Answer: a=3.20 m s⁻²

4Connected particles and pulleys

  • Connected by a light inextensible string: the tension is the same on both sides of a smooth pulley, and both particles have the same magnitude of acceleration.
  • Write F=ma for each particle separately, then solve simultaneously. Alternatively, treat the whole system as one body, but only if it moves in a straight line.
Worked example 3: Pulley system

Masses of 5 kg and 3 kg hang either side of a smooth pulley. Find the acceleration and the tension.

  1. 5 kg particle: 5g-T=5a. 3 kg particle: T-3g=3a.
  2. Adding: 2g=8a, so a=\frac g4=2.45 m s⁻².
  3. T=3g+3a=29.4+7.35.

Answer: a=2.45 m s⁻² and T=36.75 N (36.8 N)

Worked example 4: Towing a trailer

A 1200 kg car tows a 400 kg trailer with a light rigid towbar. The driving force is 2400 N, and the resistances are 300 N on the car and 100 N on the trailer. Find the acceleration and the tension in the towbar.

  1. Whole system: 2400-400=1600a, so a=1.25 m s⁻².
  2. Trailer: T-100=400\times1.25, so T=600 N.

Answer: a=1.25 m s⁻² and T=600 N

  • Force on the pulley: the two tensions combine to give a resultant force on the pulley. For vertical strings it is 2T.
Common mistakes
  • Writing R=mg on a slope, or when another force has a vertical component.
  • Using F=\mu R when the object is not moving and not on the point of moving.
  • Treating a pulley system as one body without thinking about which way each force acts.
Exam tips
  • Draw a large, clear force diagram for each particle, with the direction of the acceleration marked by a double arrow.
Summary
  • Equilibrium means zero resultant force. \mathbf F=m\mathbf a, including vector form.
  • On slopes, resolve parallel and perpendicular to the slope.
  • F\le\mu R, with equality when limiting or moving.
  • Connected particles: same tension and same acceleration; write F = ma for each.
k-force.spec: Edexcel 9MA0 Mechanics topic 8: 8.1 Newton's first law and equilibrium; 8.2 Newton's second law, including vector forms and resolving; 8.3 weight; 8.4 Newton's third law, connected particles, pulleys; 8.5 friction F ≤ μR
k-force.intro: Newton's laws link forces to motion. This topic covers force diagrams, F = ma (with vectors and on slopes), connected particles and pulleys, and friction.

k-mom.h:
1Moments

Key equations
\text{moment}=F\times d_\perp
  • d_\perp is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. Moments are measured in N m, and their sense is clockwise or anticlockwise.
  • For a force at an angle, use either F\sin\theta\times d or F\times d\sin\theta.

2Equilibrium of a rigid body

  • Resultant force = 0 (resolve in two directions) and resultant moment = 0 about any point.
  • A uniform rod has its weight acting at its midpoint. A non-uniform rod has its centre of mass at an unknown point, which you may need to find.
  • Take moments about a point where an unknown force acts, so that force is eliminated.
Worked example 1: Beam on two supports

A uniform 6 m plank of mass 20 kg rests on supports at A (0 m) and B (5 m). A 50 kg child stands 4 m from A. Find the reactions.

  1. Moments about A: R_B\times5=20g\times3+50g\times4=260g, so R_B=52g=509.6 N.
  2. Vertically: R_A+R_B=70g, so R_A=18g=176.4 N.

Answer: R_A=176 N and R_B=510 N

3Tilting

  • When a rod is on the point of tilting about a support, the reaction at the other support is zero.
Worked example 2: On the point of tilting

In the plank example, how far beyond B can the child stand before the plank tilts?

  1. On the point of tilting about B, R_A=0.
  2. Moments about B: the plank's weight acts 2 m to the left of B, so 20g\times2=50g\times x.

Answer: x=0.8 m beyond B, which is 5.8 m from A.

Worked example 3: Non-uniform rod

A non-uniform 4 m rod of weight 60 N is suspended horizontally by two vertical strings at its ends. The tensions are 25 N and 35 N. Find the position of its centre of mass.

  1. Moments about the 25 N end: 35\times4=60x.

Answer: x=2.33 m from the end with the 25 N tension.

Rods held by strings at an angle

  • If a rod is held by a string at an angle, resolve the tension into horizontal and vertical components. Only the component perpendicular to the rod produces a moment about a point on the rod.
  • A hinge (or pivot) exerts a reaction with both horizontal and vertical components, X and Y. Take moments about the hinge to eliminate both of them at once.

4Ladders and rods with friction (A level)

  • A ladder leaning against a smooth wall on rough ground has: weight at its centre, a normal reaction from the ground R, friction at the ground F (towards the wall), and a normal reaction from the wall S (perpendicular to the wall).
  • Resolve horizontally (F=S) and vertically (R=W), then take moments about the foot of the ladder.
Worked example 4: Ladder

A uniform 4 m ladder of weight W rests against a smooth wall at 60° to the ground. Find the least coefficient of friction needed for equilibrium.

  1. Moments about the foot: S\times4\sin60°=W\times2\cos60°, so S=\frac{W}{2\tan60°}=0.289W.
  2. F=S and R=W, so we need \mu\ge\frac FR=0.289.

Answer: \mu_{\min}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt3}\approx0.289

Common mistakes
  • Using the distance along the rod instead of the perpendicular distance when a force is at an angle.
  • Forgetting the weight of the rod.
  • Giving friction at the wall when the wall is described as smooth.
Exam tips
  • Taking moments about a point where two unknown forces meet removes both of them in one step.
Summary
  • Moment = F\times d_\perp.
  • Equilibrium: no resultant force and no resultant moment.
  • Uniform rods have their weight at the midpoint; on the point of tilting, the other reaction is 0.
  • Ladders: resolve both ways and take moments; friction is limited by F\le\mu R.
k-mom.spec: Edexcel 9MA0 Mechanics topic 9: 9.1 moments; equilibrium of rigid bodies, including rods on supports, tilting, ladders and non-uniform rods
k-mom.intro: A moment measures the turning effect of a force. Taking moments lets us solve problems with beams, rods, see-saws and ladders. In equilibrium, both the forces and the moments must balance.

p-1.h:
1Planning

  • Independent variable: the variable you change. Dependent variable: the variable you measure. Control variables: the variables you keep constant so the test is fair.
  • Choose apparatus with a suitable range and resolution. For example, use a micrometer (0.01 mm) for wire diameter, but a metre rule (1 mm) for length.
  • Include a risk assessment: identify the hazard, the risk and a control measure. Examples are goggles when wires under tension might snap, and a protective resistor to limit current.
  • Decide how many readings to take (at least 5–6 values across the range), plus repeats, and how you will analyse them (usually with a straight-line graph).

2Implementing

  • Record raw data in a table with quantity / unit headings, using a consistent number of decimal places that matches the instrument's resolution.
  • Use appropriate techniques. For example, take readings at eye level to avoid parallax, check for zero errors, use fiducial markers, and time many oscillations instead of one.

3Analysing data

Key definitions

Accuracy: how close a measurement is to the true value.

Precision: how close repeated measurements are to each other (small spread).

Random error: unpredictable scatter about the mean. It is reduced by repeating and averaging.

Systematic error: a consistent shift in every reading, such as a zero error. Repeating does not reduce it.

Uncertainty: the interval within which the true value is expected to lie, e.g. 2.40 ± 0.05 V.

Key equations
\text{absolute uncertainty of a mean}\approx\tfrac12(\text{max}-\text{min})
\%\text{ uncertainty}=\frac{\text{absolute uncertainty}}{\text{value}}\times100\%

Combining uncertainties:

  • When adding or subtracting quantities, add the absolute uncertainties.
  • When multiplying or dividing, add the percentage uncertainties.
  • When raising to a power n, **multiply the percentage uncertainty by n**.
Worked example 1: Combining uncertainties

A wire has diameter d = 0.50 ± 0.01 mm. Find the percentage uncertainty in its cross-sectional area, A=\pi d^2/4.

  1. The percentage uncertainty in d is 0.01/0.50 × 100 = 2%.
  2. A depends on d², so double it: 2 × 2% = 4%.

Answer: 4%. π and 4 are exact, so they add no uncertainty.

4Graphs, gradients and error bars

  • Plot the independent variable on the x-axis. Choose scales that make the points fill more than half the grid, and label the axes with their units.
  • Draw error bars for each point. The best-fit line passes through as many error bars as possible. The worst-fit line is the steepest or shallowest line that still goes through all the error bars.
Key equations
\%\text{ uncertainty in gradient}=\frac{|\,m_\text{best}-m_\text{worst}\,|}{m_\text{best}}\times100\%
  • Linearise relationships by comparing them with y=mx+c. For example, plot T^2 against l for a pendulum. For power laws y=kx^n, plot \lg y against \lg x: the gradient is n and the intercept is \lg k.
Worked example 2: Gradient uncertainty

The best-fit gradient is 4.8 N m⁻¹ and the worst-fit gradient is 5.3 N m⁻¹. Give the result with its uncertainty.

  1. The absolute uncertainty is |5.3 − 4.8| = 0.5 N m⁻¹.
  2. The percentage uncertainty is 0.5/4.8 × 100 ≈ 10%.

Answer: k = 4.8 ± 0.5 N m⁻¹ (10%).

5Evaluating

  • Compare your result with the accepted value: percentage difference = |experimental − accepted| ÷ accepted × 100%. If the difference is smaller than the percentage uncertainty, the result agrees with the accepted value within experimental error.
  • Identify the largest source of uncertainty and suggest a specific improvement. For example, use a longer length of wire, use light gates instead of a stopwatch, or use a data logger.
The twelve PAGs (Practical Activity Groups)
  • 1 motion (e.g. finding g); 2 materials (the Young modulus); 3 electrical properties (I–V characteristics, resistivity); 4 circuits (internal resistance, potential dividers); 5 waves (diffraction gratings, stationary waves, the speed of sound); 6 quantum effects (the Planck constant using LEDs); 7 ideal gases (Boyle's law, absolute zero); 8 thermal properties (specific heat capacity, specific latent heat); 9 capacitors (charging and discharging); 10 SHM (pendulums, mass–spring systems); 11 nuclear decay (half-life models); 12 research skills.
Common mistakes
  • Saying that repeating readings reduces a systematic error. It does not; only a correction or recalibration does.
  • Giving a final answer with too many significant figures. Match the data, usually to 2 or 3 s.f.
  • Forcing a line through the origin when the data do not support it.
Exam tips
  • "Precise" and "accurate" are not interchangeable. Use them exactly as defined above.
  • When asked for an improvement, name the apparatus and explain how it reduces the uncertainty.
Summary
  • Plan with clear variables, suitable apparatus and a risk assessment.
  • Uncertainties: add absolute values for sums and differences, add percentages for products and quotients, and multiply by n for powers.
  • Error bars and worst-fit lines give the uncertainty in a gradient.
  • Evaluate by comparing with accepted values and suggesting specific improvements.
p-1.spec: OCR H556 Module 1 (1.1.1–1.1.4, 1.2.1–1.2.2) and the Practical Endorsement (PAG 1–12)
p-1.intro: Module 1 is assessed through every written paper and the Practical Endorsement. It covers planning experiments, carrying them out safely, analysing data with uncertainties, and evaluating your conclusions.

p-2-1.h:
1Physical quantities

  • A physical quantity has a numerical value and a unit, for example 9.81 m s⁻².
  • You should be able to estimate physical quantities to an order of magnitude. A typical person is about 70 kg, a car travels at about 30 m s⁻¹ on a motorway, a mains supply is 230 V, and the wavelength of visible light is about 500 nm.
Worked example 1: Estimating a quantity

Estimate the kinetic energy of a sprinter in a 100 m race.

  1. Assume a mass of about 70 kg and a top speed of about 10 m s⁻¹.
  2. E = ½mv² = ½ × 70 × 10² = 3500 J.

Answer: About 4 × 10³ J (an order of magnitude of 10³ J).

2S.I. base units

QuantityBase unitSymbol
masskilogramkg
lengthmetrem
timeseconds
currentampereA
temperaturekelvinK
amount of substancemolemol
  • All other units are derived units, built from base units. For example, 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻², 1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻², 1 W = 1 kg m² s⁻³, 1 C = 1 A s, and 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹ = 1 kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹.
Worked example 2: Finding base units

Express the ohm (Ω) in S.I. base units.

  1. R=V/I, and V has base units kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹.
  2. Divide by A.

Answer: 1 Ω = 1 kg m² s⁻³ A⁻².

3Homogeneity of equations

  • In a physically correct equation, every term has the same base units. This is called homogeneity. Checking it can show that an equation is wrong, but it cannot prove an equation right, because dimensionless constants (such as ½) cannot be checked.
Worked example 3: Checking an equation

Show that s=ut+\tfrac12at^2 is homogeneous.

  1. s has units of m.
  2. ut has units of m s⁻¹ × s = m.
  3. at² has units of m s⁻² × s² = m.

Answer: Every term has units of m, so the equation is homogeneous.

4Prefixes

PrefixSymbolFactor
picop10⁻¹²
nanon10⁻⁹
microμ10⁻⁶
millim10⁻³
centic10⁻²
kilok10³
megaM10⁶
gigaG10⁹
teraT10¹²
Worked example 4: Converting units

Convert a density of 2.7 g cm⁻³ to kg m⁻³.

  1. 1 g = 10⁻³ kg, and 1 cm³ = (10⁻² m)³ = 10⁻⁶ m³.
  2. 2.7 × 10⁻³ / 10⁻⁶ = 2.7 × 10³.

Answer: 2700 kg m⁻³.

Common mistakes
  • Converting area or volume units with the linear factor. For example, 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², not 10⁻² m².
  • Treating the joule or the newton as base units. They are derived.
  • Confusing m (milli) with M (mega).
Exam tips
  • Write the quantity in standard form with the unit before calculating, to avoid prefix slips.
  • In estimates, show one significant figure and state your assumptions.
Summary
  • The six base units are kg, m, s, A, K and mol; all others are derived.
  • A homogeneous equation has the same base units in every term.
  • Learn the prefixes from pico to tera, and square or cube them for area and volume.
p-2-1.spec: OCR H556 2.1.1 Physical quantities; 2.1.2 S.I. units
p-2-1.intro: Every measurement in physics is a number with a unit. This topic covers the base S.I. units, how other units are built from them, prefixes, and checking equations for homogeneity.

p-2-2.h:
1Errors and uncertainties

Key definitions

Systematic error: a consistent shift in every reading in the same direction, caused for example by a zero error or a miscalibrated instrument. It affects accuracy.

Random error: unpredictable variation between readings. It affects precision and is reduced by repeating and averaging.

Precision: how close repeated readings are to each other.

Accuracy: how close a reading or result is to the true value.

Absolute uncertainty: the ± range of a value, e.g. 12.3 ± 0.2 cm.

Fractional uncertainty: absolute uncertainty ÷ value. Multiply it by 100% to get the percentage uncertainty.

  • The uncertainty of a single reading is often taken as half the resolution of an analogue scale, or ±1 in the last digit of a digital meter.
  • For repeated readings, uncertainty ≈ ½ × range. Leave out anomalous readings before averaging.

2Combining uncertainties

OperationRule
y=a\pm badd the absolute uncertainties: Δy = Δa + Δb
y=ab or a/badd the percentage uncertainties
y=a^npercentage uncertainty in y = n × percentage uncertainty in a
Worked example 1: Density uncertainty

A cube has side 2.00 ± 0.02 cm and mass 64.0 ± 0.5 g. Find its density and the percentage uncertainty.

  1. V = 2.00³ = 8.00 cm³, so ρ = 64.0/8.00 = 8.00 g cm⁻³.
  2. Percentage uncertainty in the side: 0.02/2.00 = 1%. Volume depends on side³, so its uncertainty is 3%.
  3. Percentage uncertainty in mass: 0.5/64.0 = 0.8%.
  4. Total: 3% + 0.8% ≈ 3.8%, which is ±0.3 g cm⁻³.

Answer: ρ = 8.0 ± 0.3 g cm⁻³ (3.8%).

Worked example 2: Difference of two readings

Two thermometer readings are 21.5 ± 0.5 °C and 35.0 ± 0.5 °C. Give the temperature rise and its percentage uncertainty.

  1. Rise = 35.0 − 21.5 = 13.5 °C.
  2. For a difference, add the absolute uncertainties: ±1.0 °C.
  3. Percentage uncertainty = 1.0/13.5 × 100 = 7.4%.

Answer: 13.5 ± 1.0 °C (7.4%). Small differences have large percentage uncertainties.

3Graphs

  • Straight-line graphs: compare with y=mx+c. The gradient gives one quantity and the y-intercept another.
  • For an exponential relationship y=Ae^{kx}, plot ln y against x: the gradient is k and the intercept is ln A.
  • For a power law y=kx^n, plot log y against log x: the gradient is n and the intercept is log k.
  • The area under a graph can be meaningful. For example, the area under a velocity–time graph is displacement, and the area under a force–extension graph is work done.
  • Error bars show the uncertainty of each point. The worst acceptable line passes through all the error bars, and the uncertainty in the gradient = |best gradient − worst gradient|.
Worked example 3: Linearising data

The period of a pendulum is T=2\pi\sqrt{l/g}. Which graph gives a straight line, and how do you find g?

  1. Square both sides: T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{g}l.
  2. Plot T² on the y-axis against l on the x-axis. This gives a straight line through the origin.

Answer: The gradient is 4π²/g, so g = 4π² ÷ gradient.

Common mistakes
  • Adding absolute uncertainties when multiplying. For products and quotients, add the percentages.
  • Quoting an uncertainty to more than 1–2 significant figures, or a value to more decimal places than its uncertainty.
  • Including an anomalous point in the best-fit line.
Exam tips
  • Write uncertainties to 1 s.f. (or 2 s.f. if the first digit is 1), and round the value to the same decimal place.
Summary
  • Systematic errors affect accuracy; random errors affect precision.
  • For sums and differences add absolute uncertainties; for products and quotients add percentages; for a power n, multiply the percentage by n.
  • Linearise graphs to find constants; gradient uncertainty comes from best and worst lines.
p-2-2.spec: OCR H556 2.2.1 Measurements and uncertainties; 2.2.2 Graphs
p-2-2.intro: Every measurement has an uncertainty. This topic is about expressing uncertainty, combining uncertainties through calculations, and using graphs to find gradients and intercepts with their uncertainties.

p-2-3.h:
1Scalars and vectors

Key definitions

Scalar: a quantity with magnitude only, e.g. mass, distance, speed, time, energy, temperature.

Vector: a quantity with magnitude and direction, e.g. displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum.

2Adding vectors

  • Triangle of vectors: draw the vectors tip to tail. The resultant goes from the start of the first vector to the end of the last.
  • For two perpendicular vectors, use Pythagoras to find the magnitude and trigonometry to find the angle.
R=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}
\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)
  • For non-perpendicular vectors, draw an accurate scale diagram, or use the cosine rule.
Worked example 1: Perpendicular forces

Forces of 6.0 N east and 8.0 N north act on a body. Find the resultant.

  1. R = √(6.0² + 8.0²) = √100 = 10 N.
  2. θ = tan⁻¹(8.0/6.0) = 53° north of east.

Answer: 10 N at 53° north of east (a bearing of 037°).

3Non-perpendicular vectors and vector subtraction

  • For two vectors at angle θ to each other, the cosine rule gives the magnitude of the resultant directly.
  • To subtract a vector, add its negative: Δv = v − u = v + (−u). Reverse the arrow for u, then add tip to tail.
Worked example 2: Cosine rule

A plane flies at 200 m s⁻¹ due north. A wind of 50 m s⁻¹ blows towards the north-east. Find the resultant speed.

  1. The angle between the two vectors is 45°, so the angle inside the vector triangle is 180° − 45° = 135°.
  2. R² = 200² + 50² − 2(200)(50) cos 135° = 40000 + 2500 + 14142 = 56642.

Answer: R ≈ 238 m s⁻¹.

Worked example 3: Change in velocity

A ball hits a wall at 8.0 m s⁻¹ and rebounds along the same line at 6.0 m s⁻¹. Find the change in velocity.

  1. Take towards the wall as positive. Then u = +8.0 m s⁻¹ and v = −6.0 m s⁻¹.
  2. Δv = v − u = −6.0 − 8.0 = −14 m s⁻¹.

Answer: 14 m s⁻¹ directed away from the wall. The change in speed is only 2 m s⁻¹, but the change in velocity is 14 m s⁻¹.

4Resolving vectors

  • Any vector F can be split into two perpendicular components: F cos θ along the direction at angle θ to F, and F sin θ perpendicular to it.
  • On a slope at angle θ, the weight resolves into mg sin θ down the slope and mg cos θ perpendicular to the slope.
Key equations
F_x=F\cos\theta
F_y=F\sin\theta
Worked example 4: Resolving on a slope

A 5.0 kg block rests on a frictionless 30° slope. Find the components of its weight (g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹).

  1. W = 5.0 × 9.81 = 49.1 N.
  2. Down the slope: 49.1 sin 30° = 24.5 N.
  3. Perpendicular to the slope: 49.1 cos 30° = 42.5 N, balanced by the normal contact force.

Answer: 24.5 N down the slope and 42.5 N into the slope.

5Equilibrium and closed triangles

  • If three coplanar forces keep a body in equilibrium, the vectors drawn tip to tail form a closed triangle, because the resultant is zero.
  • Alternatively, resolve the forces in two perpendicular directions and set each sum to zero.
Worked example 5: Hanging sign

A 20 N sign hangs from two cords, each at 30° to the horizontal. Find the tension in each cord.

  1. By symmetry, both tensions are equal, T.
  2. Vertically: 2T sin 30° = 20, so T = 20 N.

Answer: Each tension is 20 N.

Common mistakes
  • Adding vector magnitudes directly, e.g. claiming 6 N + 8 N = 14 N whatever the directions.
  • Swapping sin and cos. The component adjacent to the angle uses cos.
  • Giving a vector answer without a direction.
Exam tips
  • Always draw a sketch with the angle marked before resolving.
Summary
  • Scalars have magnitude only; vectors have magnitude and direction.
  • Add vectors tip to tail, using Pythagoras or a scale drawing.
  • Resolve into components F cos θ and F sin θ.
  • In equilibrium the forces form a closed triangle.
p-2-3.intro: Some quantities have only a size; others also have a direction. Handling directions properly, by adding and resolving vectors, underlies all of mechanics.

p-3-1.h:
1Key quantities

Key definitions

Displacement (s): distance moved in a given direction (a vector, in m).

Velocity (v): rate of change of displacement, v=\Delta s/\Delta t (a vector, in m s⁻¹).

Speed: rate of change of distance (a scalar). Instantaneous speed is the speed at a particular instant; average speed = total distance ÷ total time.

Acceleration (a): rate of change of velocity, a=\Delta v/\Delta t (in m s⁻²).

2Motion graphs

GraphGradientArea under the graph
displacement–timevelocity—
velocity–timeaccelerationdisplacement
acceleration–time—change in velocity
  • For a curved displacement–time graph, draw a tangent to find the instantaneous velocity.

3The suvat equations (constant acceleration only)

Key equations
v=u+at
s=\tfrac12(u+v)t
s=ut+\tfrac12at^2
v^2=u^2+2as
Worked example 1: Braking car

A car travelling at 25 m s⁻¹ brakes uniformly to rest in 50 m. Find the deceleration and the braking time.

  1. v² = u² + 2as gives 0 = 625 + 2a(50), so a = −6.25 m s⁻².
  2. v = u + at gives 0 = 25 − 6.25t, so t = 4.0 s.

Answer: The deceleration is 6.25 m s⁻² and the time is 4.0 s.

4Free fall and determining g

  • In free fall near the Earth's surface with no air resistance, the acceleration is g = 9.81 m s⁻², the same for all masses.
PAG 1: determining g
  • Drop a ball through a measured height h, using light gates or an electromagnet with a timer, or record it with a video camera and frame-by-frame analysis.
  • Since h=\tfrac12gt^2, plot h against t²: the gradient is g/2.
  • Alternatively, use two light gates and v^2=u^2+2gh.
  • Reduce uncertainty by using larger heights, repeating each drop, and using a dense, small ball to reduce drag.

5Stopping distances

  • Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.
  • Thinking distance = speed × reaction time. It is increased by tiredness, alcohol, drugs and distractions.
  • Braking distance is proportional to v², from v² = 2as. It is increased by wet or icy roads, worn tyres or brakes, and greater mass.
Worked example 2: Stopping distance

A driver with a reaction time of 0.70 s is travelling at 20 m s⁻¹. The car decelerates at 5.0 m s⁻². Find the stopping distance.

  1. Thinking distance = 20 × 0.70 = 14 m.
  2. Braking distance = v²/2a = 400/10 = 40 m.

Answer: Stopping distance = 54 m.

6Projectile motion

  • The horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Horizontally there is no force (ignoring air resistance), so the velocity is constant. Vertically, the acceleration is g downwards.
  • Resolve the launch velocity: u_x=u\cos\theta and u_y=u\sin\theta. The time of flight comes from the vertical motion.
Worked example 3: Horizontal launch

A ball rolls off a 1.25 m high table at 3.0 m s⁻¹. How far from the table does it land?

  1. Vertically: 1.25 = ½ × 9.81 × t², so t = 0.505 s.
  2. Horizontally: x = 3.0 × 0.505 = 1.5 m.

Answer: About 1.5 m from the table.

Common mistakes
  • Using the suvat equations when the acceleration is not constant.
  • Giving vertical acceleration the same sign as upward velocity. Choose a positive direction and stick to it.
  • Thinking a projectile's horizontal speed decreases (when air resistance is ignored).
Exam tips
  • List s, u, v, a and t, mark the unknown, and choose the equation that leaves out the quantity you don't need.
Summary
  • On a velocity–time graph, the gradient is acceleration and the area is displacement.
  • The suvat equations apply only to constant acceleration; g = 9.81 m s⁻².
  • Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance; braking distance ∝ v².
  • In projectiles, horizontal velocity is constant and vertical acceleration is g.
p-3-1.spec: OCR H556 3.1.1 Kinematics; 3.1.2 Linear motion; 3.1.3 Projectile motion (PAG 1)
p-3-1.intro: Kinematics describes how things move: displacement, velocity and acceleration. It does not ask why they move. This topic covers motion graphs, the suvat equations, experiments to find g, stopping distances and projectiles.

p-3-2.h:
1Net force and weight

  • Newton's second law (simple form): F=ma, where F is the net force. 1 N is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻².
  • Weight, W=mg, is the gravitational force on a mass.
  • Other forces you need to know: tension, normal contact force, upthrust, friction and drag.
  • A free-body diagram shows all the forces acting on one object, drawn as labelled arrows from the object.

2Drag and terminal velocity

  • Drag increases with speed. It also depends on the cross-sectional area, the shape and the density of the fluid.
  • When an object falls, initially only weight acts, so a = g. As its speed increases, drag increases, the net force decreases, and the acceleration decreases.
  • When drag = weight, the net force is zero and the object falls at terminal velocity.
Worked example 1: Skydiver

A 75 kg skydiver experiences 450 N of drag. Find her acceleration.

  1. Net force = mg − D = 75 × 9.81 − 450 = 736 − 450 = 286 N.
  2. a = F/m = 286/75 = 3.8 m s⁻².

Answer: 3.8 m s⁻² downwards. She reaches terminal velocity when drag is 736 N.

3Moments, couples and equilibrium

Key definitions

Moment of a force: force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force (in N m).

Couple: a pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces that produces rotation only. Torque of a couple = one force × the perpendicular distance between the forces.

Principle of moments: for a body in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point = the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point.

Centre of gravity: the point at which the whole weight of the body may be taken to act.

  • For equilibrium, the resultant force is zero and the resultant moment is zero.
Worked example 2: Seesaw

A 1.0 m uniform beam weighing 20 N is pivoted at its centre. A 30 N load hangs 0.20 m to the left of the pivot. Where must a 15 N weight hang to balance it?

  1. The beam's own weight acts at the pivot, so it has no moment.
  2. 30 × 0.20 = 15 × d, so d = 0.40 m.

Answer: 0.40 m to the right of the pivot.

4Density and pressure

Key equations
\rho=\frac{m}{V}
p=\frac{F}{A}
p=h\rho g
  • The pressure in a fluid increases with depth: \Delta p=h\rho g.
  • Upthrust arises because the pressure at the bottom of an object is greater than the pressure at the top.
  • Archimedes' principle: upthrust = the weight of fluid displaced.
Worked example 3: Upthrust

A 0.0020 m³ block is fully submerged in water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³). Find the upthrust.

  1. Mass of water displaced = 1000 × 0.0020 = 2.0 kg.
  2. Upthrust = 2.0 × 9.81 = 19.6 N.

Answer: About 20 N.

Common mistakes
  • Measuring the distance for a moment along the beam when the force is at an angle. The distance must be perpendicular to the line of action.
  • Forgetting the weight of the beam itself when it is not pivoted at its centre.
  • Saying that drag decreases as speed increases.
Exam tips
  • Take moments about the point where an unknown force acts. That force then has no moment and drops out of the equation.
Summary
  • F = ma for the net force; W = mg.
  • Terminal velocity is reached when drag = weight.
  • Moment = F × perpendicular distance. In equilibrium, the net force and net moment are both zero.
  • p = F/A, p = hρg, and upthrust = weight of fluid displaced.
p-3-2.spec: OCR H556 3.2.1 Dynamics; 3.2.2 Motion with non-uniform acceleration; 3.2.3 Equilibrium; 3.2.4 Density and pressure
p-3-2.intro: Forces change motion. This topic covers net force, drag and terminal velocity, moments and equilibrium, and pressure in fluids, including upthrust.

p-3-3.h:
1Work done

Key definitions

Work done: force × distance moved in the direction of the force. 1 J is the work done when a force of 1 N moves its point of application 1 m in the direction of the force.

W=Fx\cos\theta
Worked example 1: Pulling a sledge

A rope pulls a sledge 20 m with a force of 50 N at 30° above the horizontal. Find the work done.

  1. Only the horizontal component does work: 50 cos 30° = 43.3 N.
  2. W = 43.3 × 20 = 866 J.

Answer: About 870 J.

2Conservation of energy

  • The principle of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one form to another. The total energy of a closed system stays constant.
  • Energy stores include kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical and nuclear.

3Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

Key equations
E_k=\tfrac12mv^2
E_p=mgh
  • Derivation of E_k. A force F accelerates a mass m from rest over a distance x. Then W = Fx = ma·x, and v² = 2ax gives ax = v²/2. So W = ½mv².
  • Derivation of E_p. Lifting mass m at a steady speed through height h needs a force mg, so the work done is mgh.
  • For a falling object with no air resistance: mgh = ½mv², so v=\sqrt{2gh}, which is independent of the mass.
Worked example 2: Roller coaster

A cart starts from rest 20 m above the lowest point of a track. Find its speed at the bottom (ignore friction).

  1. mgh = ½mv², and the mass cancels.
  2. v = √(2 × 9.81 × 20) = √392.4 = 19.8 m s⁻¹.

Answer: About 20 m s⁻¹.

Worked example 3: Energy lost to friction

A 2.0 kg box slides down a 3.0 m high slope and reaches the bottom at 6.0 m s⁻¹. How much energy is transferred to thermal energy?

  1. Loss of E_p = 2.0 × 9.81 × 3.0 = 58.9 J.
  2. Gain of E_k = ½ × 2.0 × 6.0² = 36 J.

Answer: 58.9 − 36 = 22.9 J is transferred to thermal energy by friction.

4Work done against resistive forces

  • When an object moves at constant velocity, the driving force does work against friction or drag at the same rate. The energy goes into thermal energy, so the kinetic energy does not change.
  • Work done by a variable force = the area under its force–displacement graph.

5Power and efficiency

Key definitions

Power: the rate of doing work (or of transferring energy), P=W/t. 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.

Efficiency: useful output energy ÷ total input energy × 100%.

  • For a force moving at a constant velocity: P=Fv, because P = Fx/t = Fv.
Worked example 4: Car power

A car moves at a steady 30 m s⁻¹ against a total resistive force of 600 N. Its engine is 25% efficient. Find the input power.

  1. Useful power = Fv = 600 × 30 = 18 kW.
  2. Input power = 18 / 0.25 = 72 kW.

Answer: 72 kW.

Common mistakes
  • Using W = Fx when the force is at an angle to the motion. Include cos θ.
  • Using a vertical distance when the motion is along a slope (or the other way round). For E_p, h is always the vertical height.
  • Giving an efficiency greater than 100%.
Exam tips
  • In energy questions, state "loss of E_p = gain of E_k (+ work done against friction)" before substituting.
Summary
  • W = Fx cos θ; energy is conserved.
  • E_k = ½mv² and E_p = mgh; both can be derived from W = Fx.
  • P = W/t = Fv; efficiency = useful output ÷ total input.
p-3-3.spec: OCR H556 3.3.1 Work and conservation of energy; 3.3.2 Kinetic and potential energies; 3.3.3 Power
p-3-3.intro: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred. Work is how a force transfers energy, and power is how quickly the transfer happens.

p-3-4.h:
1Springs and Hooke's law

Key definitions

Hooke's law: the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded: F=kx.

Force constant (k): the force per unit extension (in N m⁻¹). A stiffer spring has a larger k.

Elastic deformation: the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed.

Plastic deformation: permanent deformation, which remains after the force is removed.

  • Springs in series: 1/k=1/k_1+1/k_2, so the combination is less stiff. Springs in parallel: k=k_1+k_2.

2Elastic potential energy

  • The work done in stretching = the area under the force–extension graph. In the Hooke's law region:
E=\tfrac12Fx=\tfrac12kx^2
  • During loading and unloading, if the unloading curve is different (as for rubber), the area between the curves is the energy transferred to thermal energy.
Worked example 1: Spring energy

A spring with k = 200 N m⁻¹ is stretched by 0.15 m. Find the energy stored.

  1. E = ½kx² = ½ × 200 × 0.15².
  2. E = 100 × 0.0225 = 2.25 J.

Answer: 2.25 J

Worked example 2: Springs in series and parallel

Two springs, each with k = 100 N m⁻¹, are joined (a) in series and (b) in parallel. Find the combined force constant in each case.

  1. Series: 1/k = 1/100 + 1/100, so k = 50 N m⁻¹.
  2. Parallel: k = 100 + 100 = 200 N m⁻¹.

Answer: (a) 50 N m⁻¹ (b) 200 N m⁻¹

3Stress, strain and the Young modulus

Key equations
\text{stress }\sigma=\frac{F}{A}\ (\text{Pa})
\text{strain }\varepsilon=\frac{x}{L}\ (\text{no units})
E=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}
  • Ultimate tensile strength (UTS): the maximum stress a material can withstand before breaking.
Material typeBehaviourExample
ductilelarge plastic region; can be drawn into wirescopper
brittlebreaks with little or no plastic deformationglass, cast iron
polymericlarge extension; rubber shows hysteresisrubber, polythene
Worked example 3: Young modulus

A 2.0 m steel wire of cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ m² stretches 2.0 mm under a 20 N load. Find E.

  1. σ = 20 / 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ = 2.0 × 10⁸ Pa.
  2. ε = 2.0 × 10⁻³ / 2.0 = 1.0 × 10⁻³.
  3. E = σ/ε = 2.0 × 10⁸ / 1.0 × 10⁻³ = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa.

Answer: E = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa, a typical value for steel.

PAG 2: determining the Young modulus
  • Use a long, thin wire, clamped at one end and passing over a pulley, with a marker against a fixed scale. Alternatively, use Searle's apparatus.
  • Measure the diameter with a micrometer at several points along the wire and take the mean. Then A = πd²/4.
  • Add masses in steps. Record the extension each time, then unload to check for plastic deformation.
  • Plot stress against strain. The gradient of the linear region is E.
  • Wear goggles, because the wire may snap, and keep feet clear of the masses.
Common mistakes
  • Using the diameter instead of the radius in A = πr² (or forgetting to square it).
  • Forgetting to convert mm to m before calculating strain.
  • Saying that "strain has units of m". It is a ratio, so it has no units.
Exam tips
  • The gradient of a force–extension graph is k, but the gradient of a stress–strain graph is E. Don't confuse them.
Summary
  • F = kx up to the limit of proportionality; E = ½kx² is the area under the F–x graph.
  • Stress = F/A, strain = x/L, and E = stress/strain.
  • Ductile, brittle and polymeric materials have characteristic stress–strain curves.
p-3-4.spec: OCR H556 3.4.1 Springs; 3.4.2 Mechanical properties of matter (PAG 2)
p-3-4.intro: Materials stretch when a force acts on them. This topic covers Hooke's law, elastic potential energy, and stress, strain and the Young modulus, which describe a material regardless of its size.
secs: Stress, strain and the Young modulus

p-3-5.h:
1Newton's laws

Key definitions

First law: an object stays at rest or moves with constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it.

Second law: the resultant force is equal to the rate of change of momentum: F=\Delta p/\Delta t. For constant mass, this gives F = ma.

Third law: when body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts an equal and opposite force of the same type on A.

  • Third-law pairs act on different bodies and are the same type of force. Weight and the normal contact force on a book on a table are not a third-law pair.

2Momentum and impulse

Key equations
p=mv
\text{impulse}=F\Delta t=\Delta p
  • Momentum is a vector, measured in kg m s⁻¹ (or N s).
  • Impulse is the area under a force–time graph.
  • Crumple zones, airbags and helmets increase the collision time, so for the same change in momentum the force is reduced.
Worked example 1: Impulse on a ball

A 0.15 kg ball reaches a bat at 20 m s⁻¹ and leaves at 30 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. The contact time is 5.0 ms. Find the average force.

  1. Take the outgoing direction as positive. Δp = 0.15(30 − (−20)) = 7.5 kg m s⁻¹.
  2. F = Δp/Δt = 7.5/0.0050 = 1500 N.

Answer: 1500 N, in the direction of the outgoing ball.

3Conservation of momentum

  • The principle of conservation of momentum: for a closed system, the total momentum before an interaction equals the total momentum after it.
Key definitions

Perfectly elastic collision: both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.

Inelastic collision: momentum is conserved, but some kinetic energy is transferred to other forms, such as thermal energy and sound.

  • Total energy is always conserved. It is only kinetic energy that may not be.
Worked example 2: Coupling trucks

A 2000 kg truck moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ couples with a stationary 1000 kg truck. Find their common speed and the kinetic energy lost.

  1. Momentum before = 2000 × 3.0 = 6000 kg m s⁻¹, so v = 6000 / 3000 = 2.0 m s⁻¹.
  2. E_k before = ½ × 2000 × 9 = 9000 J. E_k after = ½ × 3000 × 4 = 6000 J.

Answer: v = 2.0 m s⁻¹ and 3000 J of kinetic energy is lost. The collision is inelastic.

Worked example 3: Explosion

A 60 kg skater pushes off a 40 kg skater, starting from rest. The 60 kg skater moves at 2.0 m s⁻¹. Find the velocity of the other skater.

  1. The total momentum is zero before, so it is zero after: 60 × 2.0 + 40v = 0.
  2. v = −3.0 m s⁻¹.

Answer: 3.0 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction.

4Collisions in two dimensions

  • Conserve momentum separately in two perpendicular directions, using components. Then combine the final components with Pythagoras to find the resultant velocity.
  • Momentum before and after can also be drawn as a closed vector triangle.
  • Rockets and jets use the same idea: the momentum given to the exhaust gases backwards equals the momentum gained by the rocket forwards. The thrust is the rate of change of the gas's momentum, F = (Δm/Δt)v.
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting signs (directions) for velocities in momentum calculations.
  • Saying that momentum is lost in an inelastic collision. It is kinetic energy that is lost.
  • Picking weight and the normal contact force as a third-law pair.
Exam tips
  • Draw "before" and "after" diagrams with the masses, velocities and a positive direction marked.
Summary
  • Newton's laws: inertia; F = Δp/Δt; equal and opposite forces on different bodies.
  • Impulse = FΔt = Δp, which is the area under the F–t graph.
  • Momentum is always conserved in a closed system; kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions.
p-3-5.spec: OCR H556 3.5.1 Newton's laws of motion; 3.5.2 Collisions
p-3-5.intro: Newton's three laws explain why things move as they do. Momentum, and the impulse that changes it, are the tools for analysing collisions and explosions.

p-4-1.h:
1Charge and current

Key definitions

Electric current (I): the rate of flow of charge, I=\Delta Q/\Delta t. The unit is the ampere (A).

Coulomb (C): the charge that passes a point when a current of 1 A flows for 1 s. 1 C = 1 A s.

Elementary charge: e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Charge is quantised: any charge is a whole-number multiple of e.

  • In metals the charge carriers are electrons; in electrolytes they are ions.
  • Conventional current flows from + to −. Electrons flow the opposite way.
Worked example 1: Counting electrons

A current of 0.40 A flows for 2.0 minutes. How many electrons pass a point?

  1. Q = It = 0.40 × 120 = 48 C.
  2. N = Q/e = 48 / 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.0 × 10²⁰.

Answer: 3.0 × 10²⁰ electrons

2Kirchhoff's first law

  • Kirchhoff's first law: the sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum of the currents leaving it.
  • This is a consequence of conservation of charge: charge cannot build up at a junction.
Worked example 2: Junction

Currents of 2.0 A and 1.5 A enter a junction. One wire leaves carrying 0.5 A. Find the current in the other wire leaving.

  1. Total in = 3.5 A.
  2. Out: 0.5 + I = 3.5.

Answer: I = 3.0 A

3Mean drift velocity

Key equations
I=Anev
  • A = cross-sectional area (m²), n = number density of charge carriers (m⁻³), e = charge on each carrier, and v = mean drift velocity.
  • Electrons in a wire move randomly at high speeds, but their average drift along the wire is very slow, typically less than 1 mm s⁻¹. The signal (the electric field) travels at close to the speed of light, so a lamp lights almost instantly.
  • In a wire that gets thinner while carrying the same current, v must increase, because A is smaller.
Worked example 3: Drift velocity in copper

A copper wire (n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³) of area 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² carries 2.0 A. Find the drift velocity.

  1. v = I/(Ane).
  2. v = 2.0 / (1.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 8.5 × 10²⁸ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹).

Answer: v = 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ (0.15 mm s⁻¹)

  • Charge on ions is a multiple of e too. For example, a Cu²⁺ ion carries +2e = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

4Conductors, semiconductors and insulators

TypeNumber density nExample
conductorvery high (~10²⁸ m⁻³)copper
semiconductormuch lower (~10¹⁷–10²³ m⁻³); increases with temperaturesilicon
insulatoralmost zeroplastic
  • For the same current, a semiconductor needs a much higher drift velocity, because n is much smaller.
  • Heating a semiconductor frees more charge carriers, so n rises and the resistance falls. This is how a thermistor works.
Common mistakes
  • Thinking electrons travel round a circuit quickly. The drift velocity is tiny.
  • Forgetting to convert minutes to seconds in Q = It.
  • Using the diameter as the area in I = Anev.
Exam tips
  • Learn e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. It is in the data booklet, but you will use it constantly.
  • When comparing two wires, write I = Anev for both and cancel the quantities that are equal.
Summary
  • I = ΔQ/Δt; charge is quantised in units of e.
  • Kirchhoff's first law (charge conservation): current in = current out at a junction.
  • I = Anev. Conductors, semiconductors and insulators differ in n.
p-4-1.spec: OCR H556 4.1.1 Charge; 4.1.2 Mean drift velocity
p-4-1.intro: Electric current is the flow of charged particles. This topic links what we measure in circuits (current and charge) to the motion of electrons inside a conductor.

p-4-2.h:
1E.m.f. and potential difference

Key definitions

Potential difference (p.d.): the energy transferred from electrical energy to other forms, per unit charge: V=W/Q.

Electromotive force (e.m.f.): the energy transferred to electrical energy from other forms (for example, chemical energy in a cell), per unit charge.

Volt: 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.

Electronvolt: the energy gained by an electron accelerated through 1 V. 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

  • The energy transferred to an electron accelerated through a p.d. V is eV=\tfrac12mv^2.
Worked example 1: Accelerated electron

An electron is accelerated from rest through 500 V. Find its speed (mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg).

  1. Energy gained = eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 500 = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ J.
  2. v = √(2E/m) = √(2 × 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ / 9.11 × 10⁻³¹).

Answer: v = 1.3 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹

2Resistance and I–V characteristics

  • Resistance, R = V/I. 1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹.
  • Ohm's law: for a metallic conductor at constant temperature, the current is directly proportional to the p.d.
ComponentI–V characteristic
fixed resistorstraight line through the origin (ohmic)
filament lampa curve that flattens as I increases. The filament heats up, the ions vibrate more, collisions with electrons increase, and R rises
diode / LEDalmost no current in reverse; conducts above a threshold p.d. (about 0.6 V for silicon, more for LEDs)
NTC thermistorresistance falls as temperature rises, because n increases
LDRresistance falls as light intensity rises

3Resistivity

Key equations
R=\frac{\rho L}{A}
  • Resistivity, ρ (in Ω m), is a property of the material and depends on temperature. For metals, ρ increases with temperature. For semiconductors, ρ decreases.
PAG 3: determining resistivity
  • Measure the diameter of a wire with a micrometer at several places, and work out A.
  • Connect lengths L of wire (using crocodile clips) and measure V and I to find R. Plot R against L: the gradient is ρ/A.
  • Keep the current small, or switch off between readings, so that the wire does not heat up and change its resistance.
Worked example 2: Resistivity

A 2.0 m nichrome wire has a diameter of 0.40 mm and a resistance of 17.5 Ω. Find ρ.

  1. A = π(0.20 × 10⁻³)² = 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ m².
  2. ρ = RA/L = 17.5 × 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ / 2.0.

Answer: ρ = 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m

4Electrical power and energy

Key equations
P=VI=I^2R=\frac{V^2}{R}
W=VIt
  • The kilowatt-hour (kW h) is the energy transferred by a 1 kW device in 1 hour: 1 kW h = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
  • Cost = energy used (in kW h) × the price per kW h.
Worked example 3: Cost of a kettle

A 2.5 kW kettle runs for 4.0 minutes a day for 30 days at 28p per kW h. Find the cost.

  1. Energy = 2.5 kW × (4/60 h) × 30 = 5.0 kW h.
  2. Cost = 5.0 × 28p.

Answer: £1.40

Common mistakes
  • Mixing up e.m.f. (energy given to charges) and p.d. (energy taken from charges).
  • Using the radius as the diameter in A = πr².
  • Saying that a filament lamp's resistance rises "because current increases". It rises because the temperature increases.
Exam tips
  • Choose the power equation that uses the quantity that is the same for every component: I²R in series, V²/R in parallel.
Summary
  • V = W/Q; e.m.f. is energy transferred to electrical energy per unit charge; 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
  • Learn the I–V shapes for a resistor, lamp, diode, thermistor and LDR.
  • R = ρL/A. P = VI = I²R = V²/R, and 1 kW h = 3.6 MJ.
p-4-2.spec: OCR H556 4.2.1 Circuit symbols; 4.2.2 E.m.f. and p.d.; 4.2.3 Resistance; 4.2.4 Resistivity; 4.2.5 Power (PAG 3)
p-4-2.intro: This topic is about energy in circuits: the difference between e.m.f. and p.d., resistance and the I–V characteristics of components, resistivity, and electrical power.

p-4-3.h:
1Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law (conservation of charge): the total current into a junction equals the total current out.
  • Second law (conservation of energy): around any closed loop, the sum of the e.m.f.s equals the sum of the p.d.s.
Key equations
\text{series: } R=R_1+R_2+\dots
\text{parallel: }\frac1R=\frac1{R_1}+\frac1{R_2}+\dots
  • In series, the current is the same everywhere and the p.d.s add up. In parallel, the p.d. is the same across each branch and the currents add up.
  • A parallel combination always has a smaller resistance than its smallest branch.
Worked example 1: Combined resistance

A 4.0 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω. The supply is 12 V with no internal resistance. Find the current from the supply.

  1. Parallel pair: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so R = 2.0 Ω.
  2. Total resistance = 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 Ω.

Answer: I = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A

2Internal resistance

Key definitions

Internal resistance (r): the resistance of the source itself, which causes "lost volts" inside it.

Terminal p.d. (V): the p.d. across the terminals of the source when it delivers current.

Key equations
\varepsilon=I(R+r)
V=\varepsilon-Ir
  • As the current increases, the lost volts (Ir) increase and the terminal p.d. falls.
  • A graph of V against I is a straight line: the y-intercept is ε and the gradient is −r.
PAG 4: determining e.m.f. and internal resistance
  • Connect a cell to a variable resistor, with an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across the cell.
  • Vary R and record V and I for each setting. Then plot V against I.
  • Add a small fixed resistor in series to protect the cell, and do not leave the current flowing for long, because r changes as the cell warms up.
Worked example 2: Lost volts

A cell with ε = 1.5 V and r = 0.50 Ω drives a current of 0.60 A. Find the terminal p.d. and the external resistance.

  1. V = 1.5 − 0.60 × 0.50 = 1.2 V.
  2. R = V/I = 1.2/0.60 = 2.0 Ω.

Answer: V = 1.2 V and R = 2.0 Ω

3Potential dividers

Key equations
V_\text{out}=\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}\times V_\text{in}
\frac{V_1}{V_2}=\frac{R_1}{R_2}
  • Replace one resistor with an LDR or thermistor to make a sensing circuit. For example, with the thermistor as R₁ and V_out taken across a fixed R₂: as the temperature rises, the thermistor's resistance falls, so V_out rises.
  • A potentiometer is a variable potential divider that gives a continuously variable output, from 0 to V_in.
Worked example 3: Light sensor

A 10 kΩ fixed resistor is in series with an LDR across a 9.0 V supply. V_out is taken across the LDR. The LDR is 2.0 kΩ in bright light and 50 kΩ in the dark. Find V_out in each case.

  1. Bright: V_out = 2/(2 + 10) × 9.0 = 1.5 V.
  2. Dark: V_out = 50/(50 + 10) × 9.0 = 7.5 V.

Answer: 1.5 V in bright light and 7.5 V in the dark. V_out rises as it gets darker, which could switch on a lamp.

Common mistakes
  • Forgetting the internal resistance when finding the current from a real cell.
  • Adding parallel resistances directly.
  • Getting the output the wrong way round. Check which resistor V_out is measured across.
Exam tips
  • With several loops, write Kirchhoff's second law for each loop and solve the equations simultaneously.
Summary
  • Kirchhoff's first law conserves charge; his second law conserves energy.
  • Series: R = ΣR. Parallel: 1/R = Σ1/R.
  • ε = I(R + r). On a V–I graph, the intercept is ε and the gradient is −r.
  • Potential dividers with LDRs or thermistors make sensors.
p-4-3.spec: OCR H556 4.3.1 Series and parallel circuits; 4.3.2 Internal resistance; 4.3.3 Potential dividers (PAG 4)
p-4-3.intro: Real circuits combine resistors, sources and sensors. This topic covers Kirchhoff's laws, combining resistances, internal resistance, and potential divider circuits used with sensors.

p-4-4.h:
1Describing waves

Key definitions

Displacement: the distance of a point from its equilibrium position.

Amplitude (A): the maximum displacement.

Wavelength (λ): the minimum distance between two points oscillating in phase.

Period (T): the time for one complete oscillation; f = 1/T.

Phase difference: how far one oscillation is ahead of another, as a fraction of a cycle, measured in degrees or radians.

Intensity: power per unit area, I = P/A, in W m⁻². Intensity is proportional to amplitude²: I ∝ A².

  • Wave equation: v = fλ.
  • Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (light, waves on strings). Longitudinal waves oscillate parallel to it, with compressions and rarefactions (sound).
  • Polarisation confines the oscillations to a single plane. Only transverse waves can be polarised. Examples are Polaroid filters and the polarisation of microwaves by a metal grille.
  • Waves undergo reflection, refraction and diffraction. Diffraction is greatest when the gap is about the same size as the wavelength.
Worked example 1: Wave speed

A sound wave has a frequency of 680 Hz and a wavelength of 0.50 m. Find its speed, and the phase difference between two points 0.125 m apart along the wave.

  1. v = fλ = 680 × 0.50 = 340 m s⁻¹.
  2. 0.125 m is λ/4, so the phase difference is 90° (π/2 rad).

Answer: 340 m s⁻¹ and 90°

2Electromagnetic waves and refraction

  • All EM waves travel at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum. In order of decreasing wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible (about 400–700 nm), ultraviolet, X-rays and γ-rays.
Key equations
n=\frac{c}{v}
n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2
\sin C=\frac1n
  • Total internal reflection happens when light travels from a higher to a lower refractive index and the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle C. It is used in optical fibres.

3Superposition and interference

  • Principle of superposition: when waves meet, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements.
  • Coherent sources have a constant phase difference and the same frequency.
  • Constructive interference occurs where the path difference is nλ. Destructive interference occurs where it is (n + ½)λ.
Key equations
\lambda=\frac{ax}{D}\ \ (\text{Young's double slits})
d\sin\theta=n\lambda\ \ (\text{diffraction grating})
Worked example 2: Diffraction grating

A grating with 300 lines per mm is lit with light of wavelength 600 nm. Find the angle of the 2nd-order maximum, and the highest order visible.

  1. d = 1/300000 = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m.
  2. sin θ = 2 × 600 × 10⁻⁹ / 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.36, so θ = 21°.
  3. The maximum order is when sin θ ≤ 1: n ≤ d/λ = 5.6, so n = 5.

Answer: 21°, and the highest order is 5.

4Stationary waves

  • A stationary wave forms when two waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions superpose, for example a wave and its reflection.
  • Nodes have zero amplitude; antinodes have maximum amplitude. Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart.
  • Stationary waves store energy; they do not transfer it. All points between adjacent nodes are in phase.
SystemFundamental (1st harmonic)
string fixed at both endsL = λ/2
tube closed at one endL = λ/4; only odd harmonics occur
tube open at both endsL = λ/2
PAG 5: speed of sound using a resonance tube
  • Hold a tuning fork over a tube in water. Adjust the length of the air column until the first resonance (the loudest sound) is heard. Then L + end correction = λ/4.
  • Find the next resonance at 3λ/4. The difference in length is λ/2, so the end correction cancels. Then v = fλ.
Common mistakes
  • Saying that sound can be polarised. It is longitudinal, so it cannot.
  • Using the slit width instead of the slit separation in λ = ax/D.
  • Confusing node spacing (λ/2) with wavelength.
Exam tips
  • For a grating, convert "lines per mm" to d in metres before doing anything else.
Summary
  • v = fλ; I = P/A ∝ A²; only transverse waves can be polarised.
  • n = c/v; Snell's law; TIR when θ > C.
  • Interference: λ = ax/D and d sin θ = nλ.
  • Stationary waves have nodes λ/2 apart and harmonics set by the boundary conditions.
p-4-4.spec: OCR H556 4.4.1 Wave motion; 4.4.2 Electromagnetic waves; 4.4.3 Superposition; 4.4.4 Stationary waves (PAG 5)
p-4-4.intro: Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. This topic covers wave properties, the electromagnetic spectrum, polarisation, refraction, interference and stationary waves.

p-4-5.h:
1Photons

Key definitions

Photon: a quantum (a discrete packet) of electromagnetic energy.

Key equations
E=hf=\frac{hc}{\lambda}
h=6.63\times10^{-34}\text{ J s}
  • To convert from J to eV, divide by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹. Visible photons have energies of about 2–3 eV.
Worked example 1: Photon energy

Find the energy, in J and in eV, of a photon of wavelength 500 nm.

  1. E = hc/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸ / 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ = 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
  2. In eV: 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.49 eV.

Answer: 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or 2.49 eV

PAG 6: estimating h using LEDs
  • Each LED emits light of a known wavelength when the p.d. across it reaches the threshold p.d. V₀. At that point, the energy given to one electron, eV₀, roughly equals the photon energy hc/λ.
  • Find V₀ for several LEDs, for example by increasing V until the LED just lights (viewed through a tube to block other light), or from the I–V graph.
  • Plot V₀ against 1/λ. The gradient is hc/e, so h = gradient × e/c.

2The photoelectric effect

  • When EM radiation of a high enough frequency falls on a metal, electrons are emitted (photoelectrons). This can be shown with a charged gold-leaf electroscope: UV light makes the leaf of a negatively charged zinc plate fall.

Key observations, which the wave model cannot explain:

  1. There is a threshold frequency f₀ below which no electrons are emitted, however intense the light.
  2. Emission is instantaneous.
  3. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons depends on the frequency, not on the intensity.
  4. A higher intensity (above f₀) gives more electrons per second, but not faster ones.
  • Explanation. One photon interacts with one electron, in a one-to-one interaction. The electron needs at least the work function φ to escape the surface.
Key equations
hf=\phi+KE_\text{max}
\phi=hf_0
  • A graph of KE_max against f is a straight line with gradient h. The x-intercept is f₀, and the y-intercept is −φ.
Worked example 2: Photoelectric equation

UV light of frequency 1.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz falls on zinc (φ = 4.3 eV). Find the maximum KE of the photoelectrons.

  1. hf = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 1.5 × 10¹⁵ = 9.95 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 6.2 eV.
  2. KE_max = 6.22 − 4.3 = 1.9 eV, which is 1.92 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

Answer: 1.9 eV (3.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)

3Wave–particle duality

  • Electron diffraction: a beam of electrons passing through thin graphite forms rings on a fluorescent screen. Diffraction is a wave property, so this is evidence that particles behave as waves.
Key equations
\lambda=\frac{h}{p}=\frac{h}{mv}
(\text{de Broglie})
  • Diffraction is noticeable when λ is similar to the atomic spacing (about 10⁻¹⁰ m).
Worked example 3: de Broglie wavelength

Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at 4.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

  1. p = mv = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 4.0 × 10⁶ = 3.64 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹.
  2. λ = h/p = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / 3.64 × 10⁻²⁴.

Answer: λ = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, similar to atomic spacings, so it would diffract.

  • Energy levels of electrons in atoms, and line spectra, follow from photons. They are covered in topic 5.5, but they use the same E = hf.
Common mistakes
  • Saying that brighter light gives "faster" electrons. It gives more electrons.
  • Forgetting the eV to J conversion before using hf = φ + KE.
  • Saying that photoelectrons "absorb several photons". It is one photon per electron.
Exam tips
  • In explanations, use the key phrases: one-to-one interaction; energy is conserved; the work function is the minimum energy needed to free an electron.
Summary
  • E = hf = hc/λ; LEDs can be used to estimate h.
  • Photoelectric effect: hf = φ + KE_max; there is a threshold frequency; intensity affects only the number of electrons.
  • Electron diffraction shows that particles have wavelength λ = h/mv.
p-4-5.spec: OCR H556 4.5.1 Photons; 4.5.2 The photoelectric effect; 4.5.3 Wave–particle duality (PAG 6)
p-4-5.intro: Light sometimes behaves as particles, called photons, and particles such as electrons sometimes behave as waves. This topic covers the evidence: the photoelectric effect and electron diffraction.

p-5-1.h:
1Temperature and the kinetic model

  • Thermal equilibrium: there is no net flow of thermal energy between objects at the same temperature.
  • Absolute zero (0 K = −273 °C) is the lowest possible temperature, at which particles have minimum internal energy. T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.
  • Kinetic model: solids have particles vibrating about fixed positions; liquids have particles close together but able to move past each other; gases have particles far apart, moving fast and randomly.
  • Brownian motion (for example, smoke particles seen jiggling under a microscope) is evidence for the random motion of the much smaller, unseen air molecules colliding with them.
Key definitions

Internal energy: the sum of the randomly distributed kinetic and potential energies of the particles in a system.

  • During a change of state, the potential energy changes but the kinetic energy (and therefore the temperature) stays constant.

2Specific heat capacity and latent heat

Key equations
E=mc\Delta\theta
E=mL
  • Specific heat capacity, c: the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K (in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹).
  • Specific latent heat, L: the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature. L_f is for fusion (melting) and L_v for vaporisation.
Worked example 1: Ice to water

How much energy is needed to turn 0.20 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 20 °C? (L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)

  1. Melting: 0.20 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 66 800 J.
  2. Warming: 0.20 × 4200 × 20 = 16 800 J.

Answer: Total = 83 600 J ≈ 8.4 × 10⁴ J

PAG 8: specific heat capacity using the electrical method
  • Heat an insulated metal block with an immersion heater. Measure V, I and t, and the rise in temperature.
  • Then c = VIt / (mΔθ). Insulating the block reduces heat loss, which would otherwise make c appear too large.

3Ideal gases

Key equations
pV=nRT
pV=NkT
pV=\tfrac13Nm\overline{c^2}
  • R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
  • Boyle's law: pV = constant at constant T. Pressure is also ∝ T at constant volume.
  • Assumptions of the kinetic theory: a large number of molecules moving randomly; elastic collisions; molecular volume negligible compared with the container; no intermolecular forces except during collisions; collision time negligible.
  • Mean kinetic energy of a molecule: \tfrac12m\overline{c^2}=\tfrac32kT. The internal energy of an ideal gas is all kinetic and is proportional to T.
  • Root-mean-square speed: c_\text{rms}=\sqrt{\overline{c^2}}.
Worked example 2: Gas in a cylinder

0.50 mol of gas is held at 300 K in a 0.010 m³ container. Find the pressure, and the mean KE of a molecule.

  1. p = nRT/V = 0.50 × 8.31 × 300 / 0.010 = 1.25 × 10⁵ Pa.
  2. Mean KE = 1.5 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 = 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Answer: p = 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa (to 2 s.f.) and mean KE = 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J

PAG 7: estimating absolute zero, and Boyle's law
  • Absolute zero: heat a flask of air in a water bath and record the pressure at several temperatures. Extrapolate the p–θ line back to p = 0. The intercept is about −273 °C.
  • Boyle's law: compress a trapped column of air with a pump and read p and V. Wait between readings so that the temperature stays constant. Plot p against 1/V to get a straight line.
Common mistakes
  • Using °C in the gas equations. Always use kelvin.
  • Saying that the temperature rises during melting.
  • Confusing n (moles) with N (number of molecules).
Exam tips
  • Choose pV = nRT when you are given moles, and pV = NkT when you are given molecules.
Summary
  • Internal energy = random KE + PE of the particles; temperature is flat during changes of state.
  • E = mcΔθ and E = mL.
  • pV = nRT = NkT = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩; mean KE = (3/2)kT.
