p-5-1.intro: Thermal physics links the large-scale properties we measure (temperature, pressure, volume) to the random motion of particles. It covers heating and changes of state, and the ideal gas model.
secs: Specific heat capacity and latent heat

p-5-2.h:
1Angular measure

Key definitions

Radian: the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius. 2π rad = 360°.

Angular velocity (ω): the rate of change of angle, \omega=\Delta\theta/\Delta t=2\pi/T=2\pi f (in rad s⁻¹).

  • The linear (tangential) speed is v=\omega r.

2Centripetal acceleration and force

Key equations
a=\frac{v^2}{r}=\omega^2r
F=\frac{mv^2}{r}=m\omega^2r
  • The velocity is tangential, and the acceleration is towards the centre. The force does no work, because it is perpendicular to the motion, so the speed stays constant.
  • The centripetal force is not a new kind of force. It is the resultant of real forces: tension for a stone on a string, friction for a car on a bend, gravity for an orbiting satellite.
Worked example 1: Car on a bend

A 1200 kg car travels round a bend of radius 50 m at 15 m s⁻¹. What friction force is needed?

  1. F = mv²/r = 1200 × 225 / 50.

Answer: F = 5400 N, provided by friction between the tyres and the road, acting towards the centre.

Worked example 2: Angular velocity

A wheel turns at 600 revolutions per minute. Find ω, and the speed of a point 0.30 m from the axle.

  1. f = 600/60 = 10 Hz, so ω = 2π × 10 = 62.8 rad s⁻¹.
  2. v = ωr = 62.8 × 0.30 = 18.8 m s⁻¹.

Answer: ω = 63 rad s⁻¹ and v = 19 m s⁻¹

3Why a centripetal force is needed

  • By Newton's first law, without a resultant force an object would carry on in a straight line along the tangent. A resultant force perpendicular to the velocity keeps changing the direction but not the speed.
  • If the force is removed (for example, the string breaks), the object flies off along the tangent, not outwards along the radius.

4Vertical circles

  • At the top of a vertical circle (for a mass on a string): T + mg = mv²/r. At the bottom: T − mg = mv²/r, so the tension is greatest at the bottom.
  • The minimum speed at the top occurs when T = 0: v=\sqrt{gr}.
Worked example 3: Bucket of water

A bucket is swung in a vertical circle of radius 0.80 m. What is the minimum speed at the top so that the water stays in?

  1. At the minimum speed, gravity alone provides the centripetal force: mg = mv²/r.
  2. v = √(9.81 × 0.80) = 2.8 m s⁻¹.

Answer: 2.8 m s⁻¹

Worked example 4: Tension at the bottom

A 0.50 kg mass moves at 4.0 m s⁻¹ at the bottom of a vertical circle of radius 0.60 m. Find the tension in the string.

  1. T − mg = mv²/r, so T = 0.50 × 9.81 + 0.50 × 16 / 0.60.
  2. T = 4.9 + 13.3 = 18.2 N.

Answer: About 18 N, far more than the weight of 4.9 N.

Investigating F = mv²/r
  • Whirl a rubber bung on a string through a glass tube, with a hanging mass providing the tension. Measure the radius and time 10 revolutions.
  • Then vary the hanging mass and check that F ∝ v² at a fixed radius. Wear goggles and keep the area clear.
Common mistakes
  • Drawing a "centrifugal force" outwards on a free-body diagram. In an inertial frame there is no such force.
  • Using degrees instead of radians in ω calculations.
  • Saying that the speed changes in uniform circular motion. It is the velocity that changes.
Exam tips
  • Identify which real force provides the centripetal force before writing F = mv²/r.
Summary
  • ω = 2π/T and v = ωr.
  • a = v²/r = ω²r, directed towards the centre; F = mv²/r.
  • The centripetal force is the resultant of real forces and does no work.
p-5-2.spec: OCR H556 5.2.1 Kinematics of circular motion; 5.2.2 Centripetal force
p-5-2.intro: An object moving in a circle at a constant speed is accelerating, because its direction keeps changing. A resultant force towards the centre, the centripetal force, causes this acceleration.
secs: Why a centripetal force is needed

p-5-3.h:
1Defining SHM

Key definitions

Simple harmonic motion: oscillation in which the acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement from the equilibrium position and is directed towards that position: a=-\omega^2x.

  • The terms (amplitude, period, frequency, angular frequency ω = 2πf, and phase difference) are the same as for waves.
  • The period of SHM is independent of the amplitude. This is why a pendulum is such a good timer (for small angles).
Key equations
x=A\cos\omega t\ \ (\text{or }A\sin\omega t)
v=\pm\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2}
v_\text{max}=\omega A
  • Velocity is the gradient of the x–t graph, and it is ¼ cycle (90°) ahead of displacement. Acceleration is in antiphase with displacement.
Worked example 1: Mass on a spring

A mass oscillates with SHM, with amplitude 0.050 m and frequency 2.0 Hz. Find the maximum speed, the maximum acceleration, and the speed at x = 0.030 m.

  1. ω = 2π × 2.0 = 12.6 rad s⁻¹, so v_max = 12.6 × 0.050 = 0.63 m s⁻¹.
  2. a_max = ω²A = 158 × 0.050 = 7.9 m s⁻².
  3. v = 12.6 × √(0.050² − 0.030²) = 12.6 × 0.040 = 0.50 m s⁻¹.

Answer: 0.63 m s⁻¹, 7.9 m s⁻² and 0.50 m s⁻¹

2Energy in SHM

  • Energy is continually exchanged between kinetic and potential energy, but the total stays constant (if there is no damping).
  • The kinetic energy is maximum at x = 0. The potential energy is maximum at x = ±A.
  • Total energy is proportional to A²: E=\tfrac12m\omega^2A^2.
Worked example 2: Energy of an oscillator

A 0.20 kg mass oscillates with ω = 10 rad s⁻¹ and A = 0.040 m. Find the total energy.

  1. E = ½ × 0.20 × 100 × 0.040².

Answer: E = 0.016 J

3Damping, forced oscillations and resonance

Key definitions

Damping: a loss of energy to the surroundings (usually by friction), which reduces the amplitude.

Free oscillation: an oscillation at the natural frequency with no driving force.

Forced oscillation: an oscillation driven by a periodic external force at the driving frequency.

Resonance: a maximum amplitude, which occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency.

  • Light damping: the amplitude decays gradually, often exponentially. Critical damping: the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating (as in car suspension). Heavy damping: a slow return with no oscillation.
  • More damping lowers and broadens the resonance peak, and shifts it slightly to a lower frequency.
  • Examples of resonance: useful in musical instruments, radio tuning and microwave ovens; harmful in bridges (the Millennium Bridge) and machinery.
PAG 10: investigating SHM
  • Time 10 or more oscillations of a mass on a spring, starting the timer as the mass passes the equilibrium position, using a fiducial marker.
  • For a spring, T = 2π√(m/k), so plot T² against m to find k. For a pendulum, T = 2π√(l/g).
  • Use a motion sensor or a data logger to plot displacement–time graphs and observe damping.
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting the minus sign in a = −ω²x. It shows that the acceleration is directed towards the centre.
  • Saying that resonance happens at "any high frequency". It happens at the natural frequency.
  • Mixing up sin and cos. Use cos if timing starts at maximum displacement, and sin if it starts at equilibrium.
Exam tips
  • Write ω = 2πf first. Most SHM calculations need ω.
Summary
  • SHM: a = −ω²x; the period is independent of the amplitude.
  • x = A cos ωt; v_max = ωA; v = ±ω√(A² − x²).
  • KE and PE interchange; E ∝ A².
  • Damping types and resonance at the natural frequency.
p-5-3.spec: OCR H556 5.3.1 Simple harmonic oscillations; 5.3.2 Energy of a simple harmonic oscillator; 5.3.3 Damping (PAG 10)
p-5-3.intro: Pendulums, masses on springs and vibrating molecules all oscillate. Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is the model behind them all, and resonance explains why bridges sway and why microwave ovens heat food.

p-5-4.h:
1Gravitational fields

Key definitions

Gravitational field strength (g): the force per unit mass at a point, g=F/m (in N kg⁻¹).

Gravitational field: a region in which a mass experiences a force.

  • Field lines show the direction of the force on a mass. A spherical mass behaves as if all its mass were at its centre, giving a radial field.
  • Close to the Earth's surface, the field is approximately uniform (parallel lines), with g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

2Newton's law of gravitation

Key equations
F=-\frac{GMm}{r^2}
g=-\frac{GM}{r^2}
G=6.67\times10^{-11}\text{ N m}^2\text{ kg}^{-2}
  • The force is attractive and follows an inverse-square law: doubling r makes F one quarter as large. The minus sign shows attraction.
Worked example 1: Field strength of the Moon

Find g at the Moon's surface (M = 7.35 × 10²² kg, r = 1.74 × 10⁶ m).

  1. g = GM/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.35 × 10²² / (1.74 × 10⁶)².

Answer: g = 1.62 N kg⁻¹, about one sixth of the Earth's.

3Planetary motion and satellites

  • Kepler's laws:
  1. Planets move in ellipses, with the Sun at one focus.
  2. A line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times.
  3. T² ∝ r³.
  • For a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, which gives T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3.
  • Geostationary satellites orbit above the equator with T = 24 h, moving in the same direction as the Earth spins, at about 36 000 km above the surface. They stay above the same point, so they are useful for communications.
Worked example 2: Geostationary orbit

Find the orbital radius of a geostationary satellite (M_E = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg).

  1. r³ = GMT²/(4π²) = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ × (86 400)² / 39.5.
  2. r³ = 7.5 × 10²², so r = 4.2 × 10⁷ m.

Answer: About 4.2 × 10⁷ m from the Earth's centre.

Worked example 3: Orbital speed

Find the speed of a satellite in a circular orbit 400 km above the Earth's surface.

  1. r = 6.37 × 10⁶ + 0.40 × 10⁶ = 6.77 × 10⁶ m.
  2. v = √(GM/r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ / 6.77 × 10⁶).

Answer: v = 7.7 × 10³ m s⁻¹. Lower orbits are faster.

4Gravitational potential and energy

Key definitions

Gravitational potential (V_g): the work done per unit mass to bring a small mass from infinity to that point.

Key equations
V_g=-\frac{GM}{r}
E=mV_g=-\frac{GMm}{r}
v_\text{esc}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}
  • The potential is zero at infinity and negative everywhere else.
  • Work done moving a mass m = m ΔV_g. On a force–distance graph, the area under the curve is the work done.
  • Escape velocity is the minimum speed needed to escape from the surface to infinity: ½mv² = GMm/r.
Worked example 4: Escape velocity from the Earth

Find the Earth's escape velocity (r = 6.37 × 10⁶ m).

  1. v = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ / 6.37 × 10⁶).

Answer: v = 1.12 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ (11.2 km s⁻¹)

Common mistakes
  • Using the height above the surface instead of the distance from the centre for r.
  • Writing the potential as positive. It is always negative, rising to zero at infinity.
  • Forgetting to cube or square r in Kepler's third law.
Exam tips
  • For any orbit question, start from GMm/r² = mv²/r = mω²r.
Summary
  • g = F/m = GM/r²; F = GMm/r² (inverse square).
  • Kepler: T² ∝ r³. Geostationary orbits have T = 24 h, above the equator.
  • V_g = −GM/r; v_esc = √(2GM/r).
p-5-4.spec: OCR H556 5.4.1 Point and spherical masses; 5.4.2 Newton's law of gravitation; 5.4.3 Planetary motion; 5.4.4 Gravitational potential and energy
p-5-4.intro: Gravity holds planets, moons and satellites in orbit. This topic covers gravitational fields, Newton's inverse-square law, Kepler's laws, satellites, and gravitational potential and escape velocity.

p-5-5.h:
1Objects in the Universe

  • Planets, planetary satellites (moons), comets, solar systems, galaxies and the Universe.

2The life of a star

  • Formation: gravity pulls a nebula of gas and dust together. The gravitational potential energy becomes thermal energy, forming a protostar. When the core is hot enough, hydrogen fusion starts.
  • Main sequence: the outward radiation and gas pressure balances the inward pull of gravity.
  • A low-mass star (about 0.5–10 solar masses) becomes a red giant, then sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving a white dwarf. Electron degeneracy pressure supports a white dwarf, provided its mass is below the Chandrasekhar limit of 1.44 solar masses.
  • A massive star becomes a red supergiant, then a supernova. It leaves a neutron star or, above about 3 solar masses, a black hole.
  • The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram plots luminosity against surface temperature, with temperature increasing to the left. It shows the main sequence, red giants and supergiants (top right) and white dwarfs (bottom left).

3Energy levels and spectra

  • Electrons in atoms have discrete energy levels. Energies are negative, and 0 is the energy of a free electron.
  • When an electron moves down a level, it emits a photon with hf=\Delta E.
  • Hot dense sources give continuous spectra. Hot low-density gases give emission line spectra. Cool gas in front of a continuous source gives absorption line spectra, which have dark lines.
  • A star's absorption lines identify the elements in its atmosphere. A diffraction grating, d\sin\theta=n\lambda, measures the wavelengths of the lines.
Worked example 1: Photon from an energy-level transition

An electron moves from the −1.51 eV level to the −3.40 eV level. Find the wavelength of the emitted photon.

  1. ΔE = 1.89 eV = 1.89 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
  2. λ = hc/ΔE = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸ / 3.02 × 10⁻¹⁹.

Answer: λ = 6.58 × 10⁻⁷ m (red light, the H-alpha line).

4Luminosity and temperature

Key equations
\lambda_\text{max}T=\text{constant}=2.9\times10^{-3}\text{ m K}\ \ (\text{Wien})
L=4\pi r^2\sigma T^4\ \ (\text{Stefan})
  • Luminosity is the total power output of a star. σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
  • Hotter stars peak at shorter wavelengths, so they appear bluer.
Worked example 2: Radius of a star

A star has λ_max = 290 nm and L = 4.0 × 10²⁸ W. Find its surface temperature and radius.

  1. T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ / 2.9 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.0 × 10⁴ K.
  2. r = √(L / 4πσT⁴) = √(4.0 × 10²⁸ / (4π × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 10¹⁶)).

Answer: T = 10 000 K and r = 2.4 × 10⁹ m

5Distances and cosmology

  • Units: the astronomical unit (1 AU = 1.50 × 10¹¹ m), the light-year (9.46 × 10¹⁵ m) and the parsec (3.1 × 10¹⁶ m).
  • Stellar parallax: d (in pc) = 1/p (in arcseconds).
  • Doppler effect: \Delta\lambda/\lambda\approx\Delta f/f\approx v/c. Light from receding galaxies is redshifted.
  • Hubble's law: v=H_0d. The Universe is expanding, and its age is approximately 1/H₀.
  • The cosmological principle: on a large scale, the Universe is homogeneous and isotropic, and the laws of physics are the same everywhere.
  • Evidence for the Big Bang: the redshift of galaxies (Hubble's law), and the cosmic microwave background radiation, which is radiation from the early Universe stretched to microwave wavelengths, corresponding to about 2.7 K.
  • Evolution of the Universe: quarks formed, then protons and neutrons, then nuclei, then atoms, then stars and galaxies.
  • Dark matter is inferred from galaxy rotation curves. Dark energy is inferred from the accelerating expansion.
Worked example 3: Age of the Universe

H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. Estimate the age of the Universe.

  1. Convert to SI units: H₀ = 70 × 10³ / 3.1 × 10²² = 2.26 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹.
  2. Age ≈ 1/H₀ = 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s.

Answer: About 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years (14 billion years).

Common mistakes
  • Drawing the HR temperature axis increasing to the right. It increases to the left.
  • Forgetting to convert Mpc to m and km to m before working out 1/H₀.
  • Saying that energy levels are positive. They are negative, with 0 for a free electron.
Exam tips
  • Wien's law gives T, and Stefan's law then gives r. This is a very common two-step question.
Summary
  • Star life cycles depend on mass, ending in white dwarfs, neutron stars or black holes.
  • Line spectra: hf = ΔE; the elements are identified by their absorption lines.
  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K. Stefan: L = 4πr²σT⁴.
  • Distances use parallax and the parsec. Hubble's law v = H₀d gives an age ≈ 1/H₀. The CMB supports the Big Bang.
p-5-5.spec: OCR H556 5.5.1 Stars; 5.5.2 Electromagnetic radiation from stars; 5.5.3 Cosmology
p-5-5.intro: Astrophysics uses the light from stars to work out what they are made of, how hot and large they are, and how far away they are. Cosmology uses the same evidence to tell the story of the whole Universe, from the Big Bang onwards.

p-6-1.h:
1Capacitance

Key definitions

Capacitance (C): the charge stored per unit p.d., C=Q/V. 1 F = 1 C V⁻¹.

  • When a capacitor charges, electrons are pushed onto one plate and pulled off the other. The plates carry equal and opposite charges.
Key equations
\text{parallel: } C=C_1+C_2+\dots
\text{series: }\frac1C=\frac1{C_1}+\frac1{C_2}+\dots
  • These are the opposite of the rules for resistors. In series, every capacitor carries the same charge Q.
Worked example 1: Combining capacitors

A 100 μF capacitor is in series with a parallel pair of 47 μF and 53 μF. Find the total capacitance.

  1. Parallel pair: 47 + 53 = 100 μF.
  2. Series: 1/C = 1/100 + 1/100, so C = 50 μF.

Answer: 50 μF

2Energy stored

  • The energy stored is the area under a Q–V graph, which is a straight line through the origin.
Key equations
W=\tfrac12QV=\tfrac12CV^2=\frac{Q^2}{2C}
  • Uses include camera flashes, back-up power supplies and defibrillators. Capacitors can deliver a large current quickly.
Worked example 2: Defibrillator

A 200 μF capacitor is charged to 2.0 kV. How much energy does it store?

  1. W = ½CV² = ½ × 200 × 10⁻⁶ × (2000)².

Answer: W = 400 J

3Discharging through a resistor

Key equations
Q=Q_0e^{-t/CR}
V=V_0e^{-t/CR}
I=I_0e^{-t/CR}
\tau=CR
  • The time constant, τ = CR, is the time for Q, V or I to fall to 1/e (about 37%) of the initial value.
  • The time to halve is t½ = 0.69CR (that is, CR ln 2).
  • The decay is exponential because the rate of loss of charge is proportional to the charge remaining: dQ/dt = −Q/CR.
  • Modelling: the change is ΔQ = −(Q/CR)Δt in each small step. A spreadsheet repeats this step to build the curve.
Worked example 3: Discharge

A 470 μF capacitor is charged to 12 V and discharges through a 10 kΩ resistor. Find V after 10 s.

  1. τ = CR = 470 × 10⁻⁶ × 10 × 10³ = 4.7 s.
  2. V = 12 e^(−10/4.7) = 12 × 0.119.

Answer: V = 1.4 V

4Charging

  • When the switch is closed, the current is largest at the start, because the capacitor has no p.d. to oppose the supply. As charge builds up, the capacitor's p.d. rises, the p.d. across the resistor falls, and the current decreases.
  • After about 5CR, the capacitor is effectively fully charged to the supply p.d.
Key equations
V=V_0\left(1-e^{-t/CR}\right)
Q=Q_0\left(1-e^{-t/CR}\right)
  • The current still decays exponentially during charging, I=I_0e^{-t/CR}.
Worked example 4: Time to charge

A 220 μF capacitor charges through a 4.7 kΩ resistor from a 6.0 V supply. How long does it take to reach 3.0 V?

  1. τ = 220 × 10⁻⁶ × 4700 = 1.03 s.
  2. 3.0 = 6.0(1 − e^(−t/τ)) gives e^(−t/τ) = 0.5, so t = τ ln 2.

Answer: t = 0.72 s

PAG 9: finding the time constant
  • Charge a capacitor, then discharge it through a known resistor. Record V every 10 s with a voltmeter or a data logger.
  • Plot ln V against t. This gives a straight line with gradient −1/CR, so you can find C.
  • Use a large CR, so that readings can be taken by hand. Repeat the run and average the results.
Common mistakes
  • Using the resistor combination rules for capacitors. They are the other way round.
  • Forgetting the 1 − e⁻ form for charging.
  • Leaving μF unconverted. 1 μF = 10⁻⁶ F.
Exam tips
  • To find t from V, take logs: t = −CR ln(V/V₀).
Summary
  • C = Q/V. In parallel C adds; in series 1/C adds.
  • W = ½QV = ½CV².
  • Discharge: x = x₀e^(−t/CR); τ = CR. A graph of ln V against t has gradient −1/CR.
p-6-1.spec: OCR H556 6.1.1 Capacitors; 6.1.2 Energy; 6.1.3 Charging and discharging capacitors (PAG 9)
p-6-1.intro: A capacitor stores charge, and therefore energy, on two conducting plates separated by an insulator. Its charging and discharging follow an exponential pattern that turns up all over physics.

p-6-2.h:
1Electric fields

Key definitions

Electric field strength (E): the force per unit positive charge, E=F/Q (in N C⁻¹, or V m⁻¹).

  • Field lines run from + to −. A charged sphere behaves as if its charge were at its centre.

2Coulomb's law

Key equations
F=\frac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}
E=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}
\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\text{ F m}^{-1}
  • Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. The force is an inverse-square law, just like gravity.
Worked example 1: Force in a hydrogen atom

Find the force between a proton and an electron 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m apart.

  1. F = (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)² / (4π × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × (5.3 × 10⁻¹¹)²).

Answer: F = 8.2 × 10⁻⁸ N (attractive), which is about 10³⁹ times the gravitational force between them.

3Uniform fields and capacitors

Key equations
E=\frac{V}{d}
C=\frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}\ \ (\text{or }\frac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_rA}{d}\text{ with a dielectric})
  • A dielectric increases C, by a factor of the relative permittivity, ε_r. Its polar molecules align with the field.
Worked example 2: Parallel plates

Two plates 2.0 mm apart have an area of 0.040 m² and a p.d. of 500 V. Find E, and C with air between the plates.

  1. E = 500 / 2.0 × 10⁻³ = 2.5 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹.
  2. C = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 0.040 / 2.0 × 10⁻³ = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ F.

Answer: E = 2.5 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ and C = 180 pF

4Charged particles in a uniform field

  • A charged particle entering at right angles to the field feels a constant force, F = EQ, perpendicular to its velocity. Its path is a parabola, just like a projectile.
  • Horizontal velocity is constant. The vertical acceleration is a = EQ/m.
Worked example 3: Deflection of an electron

An electron enters a 2.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ field at 3.0 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹, at right angles to the field. The plates are 0.050 m long. Find its vertical deflection.

  1. Time between the plates: t = 0.050 / 3.0 × 10⁷ = 1.67 × 10⁻⁹ s.
  2. a = eE/m = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁴ / 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ = 3.5 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻².
  3. y = ½at² = ½ × 3.5 × 10¹⁵ × (1.67 × 10⁻⁹)².

Answer: y = 4.9 × 10⁻³ m (about 5 mm), towards the positive plate.

5Electric potential and energy

Key equations
V=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}
E_p=\frac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}
  • Electric potential is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing it from infinity to that point. It is positive near a positive charge.
  • The area under an F–r graph is the work done. The capacitance of an isolated sphere is C = 4πε₀R.
Worked example 4: Closest approach

An alpha particle (q = +2e) with 5.0 MeV of kinetic energy approaches a gold nucleus (Q = +79e). Find its distance of closest approach.

  1. At closest approach, all the KE has become potential energy: 5.0 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 8.0 × 10⁻¹³ J.
  2. r = Qq / (4πε₀ × KE) = (79 × 2 × (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)²) / (4π × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 8.0 × 10⁻¹³).

Answer: r = 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m, which sets an upper limit on the size of the nucleus.

Common mistakes
  • Using the 1/r² law for potential. Potential goes as 1/r, and the field as 1/r².
  • Forgetting that E = V/d applies only to uniform fields.
  • Assuming the electric force is always attractive, as gravity is.
Exam tips
  • Make a table comparing gravitational and electric fields (force, field strength, potential and their units). Examiners love that comparison.
Summary
  • E = F/Q. Coulomb: F = Qq/4πε₀r²; radial E = Q/4πε₀r².
  • Uniform field: E = V/d; C = ε₀ε_rA/d; charged particles follow parabolic paths.
  • V = Q/4πε₀r; E_p = Qq/4πε₀r.
p-6-2.spec: OCR H556 6.2.1 Point and spherical charges; 6.2.2 Coulomb's law; 6.2.3 Uniform electric field; 6.2.4 Electric potential and energy
p-6-2.intro: Electric fields are closely parallel to gravitational fields, but they can repel as well as attract. This topic covers Coulomb's law, uniform fields between plates, the deflection of charged particles, and electric potential.
secs: Charged particles in a uniform field

p-6-3.h:
1Magnetic fields

  • Magnetic fields are produced by moving charges (currents) and by permanent magnets. Field lines run from N to S.
  • The field patterns to know are: around a long straight wire (concentric circles, using the right-hand grip rule), in a flat coil, and in a solenoid (uniform inside, like a bar magnet outside).

2Force on a current-carrying conductor

Key equations
F=BIL\sin\theta
  • The direction comes from Fleming's left-hand rule: First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion.
Key definitions

Magnetic flux density (B): the force per unit current per unit length on a wire at right angles to the field. 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹.

Worked example 1: Motor effect

A 0.20 m wire carrying 3.0 A is placed at 90° to a 0.050 T field. Find the force.

  1. F = BIL = 0.050 × 3.0 × 0.20.

Answer: F = 0.030 N

3Charged particles in magnetic fields

Key equations
F=BQv
r=\frac{mv}{BQ}
  • The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the particle moves in a circle, and its speed does not change: BQv = mv²/r.
  • Velocity selector: crossed electric and magnetic fields let through, undeflected, only the particles for which EQ = BQv, so v = E/B.
Worked example 2: Proton in a field

A proton moving at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ enters a 0.10 T field at right angles. Find the radius of its path (m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).

  1. r = mv/BQ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ × 2.0 × 10⁶ / (0.10 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹).

Answer: r = 0.21 m

4Electromagnetic induction

Key definitions

Magnetic flux (φ): φ = BA cos θ, in Wb (1 Wb = 1 T m²).

Magnetic flux linkage: Nφ, for a coil of N turns.

Faraday's law: the induced e.m.f. is equal to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage.

Lenz's law: the direction of the induced e.m.f. (or current) is such that it opposes the change that produced it.

Key equations
\varepsilon=-\frac{\Delta(N\phi)}{\Delta t}
  • On a graph of flux linkage against time, the gradient gives the e.m.f.
  • AC generator: a coil rotating in a field has a sinusoidal flux linkage. The e.m.f. is greatest when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, because that is when the flux linkage changes fastest.
Worked example 3: Induced e.m.f.

A 200-turn coil of area 4.0 × 10⁻³ m² sits at 90° to a 0.50 T field. The field falls to zero in 0.10 s. Find the average induced e.m.f.

  1. Change in flux linkage = 200 × 0.50 × 4.0 × 10⁻³ = 0.40 Wb turns.
  2. ε = 0.40 / 0.10.

Answer: ε = 4.0 V

5Transformers

Key equations
\frac{n_s}{n_p}=\frac{V_s}{V_p}=\frac{I_p}{I_s}\ \ (\text{for an ideal transformer})
  • An alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing flux in the iron core. This links the secondary coil and induces an e.m.f. in it.
  • Laminating the core reduces eddy currents. Transmitting power at high voltage means a low current, so the I²R losses in the cables are smaller.
Worked example 4: Step-down transformer

A transformer steps 230 V down to 11.5 V. The primary has 2000 turns. How many turns are on the secondary?

  1. n_s = n_p × V_s/V_p = 2000 × 11.5/230.

Answer: n_s = 100 turns

Common mistakes
  • Using the right hand for the motor effect. Fleming's left-hand rule is for motors.
  • Saying that the e.m.f. is maximum when the flux linkage is maximum. It is maximum when the flux linkage is changing fastest.
  • Thinking transformers work on d.c. They need a changing current.
Exam tips
  • Lenz's law is conservation of energy. If the induced current helped the change, you would get energy for nothing.
Summary
  • F = BIL sin θ (Fleming's left-hand rule); F = BQv gives circular paths with r = mv/BQ; a velocity selector passes v = E/B.
  • φ = BA cos θ; ε = −Δ(Nφ)/Δt (Faraday and Lenz).
  • Transformers: V_s/V_p = n_s/n_p; high-voltage transmission reduces losses.
p-6-3.spec: OCR H556 6.3.1 Magnetic fields; 6.3.2 Motion of charged particles; 6.3.3 Electromagnetism
p-6-3.intro: Moving charges produce magnetic fields, and magnetic fields push on moving charges. This topic covers the motor effect, charged particles in magnetic fields, and electromagnetic induction, which underlies generators and transformers.

p-6-4.h:
1The nucleus

  • Alpha-particle scattering: most alpha particles passed straight through gold foil, and a few were deflected through large angles. This showed that the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.
  • A nucleus is written ᴬ_Z X, where A is the nucleon number and Z is the proton number. Isotopes have the same Z but different A.
  • Nuclear radius: R=r_0A^{1/3}, with r₀ ≈ 1.2 fm. The density of nuclear matter is therefore roughly constant, at about 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.
  • The strong nuclear force is attractive up to about 3 fm and repulsive below about 0.5 fm. It acts between nucleons and holds the nucleus together against electrostatic repulsion.

2Fundamental particles

  • Every particle has an antiparticle, with the same mass and the opposite charge. The positron is the antiparticle of the electron.
  • Hadrons feel the strong force and are made of quarks. Baryons have 3 quarks (proton = uud; neutron = udd). Mesons are a quark plus an antiquark.
  • Leptons (electron, muon, neutrino) do not feel the strong force and are fundamental.
  • Quark charges: u = +⅔e, d = −⅓e, s = −⅓e.
  • Beta-minus decay: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ (a d quark becomes a u quark). Beta-plus decay: p → n + e⁺ + νₑ (a u quark becomes a d quark). Both are caused by the weak interaction.

3Radioactivity

RadiationNatureIonisingStopped by
αhelium nucleusstronglypaper, or a few cm of air
β⁻ / β⁺electron / positronmoderatelya few mm of aluminium
γEM photonweaklyseveral cm of lead (reduced, not fully stopped)
  • Decay is random (you cannot predict which nucleus will decay next) and spontaneous (it is not affected by external conditions).
Key equations
A=\lambda N
N=N_0e^{-\lambda t}
\lambda t_{1/2}=\ln2
Worked example 1: Activity

A sample contains 2.0 × 10²⁰ nuclei with a half-life of 8.0 days. Find its activity, and the number of nuclei remaining after 24 days.

  1. λ = 0.693 / (8.0 × 86 400) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹, so A = λN = 2.0 × 10¹⁴ Bq.
  2. 24 days is 3 half-lives, so N = 2.0 × 10²⁰ / 8.

Answer: A = 2.0 × 10¹⁴ Bq, and 2.5 × 10¹⁹ nuclei remain.

  • Carbon dating: living things keep a constant ratio of ¹⁴C to ¹²C. After death the ¹⁴C decays (t½ ≈ 5700 years), so measuring the activity gives the age.
PAG 11: modelling decay
  • Use dice or coins, or a protactinium generator, and correct each count for background radiation.
  • Plot ln A against t. The gradient is −λ. Then find t½ = ln 2 / λ.

4Mass defect, binding energy, fission and fusion

Key definitions

Mass defect: the difference between the total mass of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus.

Binding energy: the minimum energy needed to separate a nucleus completely into its nucleons. It is given by Δmc².

  • Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56. Fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei both move towards the peak, so both release energy.
  • Fission reactors: a thermal neutron is absorbed by uranium-235, which splits and releases 2–3 neutrons, giving a chain reaction. A moderator (water or graphite) slows the neutrons, control rods (boron) absorb neutrons, and coolant removes the heat. There are environmental issues with radioactive waste.
  • Fusion needs very high temperatures, so the nuclei move fast enough to overcome their electrostatic repulsion. It powers stars.
Worked example 2: Binding energy

A helium-4 nucleus has a mass defect of 0.0304 u. Find its binding energy per nucleon (1 u = 931.5 MeV).

  1. BE = 0.0304 × 931.5 = 28.3 MeV.
  2. Per nucleon: 28.3 / 4.

Answer: 7.1 MeV per nucleon

Common mistakes
  • Saying that gamma rays are stopped completely by lead. They are attenuated, not fully stopped.
  • Forgetting the neutrino or antineutrino in beta-decay equations.
  • Using t½ in days with λ in s⁻¹. Keep the units consistent.
Exam tips
  • In every nuclear equation, check that A, Z and charge balance. For particle reactions, check charge and baryon number too.
Summary
  • Alpha scattering revealed the nucleus; R = r₀A^(1/3); the strong force holds nucleons together.
  • Hadrons are made of quarks (baryons have 3, mesons have quark + antiquark); leptons are fundamental; beta decay changes the flavour of a quark.
  • A = λN; N = N₀e^(−λt); λt½ = ln 2.
  • Binding energy = Δmc²; fission and fusion both release energy; reactors use a moderator, control rods and coolant.

p-6-4.intro: This topic goes inside the atom: the nucleus and the forces that hold it together, quarks and leptons, radioactive decay, and the energy released by fission and fusion.
secs: Mass defect, binding energy, fission and fusion

p-6-5.h:
1X-rays

  • Production: electrons are accelerated through a large p.d. (tens of kV) and hit a tungsten target. Their deceleration produces X-ray photons, with a maximum energy equal to eV. Only about 1% of the energy becomes X-rays; the rest becomes heat, so the anode is rotated and cooled.
Key equations
I=I_0e^{-\mu x}
  • μ is the attenuation (absorption) coefficient. Bone has a much higher μ than soft tissue, which gives contrast on the image.
Attenuation mechanismPhoton energyWhat happens
simple scatter1–20 keVthe photon bounces off an electron with no energy change
photoelectric effectbelow about 100 keVthe photon is absorbed and an electron is ejected
Compton scattering0.5–5 MeVthe photon loses part of its energy to an electron and is scattered
pair productionabove 1.02 MeVthe photon becomes an electron–positron pair
  • Contrast media, such as barium sulfate or iodine, have a high atomic number and absorb X-rays strongly. They outline soft tissues such as the gut and blood vessels.
  • CAT scans: an X-ray tube rotates around the patient, and many detectors record slices. A computer builds a 3D image. CAT scans give better detail than an X-ray image, but a higher dose.
Worked example 1: X-ray attenuation

For a beam of X-rays in soft tissue, μ = 0.35 cm⁻¹. What fraction of the intensity is transmitted through 4.0 cm?

  1. I/I₀ = e^(−0.35 × 4.0) = e^(−1.4).

Answer: 0.25, so 25% is transmitted.

2Diagnostic methods using radioactive tracers

  • Medical tracers are radioactive substances that are injected or swallowed, and that collect in target organs. Technetium-99m emits only γ rays, has a 6-hour half-life, and is easily attached to other molecules. Fluorine-18 (in fluorodeoxyglucose) emits positrons and is used for PET.
  • Gamma camera: a collimator (lead tubes) lets through only the γ rays travelling parallel to the tubes. A scintillator (NaI crystal) converts each γ photon into light. Photomultiplier tubes turn the light into electrical pulses, and a computer forms the image.
  • PET scans: an emitted positron annihilates with an electron, producing two 511 keV γ photons travelling in opposite directions. Detectors around the patient time the arrivals of each pair to locate the source. PET shows function (for example, metabolism), not just structure.
Worked example 2: Annihilation energy

Show that each photon from positron–electron annihilation has an energy of about 0.51 MeV.

  1. Mass of each particle = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, so the total energy is 2mc² = 2 × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × (3.0 × 10⁸)² = 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J.
  2. This is shared between two photons: 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J each, which is 0.51 MeV.

Answer: About 0.51 MeV per photon.

3Ultrasound

  • Ultrasound has frequencies above 20 kHz; medical imaging uses 1–15 MHz. It is produced and detected using the piezoelectric effect: a p.d. across a crystal makes it change shape, and the reverse also happens.
Key equations
Z=\rho c
\frac{I_r}{I_0}=\frac{(Z_2-Z_1)^2}{(Z_2+Z_1)^2}
  • Acoustic impedance, Z, is density × speed of sound. A large difference in Z gives strong reflection. Between air and skin almost all the ultrasound is reflected, so coupling gel is used, because its Z is close to that of skin.
  • An A-scan measures the depth of a boundary from the echo time. A B-scan sweeps the probe to build a 2D image.
  • Doppler imaging measures the speed of blood flow from the frequency shift: Δf = 2fv cos θ / c.
Worked example 3: Reflection at a boundary

Find the fraction of ultrasound intensity reflected at a boundary between muscle (Z = 1.70 × 10⁶) and bone (Z = 7.80 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹).

  1. I_r/I₀ = (7.80 − 1.70)² / (7.80 + 1.70)² = 37.2 / 90.3.

Answer: 0.41, so about 41% is reflected.

Common mistakes
  • Saying that X-ray contrast media are "radioactive". They simply absorb X-rays strongly.
  • Forgetting the factor of 2 in the Doppler equation and the echo-time calculation (the pulse travels there and back).
  • Confusing PET (positrons and two photons) with the gamma camera (single γ photons).
Exam tips
  • Compare the methods by what they show (structure or function), the dose (ultrasound is non-ionising), the cost and the resolution.
Summary
  • X-rays: I = I₀e^(−μx); simple scatter, the photoelectric effect, Compton scattering and pair production; contrast media; CAT scans.
  • Tracers: Tc-99m with a gamma camera; F-18 with PET (two 511 keV photons).
  • Ultrasound: piezoelectric transducers; Z = ρc; gel for matching impedance; A- and B-scans; Doppler.

p-6-5.intro: Medical imaging uses physics to look inside the body without surgery. X-rays, CAT scans, radioactive tracers, PET and ultrasound each depend on a different interaction between radiation and matter.

c-1-1.h:
1Fundamental particles

Our model of the atom has changed over time as new evidence appeared. Dalton pictured solid spheres. Thomson's discovery of the electron led to the "plum pudding" model. Rutherford's gold-foil experiment showed a tiny, dense, positive nucleus. Bohr then put the electrons in fixed energy levels. The modern model uses orbitals. Each model was accepted because it explained the experimental results of its time better than the one before.

ParticleRelative massRelative chargeWhere it is found
proton1+1nucleus
neutron10nucleus
electron1/1840 (about 0.0005)−1shells (orbitals) around the nucleus
  • The nucleus contains almost all the mass but takes up only a tiny fraction of the volume of the atom.
  • A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

2Mass number and isotopes

Key definitions

Atomic (proton) number, Z: the number of protons in the nucleus. It defines the element.

Mass number, A: the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

Isotopes: atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

  • Number of neutrons = A - Z. For an ion, electrons = Z - \text{charge}. So ^{32}_{16}\text{S}^{2-} has 16 protons, 16 neutrons and 18 electrons.
  • Isotopes have the same chemical properties because they have the same electron configuration. They have slightly different physical properties, such as density and rate of diffusion, because their masses differ.

3The time-of-flight (TOF) mass spectrometer

A TOF mass spectrometer measures the mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of ions. It works in four stages.

  1. Ionisation. In electrospray ionisation, the sample is dissolved in a volatile solvent and forced through a fine, high-voltage needle. Each molecule gains a proton: \text{X(g)} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{XH}^+\text{(g)}. This is used for larger molecules because they don't break up. In electron impact, high-energy electrons from an electron gun knock an electron off each particle: \text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^+\text{(g)} + \text{e}^-. This is used for elements and small molecules, and the molecules often fragment.
  2. Acceleration. An electric field accelerates the positive ions so that they all have the same kinetic energy.
  3. Ion drift. The ions pass through a flight tube with no field. Because E_k=\frac12mv^2 is the same for all of them, lighter ions travel faster and reach the detector first.
  4. Detection. Each ion picks up an electron at the detector. This produces a current, and the current is proportional to the number of ions (the abundance).
t = d\sqrt{\frac{m}{2E_k}}
\text{(time of flight is proportional to }\sqrt{m}\text{)}
  • Uses. The pattern of isotopes identifies an element. For a molecular substance, the peak with the largest m/z (the molecular ion, M⁺, or [\text{M+H}]^+ in electrospray) gives the relative molecular mass. With electrospray you subtract 1 for the added proton.
Key equations
A_r=\frac{\sum(\text{isotopic mass}\times\text{abundance})}{\sum\text{abundance}}
Worked example 1: Relative atomic mass from a spectrum

A sample of magnesium gives peaks at m/z 24 (78.6%), 25 (10.1%) and 26 (11.3%). Calculate A_r to 1 decimal place.

  1. Multiply each mass by its abundance: 24\times78.6=1886.4, 25\times10.1=252.5, 26\times11.3=293.8.
  2. Add them: 1886.4+252.5+293.8=2432.7.
  3. Divide by the total abundance (100): 2432.7/100=24.327.

Answer: A_r = 24.3

Worked example 2: Working out abundances

Boron has isotopes ¹⁰B and ¹¹B, and its A_r is 10.8. Find the percentage of ¹⁰B.

  1. Let the percentage of ¹⁰B be x, so ¹¹B is 100-x.
  2. Then \frac{10x+11(100-x)}{100}=10.8, which gives 1100-x=1080.
  3. So x=20.

Answer: 20% ¹⁰B and 80% ¹¹B.

4Electron configuration

Electrons occupy shells (main energy levels, n=1,2,3\dots), which are split into sub-shells (s, p, d). Each sub-shell is made of orbitals. Every orbital holds up to two electrons with opposite spins.

Sub-shellOrbitalsMaximum electrons
s12
p36
d510
  • Filling order (up to Z = 36): 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p. The 4s sub-shell fills before 3d because it is slightly lower in energy.
  • Orbitals in the same sub-shell fill singly first, then pair up.
  • Exceptions: Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, because a half-full or full d sub-shell is more stable.
  • Ions of transition metals lose their 4s electrons first: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s², so Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵.
  • The block an element sits in (s, p, d) tells you the sub-shell of its highest-energy electron.

5Ionisation energies

Key definitions

First ionisation energy: the energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms, forming one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.

\text{Na(g)}\rightarrow\text{Na}^+\text{(g)}+\text{e}^-
\text{(1st IE)}
\text{Na}^+\text{(g)}\rightarrow\text{Na}^{2+}\text{(g)}+\text{e}^-
\text{(2nd IE)}

Ionisation energy depends on three things: nuclear charge (the number of protons), distance of the electron from the nucleus, and shielding by inner electrons.

  • Successive ionisation energies always increase, because each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion. A big jump shows that the next electron comes from a shell closer to the nucleus. For example, Al has jumps after the 3rd and the 11th electrons, which is evidence for the 2, 8, 3 arrangement.
  • Down Group 2 (Be–Ba), the first IE decreases. The outer electron is in a higher shell, further from the nucleus and more shielded. This outweighs the increase in nuclear charge.
  • Across Period 3 (Na–Ar), the first IE generally increases. Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays similar, so the atomic radius gets smaller.
  • Dip at Al. Al's outer electron is in a 3p orbital, which is higher in energy than 3s and slightly shielded by the 3s electrons. This is evidence for sub-shells.
  • Dip at S. S has a pair of electrons in one 3p orbital. They repel each other, so one is easier to remove. This is evidence for electron pairing in orbitals.
Worked example 3: Reading successive ionisation energies

The first five ionisation energies of element X (kJ mol⁻¹) are 578, 1817, 2745, 11 577 and 14 842. Which group is X in?

  1. Look for the large jump. Between the 3rd (2745) and 4th (11 577) IE the value roughly quadruples.
  2. The 4th electron is therefore removed from an inner shell, so X has 3 outer electrons.

Answer: Group 13 (X is aluminium).

Common mistakes
  • Writing ionisation equations without state symbols, or with an electron *added* on the left. It is always X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻.
  • Saying 4s electrons are lost *after* 3d when ions form. They are lost first.
  • Explaining isotopes as having "different numbers of protons". The protons are the same; the neutrons differ.
  • In TOF, saying the ions are "deflected" by a magnetic field. That is an older instrument; TOF separates ions by time of flight.
Exam tips
  • For a trend in IE, always mention nuclear charge, distance (or shells) and shielding. Then say which effect wins.
  • Learn the Cr and Cu exceptions and the Period 3 dips at Al (3p) and S (pairing). They are favourite 2-mark questions.
Summary
  • Protons (+1, mass 1) and neutrons (0, mass 1) are in the nucleus; electrons (−1, mass ≈ 1/1840) are around it.
  • Isotopes have the same Z and different A, so they have the same chemistry.
  • TOF mass spectrometry: ionise, accelerate (same E_k), drift (lighter ions are faster), detect. It gives isotopic masses, abundances and M_r.
  • Electron configurations use 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d. Cr and Cu are exceptions, and ions lose 4s first.
  • Ionisation energy trends are explained by nuclear charge, distance and shielding. The Period 3 dips at Al and S are evidence for sub-shells and pairing.
c-1-1.intro: Everything in chemistry comes back to atoms: how many protons, neutrons and electrons they have, and how the electrons are arranged. This topic covers the particles in an atom, isotopes and the time-of-flight mass spectrometer, and how ionisation energies give evidence for shells and sub-shells.

c-1-2.h:
1Relative masses

Key definitions

Relative atomic mass, A_r: the average mass of an atom of an element, compared with 1/12 of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.

Relative molecular mass, M_r: the average mass of a molecule, compared with 1/12 of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.

Relative formula mass: the same idea, used for ionic compounds, which do not exist as molecules.

  • M_r is the sum of the A_r values in the formula. For example, M_r(\text{CaCO}_3)=40.1+12.0+3(16.0)=100.1.
  • Relative masses have no units. Molar mass M has the same value but with units of g mol⁻¹.

2The mole and the Avogadro constant

Key definitions

Avogadro constant, L (or N_A): the number of particles in one mole, 6.022\times10^{23} mol⁻¹. You don't need to memorise it; it is given in the data booklet.

Mole: the amount of substance containing 6.022\times10^{23} particles (atoms, molecules, ions or electrons, which you must name).

Key equations
n=\frac{m}{M}
N=n\times L
n=c\times V\ (V\text{ in dm}^3)
  • Volumes in cm³ must be divided by 1000 to give dm³. Concentration is in mol dm⁻³.
  • Always state which particle you are counting. One mole of H₂O contains 3 moles of atoms.

3The ideal gas equation

pV=nRT
  • SI units are essential: p in Pa, V in m³, T in K, and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (given).
  • Conversions: 1 kPa = 10³ Pa; 1 dm³ = 10⁻³ m³; 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³; T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.
  • A typical use is finding the M_r of a volatile liquid. You measure the mass vaporised and the volume of gas, find n=pV/RT, then M_r=m/n.
Worked example 1: Ideal gas calculation

0.250 g of a volatile liquid vaporises to give 98.0 cm³ of gas at 101 kPa and 373 K. Find its M_r.

  1. Convert to SI units: V=98.0\times10^{-6} m³ and p=101\times10^3 Pa.
  2. n=\frac{pV}{RT}=\frac{101000\times98.0\times10^{-6}}{8.31\times373}=3.19\times10^{-3} mol.
  3. M_r=\frac{m}{n}=\frac{0.250}{3.19\times10^{-3}}=78.3.

Answer: M_r \approx 78

4Empirical and molecular formulae

Key definitions

Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.

Molecular formula: the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule.

  1. Divide the mass (or percentage) of each element by its A_r.
  2. Divide each answer by the smallest one.
  3. If necessary, multiply to get whole numbers (a ratio of 1.5 means ×2, 1.33 means ×3).
  4. Molecular formula = empirical formula × \frac{M_r}{M_r(\text{empirical})}.
Worked example 2: Empirical and molecular formula

A compound contains 85.7% C and 14.3% H by mass, and its M_r is 56.0. Find its molecular formula.

  1. Moles: C =85.7/12.0=7.14; H =14.3/1.0=14.3.
  2. Ratio: divide by 7.14 to get C : H = 1 : 2. The empirical formula is CH₂ (mass 14.0).
  3. 56.0/14.0=4, so multiply by 4.

Answer: C₄H₈

5Balanced equations and calculations

  • Balance atoms first, then check that charges balance in ionic equations. Spectator ions are left out. For example, the ionic equation for neutralisation is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
  • To go from one substance to another: moles of the known substance → mole ratio from the equation → moles of the unknown → mass, volume or concentration.
Key equations
\text{percentage yield}=\frac{\text{actual mass of product}}{\text{theoretical mass of product}}\times100
\text{percentage atom economy}=\frac{M_r\text{ of desired product}}{\sum M_r\text{ of all reactants}}\times100
  • High atom economy means less waste and fewer by-products to separate or dispose of. That saves money and raw materials and is better for the environment. Addition reactions have 100% atom economy.
  • Yield and atom economy are different. A reaction can have a high yield but a poor atom economy.
  • Water of crystallisation. Heat a hydrated salt to constant mass. Find the moles of anhydrous salt and the moles of water lost, then the ratio gives x in, for example, MgSO₄·xH₂O.
Worked example 3: Titration calculation

25.0 cm³ of sodium carbonate solution reacts with 22.50 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl. The equation is Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Find the concentration of the Na₂CO₃.

  1. Moles of HCl =0.100\times\frac{22.50}{1000}=2.25\times10^{-3} mol.
  2. The ratio is 1 Na₂CO₃ : 2 HCl, so moles of Na₂CO₃ =1.125\times10^{-3} mol.
  3. c=\frac{1.125\times10^{-3}}{0.0250}=0.0450 mol dm⁻³.

Answer: 0.0450 mol dm⁻³

Required practical 1: making a standard solution and titrating
  • Weigh the solid by difference. Dissolve it in a beaker of distilled water, transfer it to a volumetric flask with washings, make it up to the mark (bottom of the meniscus at eye level), then invert to mix.
  • Rinse the pipette and burette with the solutions they will hold. Use an indicator and add dropwise near the end point.
  • Repeat until you have concordant titres (within 0.10 cm³). Ignore the rough titre and any outliers when you calculate the mean titre.
  • The uncertainty in a titre is ±0.05 cm³ per reading × 2 readings = ±0.10 cm³. Percentage uncertainty = uncertainty ÷ titre × 100.
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting to convert cm³ to dm³ (÷1000), or °C to K, or kPa to Pa in pV=nRT.
  • Using the mole ratio the wrong way round. Write the ratio under the equation before you start.
  • Rounding too early. Keep extra figures until the final answer, then give the answer to the same number of significant figures as the least precise data.
Exam tips
  • Lay out multi-step calculations as "moles → ratio → moles → answer", with units at every step. Method marks are awarded even if the final answer is wrong.
  • In atom economy, use the balanced equation and include every reactant.
Summary
  • n=m/M, N=nL, n=cV and pV=nRT (in SI units).
  • Empirical formula: divide by A_r, then divide by the smallest. Molecular formula = empirical × (M_r ÷ empirical mass).
  • Use the mole ratio from the balanced equation to find masses, gas volumes and concentrations.
  • Yield compares actual with theoretical product; atom economy compares desired product with all reactants.
c-1-2.intro: The mole lets chemists count particles by weighing them. This topic covers relative masses, the Avogadro constant, concentrations, the ideal gas equation, empirical and molecular formulae, and calculations from balanced equations, including yield, atom economy and titrations.
secs: The mole and the Avogadro constant

c-1-3.h:
1Ionic bonding

Key definitions

Ionic bonding: the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice.

  • Charges come from the Periodic Table. Group 1 forms 1+, Group 2 forms 2+, Al forms 3+, Group 6 forms 2−, and Group 7 forms 1−.
  • Learn these compound ions: sulfate SO₄²⁻, hydroxide OH⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻ and ammonium NH₄⁺.
  • To write a formula, balance the charges. For example, Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ give Al₂(SO₄)₃.

2Covalent, dative and metallic bonding

Key definitions

Covalent bond: a shared pair of electrons. A double bond has two shared pairs; a triple bond has three.

Co-ordinate (dative covalent) bond: a shared pair of electrons where both electrons come from the same atom. It is drawn as an arrow from the donor atom.

Metallic bonding: the attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.

  • Examples of dative bonds: NH₄⁺ (H⁺ accepts the lone pair from N), H₃O⁺, and Al₂Cl₆ (a Cl lone pair donated to Al). Once formed, a dative bond is identical to the other covalent bonds; all four N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ are the same.
  • Metals with more delocalised electrons per atom and smaller ions (for example Mg compared with Na) have stronger metallic bonding and higher melting points.

3Crystal structures and properties

StructureExampleBondingMelting pointConducts?
ionicsodium chlorideions in a latticehighonly when molten or dissolved (ions free to move)
metallicmagnesiumpositive ions + delocalised electronshighyes, solid and liquid (delocalised electrons)
macromolecular (giant covalent)diamond, graphitecovalent networkvery highgraphite yes, diamond no
simple moleculariodine, icecovalent within molecules, weak forces between moleculeslowno
  • Diamond: each C is bonded to 4 others in a tetrahedral network. It is very hard and has no free electrons.
  • Graphite: each C is bonded to 3 others in flat layers. The fourth electron is delocalised, so graphite conducts along the layers. The layers are held by weak forces, so they slide.
  • Iodine and ice: simple molecular lattices. Melting breaks only the intermolecular forces, not the covalent bonds.
  • Changes of state need energy to overcome the forces between particles. The temperature stays constant during melting or boiling while that energy is absorbed.

4Shapes of molecules (VSEPR)

Electron pairs around the central atom repel each other and spread as far apart as possible. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair. Each lone pair closes the bond angle by about 2.5°.

Electron pairs (bonding + lone)ShapeAngleExample
2 + 0linear180°CO₂, BeCl₂
3 + 0trigonal planar120°BF₃
4 + 0tetrahedral109.5°CH₄, NH₄⁺
3 + 1trigonal pyramidal107°NH₃
2 + 2bent (V-shaped)104.5°H₂O
5 + 0trigonal bipyramidal90° and 120°PCl₅
6 + 0octahedral90°SF₆
4 + 2square planar90°XeF₄
Worked example 1: Predicting a shape

Predict the shape of, and bond angle in, PCl₄⁺.

  1. P has 5 outer electrons. Lose 1 for the positive charge, giving 4. Each Cl contributes 1 electron to a bond, giving 4 bonding pairs in total.
  2. There are 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs.

Answer: Tetrahedral, 109.5°.

Worked example 2: A shape with lone pairs

Predict the shape of ClF₃.

  1. Cl has 7 outer electrons. Three of them pair with the 3 F atoms, giving 3 bonding pairs. The remaining 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs.
  2. That is 5 electron pairs, based on a trigonal bipyramid. The two lone pairs sit in equatorial positions.

Answer: T-shaped, with bond angles slightly less than 90°.

5Electronegativity and bond polarity

Key definitions

Electronegativity: the power of an atom to attract the pair of electrons in a covalent bond.

  • Electronegativity increases across a period and up a group. F is the most electronegative element, then O, N and Cl.
  • Bonding electrons are shared unequally between atoms of different electronegativity. The result is a polar bond with partial charges, for example H^{\delta+}–Cl^{\delta-}.
  • A molecule with polar bonds can still have no overall dipole if it is symmetrical, so the dipoles cancel. Examples are CO₂, BF₃ and CCl₄. CHCl₃ and H₂O are polar.

6Forces between molecules

  1. Induced dipole–dipole (van der Waals, London or dispersion) forces act between all molecules. Electrons move at random, creating a temporary dipole that induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule. These forces are stronger for molecules with more electrons (a larger M_r) and a larger surface contact, so straight chains have higher boiling points than branched ones.
  2. Permanent dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules, for example HCl or propanone.
  3. Hydrogen bonding is the strongest of the three. It happens when H is bonded to N, O or F. The δ+ H is attracted to a lone pair on an N, O or F atom of another molecule. In a diagram, show the lone pair and the partial charges, with a bond angle of about 180° at the H.
  • Anomalous boiling points. H₂O, HF and NH₃ boil much higher than the trend in their groups predicts, because they form hydrogen bonds.
  • Ice is less dense than water. Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice, so they are further apart than in the liquid.
Worked example 3: Explaining boiling points

Explain why ethanol (M_r 46) boils at 78 °C but propane (M_r 44) boils at −42 °C.

  1. Their M_r values are similar, so their van der Waals forces are similar.
  2. Ethanol has an O–H group, so it forms hydrogen bonds between molecules. Propane has only weak van der Waals forces.
  3. More energy is needed to overcome the hydrogen bonds.

Answer: Ethanol boils higher because of its hydrogen bonding between molecules.

Common mistakes
  • Saying that covalent bonds break when a simple molecular substance boils. Only the intermolecular forces are overcome.
  • Saying that ionic solids conduct. They conduct only when molten or in solution, when the ions can move. It is the ions that carry the charge, not electrons.
  • Drawing a hydrogen bond without the lone pair, or to an H that is not bonded to N, O or F.
  • Forgetting lone pairs on the central atom when predicting shape.
Exam tips
  • For a shape question, state the numbers of bonding pairs and lone pairs, then the shape and the angle. Then say that pairs repel to be as far apart as possible and that lone pairs repel more.
  • For a melting-point question, name the structure, name the force or bond that has to be broken, and say how strong it is.
Summary
  • Ionic bonding attracts oppositely charged ions; covalent bonding is a shared pair; in a dative bond both electrons come from one atom; metallic bonding is positive ions with delocalised electrons.
  • The four structures are ionic, metallic, giant covalent and simple molecular. They explain melting points and conductivity.
  • VSEPR: count bonding and lone pairs. Lone pairs repel most, removing about 2.5° per lone pair.
  • Polarity comes from differences in electronegativity, but symmetrical molecules cancel out.
  • The intermolecular forces in order of strength are induced dipole < permanent dipole < hydrogen bond.
c-1-3.intro: The way particles are held together explains melting points, conductivity, solubility and shape. This topic covers ionic, covalent, dative and metallic bonding, the four crystal structures, VSEPR shapes, electronegativity and polarity, and the three types of intermolecular force.

c-1-4.h:
1Enthalpy change

Key definitions

Enthalpy change, ΔH: the heat energy change measured at constant pressure.

Standard conditions: 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K, with all substances in their standard states. Written ΔH⦵₂₉₈.

Standard enthalpy of combustion, ΔcH⦵: the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a substance is completely burned in oxygen, with all reactants and products in their standard states.

Standard enthalpy of formation, ΔfH⦵: the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements, with all reactants and products in their standard states.

  • Exothermic reactions have negative ΔH: heat is given out and the surroundings warm up. Examples are combustion, neutralisation and respiration.
  • Endothermic reactions have positive ΔH: heat is taken in. Examples are thermal decomposition and photosynthesis.
  • ΔfH of an element in its standard state is zero by definition.

2Calorimetry

q=mc\Delta T
\Delta H=-\frac{q}{n}
  • m is the mass of the substance being heated, usually the water or solution (1 cm³ ≈ 1 g), not the mass of fuel. c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water. ΔT is the temperature change in K (the same number as in °C).
  • Convert q from J to kJ, then divide by the moles of the limiting reactant. Add a negative sign if the temperature rose (exothermic).
Worked example 1: Enthalpy of combustion from a spirit burner

Burning 0.46 g of ethanol (M_r 46) heats 100 g of water from 20.0 °C to 34.5 °C. Calculate ΔcH.

  1. q=100\times4.18\times14.5=6061 J =6.06 kJ.
  2. n=0.46/46=0.010 mol.
  3. \Delta H=-6.06/0.010=-606 kJ mol⁻¹.

Answer: ΔcH ≈ −610 kJ mol⁻¹ (2 s.f.). The data-book value is −1367 kJ mol⁻¹.

  • The experimental value is much less exothermic than the data-book value because of heat loss to the surroundings, incomplete combustion, evaporation of the fuel, and non-standard conditions.
Required practical 2: measuring an enthalpy change
  • For reactions in solution, such as neutralisation or displacement with zinc and copper(II) sulfate, use a polystyrene cup with a lid as an insulated calorimeter.
  • Record the temperature every 30 s for a few minutes before mixing and for several minutes after. Plot temperature against time and extrapolate back to the time of mixing to find the maximum temperature change, which corrects for cooling.
  • Use an excess of one reagent. Stir, and use a thermometer with a fine resolution.

3Hess's law

Key definitions

Hess's law: the enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided the initial and final conditions are the same.

Key equations
\Delta_rH=\sum\Delta_fH(\text{products})-\sum\Delta_fH(\text{reactants})
\Delta_rH=\sum\Delta_cH(\text{reactants})-\sum\Delta_cH(\text{products})
Worked example 2: Using enthalpies of formation

Find ΔrH for C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) → C₂H₅OH(g). ΔfH values (kJ mol⁻¹): C₂H₄ +52, H₂O(g) −242, C₂H₅OH(g) −235.

  1. Sum for the products: −235.
  2. Sum for the reactants: +52 + (−242) = −190.
  3. ΔrH = −235 − (−190) = −45.

Answer: −45 kJ mol⁻¹

Worked example 3: Using enthalpies of combustion

Find ΔfH of methane. ΔcH values: C −394, H₂ −286, CH₄ −890 kJ mol⁻¹.

  1. The formation reaction is C + 2H₂ → CH₄. The combustion route goes from these reactants via CO₂ + 2H₂O.
  2. ΔfH = ΣΔcH(reactants) − ΣΔcH(products) = [−394 + 2(−286)] − (−890).
  3. That is = −966 + 890 = −76.

Answer: −76 kJ mol⁻¹

  • Hess's law can also combine two measured reactions to find one that can't be measured directly. An example is the hydration of anhydrous MgSO₄ or CuSO₄: measure the enthalpy of solution of the anhydrous and the hydrated salt, then subtract.

4Mean bond enthalpies

Key definitions

Mean bond enthalpy: the enthalpy needed to break one mole of a given covalent bond in the gaseous state, averaged over a range of compounds.

\Delta H=\sum(\text{bonds broken})-\sum(\text{bonds made})
  • Breaking bonds is endothermic and making bonds is exothermic.
  • Answers from mean bond enthalpies differ from Hess's law values for two reasons. The values are averages; the actual bond in a given molecule may be stronger or weaker. They also apply only to gases, so any substance that is a liquid adds an error.
Worked example 4: Bond enthalpy calculation

Estimate ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (all gases). Bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 464.

  1. Bonds broken: 4(413) + 2(498) = 2648.
  2. Bonds made: 2(805) + 4(464) = 3466.
  3. ΔH = 2648 − 3466 = −818.

Answer: About −818 kJ mol⁻¹

Common mistakes
  • Using the mass of the fuel or solute as m in q=mc\Delta T. Use the mass of the water or solution.
  • Forgetting the minus sign for an exothermic reaction, or not dividing by moles.
  • In a ΔfH cycle, writing reactants − products. It is products − reactants for formation, but reactants − products for combustion.
  • Multiplying only some of the terms by the stoichiometric coefficients.
Exam tips
  • Define standard enthalpies precisely: "1 mol", "standard states", "100 kPa", "298 K". Each phrase can earn a mark.
  • Give ΔH with a sign, units (kJ mol⁻¹) and sensible significant figures.
Summary
  • ΔH is the heat change at constant pressure: negative for exothermic, positive for endothermic.
  • q=mc\Delta T, then \Delta H=-q/n. Experimental values are lower because of heat loss.
  • Hess's law: ΔrH = ΣΔfH(products) − ΣΔfH(reactants), or ΣΔcH(reactants) − ΣΔcH(products).
  • Bond enthalpy: broken − made. It is approximate because the values are means and apply to gases only.
c-1-4.intro: Energetics measures the heat taken in or given out by a reaction. This topic covers enthalpy change and standard conditions, calorimetry with q = mcΔT, Hess's law cycles using formation and combustion data, and mean bond enthalpies.

c-1-5.h:
1Collision theory and rate

Key definitions

Rate of reaction: the change in concentration (or amount) of a reactant or product per unit time, for example in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

Activation energy, Eₐ: the minimum energy that particles need to collide with for a reaction to happen.

  • For particles to react they must collide, with the correct orientation and with energy at least Eₐ.
  • Most collisions do not lead to a reaction, because most particles have less energy than Eₐ or collide the wrong way round.
  • On a concentration–time graph, the rate at any time is the gradient of the tangent. The initial rate is the gradient at t=0.

2The Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution

  • The curve shows how many molecules in a gas have each energy.
  • It starts at the origin, because no molecules have zero energy.
  • It has no maximum energy: the curve approaches the energy axis but never touches it.
  • The peak is the most probable energy. The mean energy is a little to the right of the peak.
  • The area under the curve is the total number of molecules.
  • Molecules to the right of Eₐ have enough energy to react.

3Effect of temperature

  • At a higher temperature the peak moves right and lower, and the curve is more spread out. The area stays the same because the number of molecules is unchanged.
  • A small rise in temperature greatly increases the number of molecules with E \ge E_a. So a large fraction more of the collisions are successful, and the rate rises sharply. For many reactions, a 10 K rise roughly doubles the rate.
  • Collisions also become a little more frequent, but that is a much smaller effect.
Required practical 3: effect of temperature on rate
  • A typical method is sodium thiosulfate + hydrochloric acid → a sulfur precipitate. Time how long it takes for a cross under the flask to disappear, at several temperatures (use a water bath).
  • Rate is proportional to 1/time. Keep the concentrations and volumes the same. Measure the temperature of the mixture itself, not the bath.
  • Plot 1/t against temperature to show the trend.

4Effect of concentration, pressure and surface area

  • A higher concentration of a solution, or a higher pressure of a gas, puts more particles in the same volume. They collide more frequently, so there are more successful collisions per second. The *proportion* of molecules with E\ge E_a does not change.
  • A larger surface area (a powder instead of lumps) exposes more particles to collisions.
  • The effect of concentration can be followed by continuous monitoring. An example is CaCO₃ + HCl, measuring the volume of CO₂ with a gas syringe or the loss of mass over time. Draw tangents to find the rate.
Worked example 1: Rate from a gas syringe

In the reaction of marble chips with acid, 48 cm³ of CO₂ is collected in the first 30 s. Calculate the mean rate over this time.

  1. Rate = change in volume ÷ time.
  2. 48 \div 30 = 1.6.

Answer: 1.6 cm³ s⁻¹

5Catalysts

Key definitions

Catalyst: a substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being changed in chemical composition or amount at the end.

  • A catalyst provides an alternative reaction route with a lower activation energy.
  • On the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve, Eₐ moves to the left. The curve itself is unchanged, so many more molecules now have enough energy to react.
  • A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally. It does not change ΔH or the position of equilibrium.
  • Catalysts are important in industry: lower temperatures can be used, which saves energy and reduces CO₂ emissions.
Worked example 2: Explaining a rate change

Explain why increasing the temperature from 20 °C to 30 °C roughly doubles the rate of a reaction.

  1. At the higher temperature, the molecules have more kinetic energy on average.
  2. On the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve, many more molecules have energy greater than or equal to Eₐ.
  3. So a greater proportion of collisions are successful each second, and the frequency of collisions also increases slightly.

Answer: There are many more successful collisions per unit time, so the rate increases significantly.

Common mistakes
  • Saying that a higher temperature "lowers the activation energy". Only a catalyst does that.
  • Drawing the hotter Maxwell–Boltzmann curve with a higher peak, or with the curve crossing back to touch the axis.
  • Saying that a higher concentration gives particles more energy. It gives more collisions per second.
Exam tips
  • Always use the phrase "more successful collisions per unit time". Frequency matters, not just "more collisions".
  • When asked to sketch a curve at a higher temperature, keep the same start, make the peak lower and further right, and keep the tail above the original curve at high energy.
Summary
  • A reaction needs a collision with the right orientation and E\ge E_a.
  • The Maxwell–Boltzmann curve starts at the origin, never touches the axis, and its area is the number of molecules.
  • Temperature is the biggest effect: many more molecules have at least Eₐ.
  • Concentration and pressure increase collision frequency.
  • Catalysts give a route with lower Eₐ and leave the curve unchanged.
c-1-5.intro: Kinetics is about how fast reactions go. This topic covers collision theory and activation energy, the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, and how temperature, concentration, pressure and catalysts change the rate.
secs: Effect of concentration, pressure and surface area

c-1-6.h:
1Dynamic equilibrium

Key definitions

Dynamic equilibrium: in a closed system, the forward and reverse reactions happen at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.

  • Both reactions are still going on. The concentrations are constant, but they are not usually equal.
  • Equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system, where nothing can escape.

2Le Chatelier's principle

Key definitions

Le Chatelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose (minimise) that change.

ChangeEffect on position of equilibrium
increase the concentration of a reactantshifts right, using up the added reactant
increase the pressure (gases)shifts to the side with fewer gas moles
increase the temperatureshifts in the endothermic direction
add a catalystno change; equilibrium is reached faster
  • If both sides have the same number of gas moles, pressure has no effect on the position.
Worked example 1: Predicting a shift

N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Predict the effect on the yield of NH₃ of (a) increasing the pressure and (b) increasing the temperature.

  1. (a) The left side has 4 gas moles and the right side has 2. Higher pressure shifts equilibrium to the side with fewer moles, so it shifts right.
  2. (b) The forward reaction is exothermic, so the reverse reaction is endothermic. Higher temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction, so it shifts left.

Answer: (a) The yield increases. (b) The yield decreases.

3Industrial compromise

  • Ethanol by hydration of ethene: C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ C₂H₅OH(g), ΔH = −46 kJ mol⁻¹. Typical conditions are 300 °C, 6–7 MPa and a phosphoric acid catalyst. A lower temperature would give a better yield but the rate would be too slow. A higher pressure would give a better yield but costs more and needs stronger equipment. Unreacted ethene is recycled.
  • Methanol: CO(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g), ΔH is negative. The same kind of compromise applies.
  • The compromise balances a good yield, a fast rate, cost and safety.

4The equilibrium constant Kc

For a\text{A}+b\text{B}\rightleftharpoons c\text{C}+d\text{D} (all in the same phase):

K_c=\frac{[\text{C}]^c[\text{D}]^d}{[\text{A}]^a[\text{B}]^b}
  • Square brackets mean the equilibrium concentration in mol dm⁻³.
  • Units. Substitute mol dm⁻³ for each term and cancel. Kc can have no units.
  • Only temperature changes Kc. If the forward reaction is exothermic, raising the temperature decreases Kc. Changing a concentration or the pressure moves the position of equilibrium, but Kc stays the same. A catalyst does not affect Kc.
Worked example 2: Calculating Kc from equilibrium moles

1.00 mol of ethanoic acid and 1.00 mol of ethanol reach equilibrium in 0.500 dm³. At equilibrium 0.667 mol of ethyl ethanoate has formed. Calculate Kc for CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.

  1. Equilibrium moles: ester 0.667 and water 0.667. The acid and the alcohol each have 1.00-0.667=0.333.
  2. Concentrations: divide by 0.500. The volumes cancel here because there are equal numbers of moles on each side.
  3. K_c=\frac{0.667\times0.667}{0.333\times0.333}=4.01.

Answer: Kc ≈ 4.0 (no units)

Worked example 3: Finding units

Write the expression for Kc for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) and find its units.

  1. K_c=\frac{[\text{SO}_3]^2}{[\text{SO}_2]^2[\text{O}_2]}
  2. Units: \frac{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^2}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^3}=(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{-1}.

Answer: mol⁻¹ dm³

Common mistakes
  • Saying that a catalyst increases the yield. It only speeds up how quickly equilibrium is reached.
  • Using initial moles instead of equilibrium moles in Kc. Set up a table with rows for initial, change and equilibrium.
  • Saying Kc changes when the pressure or a concentration changes. Only temperature changes Kc.
Exam tips
  • For a Le Chatelier answer, state the change, the direction of the shift, and the reason (for example "to the side with fewer gas moles, to reduce the pressure").
  • Answers about industrial conditions should mention yield, rate, cost of energy or equipment, and safety.
Summary
  • Dynamic equilibrium: equal rates and constant concentrations in a closed system.
  • Le Chatelier: the system opposes the change. Pressure favours fewer gas moles; temperature favours the endothermic direction; catalysts have no effect on the position.
  • Kc = products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient. Work out the units by cancelling.
  • Only temperature changes the value of Kc.
c-1-6.intro: Many reactions are reversible and reach a dynamic equilibrium. This topic covers Le Chatelier's principle, industrial compromise conditions, and the equilibrium constant Kc, including writing expressions, calculating values and finding units.

c-1-7.h:
1Oxidation and reduction

Key definitions

Oxidation: loss of electrons, or an increase in oxidation state.

Reduction: gain of electrons, or a decrease in oxidation state.

Oxidising agent: an electron acceptor. It is reduced itself.

Reducing agent: an electron donor. It is oxidised itself.

Remember OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

2Oxidation states

Rules, in order of priority:

  1. An uncombined element is 0, for example Na, O₂ and Cl₂.
  2. The oxidation states in a neutral compound add up to 0. In an ion they add up to the ion's charge.
  3. A simple ion has the same oxidation state as its charge: Na⁺ is +1, Cl⁻ is −1.
  4. Group 1 is +1, Group 2 is +2 and Al is +3. F is always −1.
  5. H is +1, except in metal hydrides such as NaH, where it is −1.
  6. O is −2, except in peroxides such as H₂O₂, where it is −1, and in OF₂, where it is +2.
  7. Cl is −1, except when it is combined with O or F.
  • Roman numerals in names give the oxidation state: iron(III) is Fe³⁺, and in chlorate(I), ClO⁻, Cl is +1.
Worked example 1: Finding oxidation states

Find the oxidation state of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻ and of S in S₂O₃²⁻.

  1. Cr₂O₇²⁻: 2x+7(-2)=-2, so 2x=12 and x=+6.
  2. S₂O₃²⁻: 2x+3(-2)=-2, so 2x=4 and x=+2.

Answer: Cr is +6; S is +2.

3Half-equations

A half-equation shows the electrons gained or lost by one species, for example Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ or Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻.

In acidic solution, balance a half-equation in this order:

  1. Balance the element that changes oxidation state.
  2. Balance O by adding H₂O.
  3. Balance H by adding H⁺.
  4. Balance charge by adding electrons to the more positive side.
Worked example 2: Manganate(VII) half-equation

Write the half-equation for MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ in acid.

  1. Mn is balanced. Add 4H₂O on the right to balance the 4 O atoms.
  2. Add 8H⁺ on the left to balance the H.
  3. Charge on the left is −1 + 8 = +7; charge on the right is +2. Add 5e⁻ to the left.

Answer: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O

4Combining half-equations

  1. Multiply the half-equations so that the numbers of electrons are equal.
  2. Add them together and cancel the electrons, plus any H⁺ or H₂O that appear on both sides.
Worked example 3: Overall redox equation

Combine MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O with Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻.

  1. Multiply the iron half-equation by 5: 5Fe²⁺ → 5Fe³⁺ + 5e⁻.
  2. Add the two and cancel the 5e⁻.

Answer: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5Fe³⁺

  • Check the final equation: the atoms balance, the total charge is the same on both sides (+17 on each side here), and no electrons are left.
  • Disproportionation is when the same element is both oxidised and reduced. An example is Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O, where Cl goes from 0 to −1 and +1.
Common mistakes
  • Writing electrons on the wrong side. In an oxidation half-equation the electrons are products.
  • Giving oxidation states as charges ("2+") instead of "+2". Write the sign first.
  • Saying the oxidising agent is oxidised. It is reduced.
Exam tips
  • To identify what is oxidised and what is reduced, write the oxidation states above every element in the equation and look for the changes.
  • In combined equations, check both atoms and charges. Examiners check both.
Summary
  • OIL RIG. An oxidising agent gains electrons; a reducing agent loses electrons.
  • Assign oxidation states using the priority rules (F, then O, then H).
  • Balance half-equations in acid with H₂O, then H⁺, then e⁻. Combine by matching the electrons.
c-1-7.intro: Redox reactions involve transfer of electrons. This topic covers oxidation states, identifying oxidising and reducing agents, and writing and combining half-equations, including those in acidic solution.

c-2-1.h:
1Classification into blocks

  • Elements are arranged in order of atomic (proton) number, in periods (rows) and groups (columns).
  • An element's block is the sub-shell that holds its highest-energy electron:
BlockGroupsExamples
s1 and 2 (plus H and He)Na, Mg
p13–18Al to Ar
dtransition metalsSc to Zn
flanthanides and actinidesCe, U
Key definitions

Periodicity: the repeating pattern of physical and chemical properties across periods.

2Atomic radius across Period 3

  • Atomic radius decreases from Na to Ar.
  • Across the period the nuclear charge increases (one more proton each time), while the extra electrons go into the same shell, so the shielding is similar.
  • The outer electrons are therefore pulled closer to the nucleus.

3First ionisation energy across Period 3

  • The general trend is an increase from Na to Ar, for the same reason: more nuclear charge, similar shielding, a smaller radius, so the outer electron is held more strongly.
