  • Al is lower than Mg. Al's outer electron is in a 3p sub-shell, which is slightly higher in energy and is shielded by the 3s electrons.
  • S is lower than P. In S, two electrons share one 3p orbital. The repulsion between the paired electrons makes one of them easier to remove.

4Melting points across Period 3

ElementStructureBonding or force overcomeMelting point
Na, Mg, Almetallic latticemetallic bonding, which gets stronger from Na to Alrises Na < Mg < Al
Simacromolecular (giant covalent)many strong covalent bondshighest
P₄, S₈, Cl₂simple molecularweak van der Waals forceslow; S₈ > P₄ > Cl₂
Arsingle atomsvery weak van der Waals forceslowest
  • Na to Al. The ions carry more charge (1+, 2+, 3+) and are smaller. There are more delocalised electrons per atom, so the electrostatic attraction is stronger and the melting point rises.
  • Si has a giant covalent lattice, so a lot of energy is needed to break its covalent bonds.
  • S₈ > P₄ > Cl₂ > Ar. Bigger molecules have more electrons, which gives stronger van der Waals forces.
Worked example 1: Explaining a melting point difference

Explain why sulfur has a higher melting point than phosphorus.

  1. Both are simple molecular: sulfur exists as S₈ and phosphorus as P₄.
  2. S₈ has more electrons than P₄, so the van der Waals forces between its molecules are stronger.
  3. More energy is needed to overcome them.

Answer: The S₈ molecules are larger, so they have stronger van der Waals forces than P₄ molecules.

Worked example 2: Explaining an ionisation energy difference

Explain why the first ionisation energy of magnesium is greater than that of sodium.

  1. Mg has one more proton than Na.
  2. Its outer electrons are in the same 3s sub-shell, with similar shielding.
  3. Mg also has a smaller atomic radius, so its outer electron is attracted more strongly.

Answer: Mg has a greater nuclear charge, similar shielding and a smaller radius, so more energy is needed to remove its outer electron.

Common mistakes
  • Saying that atomic radius decreases because "there are more electrons". The key is the increasing nuclear charge with the same shielding.
  • Saying that silicon's covalent bonds break as "intermolecular forces". Silicon is giant covalent; it has no molecules.
  • Forgetting the molecular formulae P₄, S₈ and Cl₂ when explaining melting points.
Exam tips
  • In periodicity answers, structure the explanation as structure, then bonding or force, then strength, then energy needed.
  • For IE exceptions, give the sub-shell (3s compared with 3p) or the pairing in 3p⁴.
Summary
  • Blocks: s, p, d and f, based on the highest-energy sub-shell.
  • Across Period 3: the radius decreases and the first IE increases, with dips at Al and S.
  • Melting point: rises from Na to Al (metallic), peaks at Si (giant covalent), is low for P₄, S₈ and Cl₂ (molecular), and lowest for Ar.
c-2-1.intro: The Periodic Table is arranged so that patterns repeat across each period. This topic covers the s, p, d and f blocks and the trends in atomic radius, first ionisation energy and melting point across Period 3 (Na to Ar).

c-2-2.h:
1Physical trends down the group

PropertyTrend down Group 2Reason
atomic radiusincreasesan extra shell of electrons each time
first ionisation energydecreasesthe outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, which outweighs the extra nuclear charge
melting pointgenerally decreasesthe metal ions get larger while the charge stays 2+, so the attraction to the delocalised electrons weakens (Mg is an anomaly because its crystal structure is different)

2Reactions with water

  • Reactivity increases down the group, because the first and second ionisation energies decrease, so the atoms lose their two outer electrons more easily.
  • Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water: Mg + 2H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂. It burns in steam with a bright white flame: Mg(s) + H₂O(g) → MgO(s) + H₂(g).
  • Calcium, strontium and barium react with cold water with increasing vigour: M + 2H₂O → M(OH)₂ + H₂. The resulting solution is alkaline.

3Solubility trends

CompoundTrend down the groupExamples
hydroxides M(OH)₂solubility increasesMg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble; Ba(OH)₂ is quite soluble
sulfates MSO₄solubility decreasesMgSO₄ is soluble; BaSO₄ is insoluble

4Uses of Group 2 metals and compounds

  • Mg in the extraction of titanium: TiCl₄ + 2Mg → Ti + 2MgCl₂. This is done at high temperature in an argon atmosphere.
  • Mg(OH)₂ (milk of magnesia) is an antacid, neutralising excess stomach acid: Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O.
  • Ca(OH)₂ (slaked lime) is used in agriculture to neutralise acidic soils.
  • CaO and CaCO₃ remove SO₂ from flue gases (flue gas desulfurisation): CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃ and CaCO₃ + SO₂ → CaSO₃ + CO₂.
  • BaSO₄ in barium meals. BaSO₄ is insoluble, so the toxic Ba²⁺ ions are not absorbed by the body. Barium absorbs X-rays strongly, so the gut shows up on an X-ray.
  • Acidified BaCl₂ tests for sulfate ions. A white precipitate of BaSO₄ forms: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s). The solution is first acidified with HCl to remove carbonate ions, which would also give a white precipitate.
Worked example 1: Writing an equation for flue gas desulfurisation

Write an equation for the reaction of calcium carbonate with sulfur dioxide, and explain why this is useful.

  1. The products are calcium sulfite and carbon dioxide.
  2. CaCO₃(s) + SO₂(g) → CaSO₃(s) + CO₂(g).

Answer: This removes SO₂ from power-station emissions, which reduces acid rain.

Worked example 2: Explaining the use of barium sulfate

Barium compounds are toxic. Explain why a barium meal is safe to swallow.

  1. Barium sulfate is insoluble in water.
  2. So almost no Ba²⁺ ions dissolve or pass into the blood.

Answer: BaSO₄ is insoluble, so toxic Ba²⁺ ions are not absorbed, while barium still absorbs X-rays to outline the gut.

Required practical 4: test-tube tests for ions
  • Sulfate: add HCl(aq), then BaCl₂(aq). A white precipitate shows SO₄²⁻.
  • Group 2 cations: add NaOH(aq). Mg²⁺ gives a white precipitate of Mg(OH)₂. Ba²⁺ gives little or no precipitate, because Ba(OH)₂ is soluble.
  • Hydroxide: the solution turns red litmus blue.
  • Carbonate: add dilute acid. Effervescence occurs, and the gas turns limewater milky.
  • Ammonium: warm with NaOH(aq). Ammonia is given off, which turns damp red litmus blue.
Common mistakes
  • Saying that "Group 2 compounds" get more or less soluble without saying which compound. Hydroxides become more soluble down the group; sulfates become less soluble.
  • Forgetting to acidify before the BaCl₂ test.
  • Saying that magnesium reacts with steam to give Mg(OH)₂. It gives MgO and H₂.
Exam tips
  • Learn one balanced equation for each use: Ti extraction, an antacid, flue gas desulfurisation and the sulfate test.
Summary
  • Down Group 2: the radius increases, the IE decreases, the reactivity with water increases, and the melting point generally decreases.
  • Hydroxides become more soluble down the group; sulfates become less soluble.
  • Uses: Mg for Ti, Mg(OH)₂ as an antacid, Ca(OH)₂ for soil, CaO/CaCO₃ to remove SO₂, BaSO₄ for X-rays, and BaCl₂ to test for sulfate.
c-2-2.intro: The Group 2 metals (Be to Ba) show clear trends in reactivity and in the solubility of their compounds. Several of the compounds have important uses in medicine, farming and industry.
secs: Uses of Group 2 metals and compounds

c-2-3.h:
1Trends in physical properties

PropertyTrend down the groupReason
electronegativitydecreasesatoms are larger, so the bonding pair is further from the nucleus and more shielded
boiling pointincreaseslarger molecules with more electrons have stronger van der Waals forces
  • At room temperature, F₂ is a pale yellow gas, Cl₂ a green gas, Br₂ a red-brown liquid, and I₂ a grey-black solid (it forms a purple vapour).

2Oxidising ability and displacement

  • Oxidising ability decreases down the group: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. Larger atoms attract an extra electron less strongly.
  • A halogen displaces a less reactive halide from solution: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. The solution turns orange (or yellow, depending on concentration).
Added to →KCl(aq)KBr(aq)KI(aq)
Cl₂(aq)no changeorange (Br₂)brown (I₂)
Br₂(aq)no changeno changebrown (I₂)
I₂(aq)no changeno changeno change

3Reducing ability of halide ions

  • Reducing ability increases down the group: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻. Larger ions lose an electron more easily.
  • This shows clearly in their reactions with concentrated sulfuric acid:
HalideProductsObservationsWhat happens to S
NaF, NaClHF or HClsteamy (misty) fumesno redox; stays +6
NaBrHBr, then Br₂ and SO₂steamy fumes, orange-brown vapourreduced to +4 (SO₂)
NaIHI, then I₂, SO₂, S and H₂Sfumes, purple vapour or black solid, yellow solid, smell of rotten eggsreduced to +4, 0 and −2
2\text{HBr}+\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\rightarrow\text{Br}_2+\text{SO}_2+2\text{H}_2\text{O}
8\text{HI}+\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\rightarrow4\text{I}_2+\text{H}_2\text{S}+4\text{H}_2\text{O}

4Testing for halide ions

  1. Acidify the solution with dilute nitric acid to remove carbonate and hydroxide ions, which would otherwise form other precipitates.
  2. Add silver nitrate solution: Ag⁺(aq) + X⁻(aq) → AgX(s).
  3. Add ammonia to confirm which halide is present.
IonPrecipitateDilute NH₃Concentrated NH₃
Cl⁻white AgCldissolvesdissolves
Br⁻cream AgBrdoes not dissolvedissolves
I⁻yellow AgIdoes not dissolvedoes not dissolve
  • Fluoride gives no precipitate, because AgF is soluble.

5Chlorine and chlorate(I)

  • Chlorine in water. Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO. This is disproportionation: Cl goes from 0 to −1 and +1. Chloric(I) acid kills bacteria.
  • In sunlight: 2Cl₂ + 2H₂O → 4HCl + O₂.
  • Bleach. With cold, dilute NaOH: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O. Sodium chlorate(I), NaClO, is the active ingredient in bleach, and is used for cleaning and for treating water.
  • Benefits and risks of chlorinating water. It kills disease-causing microorganisms, and it leaves a residual effect that protects water in the pipes. However, chlorine is toxic, and it can react with organic matter to form chlorinated hydrocarbons that may be carcinogenic. On balance the health benefits are judged to outweigh the risks.
Worked example 1: Identifying a halide

A solution gives a cream precipitate with acidified AgNO₃. The precipitate does not dissolve in dilute ammonia but does dissolve in concentrated ammonia. Identify the ion and write the ionic equation.

  1. A cream precipitate that dissolves only in concentrated NH₃ is AgBr.
  2. Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s).

Answer: Bromide ions, Br⁻.

Worked example 2: Oxidation states in a reaction with sulfuric acid

State the change in oxidation state of sulfur when NaI reacts with concentrated H₂SO₄ to give H₂S.

  1. In H₂SO₄, sulfur is +6. In H₂S, it is −2.
  2. Sulfur gains 8 electrons.

Answer: From +6 to −2: sulfur is reduced, and the iodide ions are oxidised to I₂.

Common mistakes
  • Using HCl to acidify before the AgNO₃ test. HCl adds Cl⁻ ions and gives a false positive.
  • Saying that the halogens get "more reactive" down the group. Their oxidising ability decreases, while the halide ions become better reducing agents.
  • Mixing up the colours: AgCl is white, AgBr is cream, AgI is yellow.
Exam tips
  • Learn the conc. H₂SO₄ table well. Questions often ask for an observation and the name of the reduction product of sulfur for each halide.
  • For chlorine and water, state one benefit and one risk, and name the disproportionation.
Summary
  • Down Group 7: electronegativity and oxidising ability decrease, and the boiling point increases.
  • A halogen displaces the halides below it.
  • The reducing power of halides increases down the group. I⁻ reduces conc. H₂SO₄ as far as H₂S.
  • AgNO₃ test: AgCl is white, AgBr cream, AgI yellow. Confirm with ammonia.
  • Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO disinfects water. Cl₂ + 2NaOH gives bleach.
c-2-3.intro: The halogens (F to I) are reactive non-metals, and their oxidising ability falls down the group. This topic covers their trends, displacement, how halide ions reduce sulfuric acid, silver nitrate tests, and the chemistry of chlorine in water treatment and bleach.

c-3-1.h:
1Types of formula

FormulaWhat it showsExample (butan-1-ol)
empiricalsimplest whole-number ratio of atomsC₄H₁₀O
molecularactual number of atomsC₄H₁₀O
generalalgebraic formula for a homologous seriesCₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH
structuralarrangement of atoms with no bonds drawnCH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH
displayedevery atom and every bondall C–H, C–C, C–O and O–H bonds drawn
skeletalcarbon skeleton as lines; C and H on carbons not showna zig-zag of 4 carbons with OH at the end
Key definitions

Homologous series: a family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which each member differs from the next by CH₂.

Functional group: the group of atoms responsible for the characteristic reactions of a compound.

2Naming (IUPAC nomenclature)

  1. Find the longest carbon chain containing the functional group. Its length gives the stem: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-.
  2. Add the suffix for the main functional group: -ane, -ene, -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid, -nitrile.
  3. Number the chain to give the functional group, then any substituents, the lowest numbers.
  4. Put prefixes for substituents in alphabetical order: bromo-, chloro-, methyl-. Use di- or tri- for repeats.
SeriesSuffix or prefixExample
alkene-enebut-2-ene
alcohol-olpropan-2-ol
halogenoalkanehalo- prefix2-chloro-2-methylpropane
aldehyde-alethanal
ketone-onebutanone
carboxylic acid-oic acidpropanoic acid
Worked example 1: Naming a branched compound

Name CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(Br)CH₃.

  1. The longest chain has 4 carbons, so the stem is butane.
  2. Number from the end that gives the substituents the lowest numbers: Br on C2 and CH₃ on C3.
  3. Put the prefixes in alphabetical order: bromo before methyl.

Answer: 2-bromo-3-methylbutane

3Reaction mechanisms

  • Curly arrows show the movement of a pair of electrons. An arrow starts from a lone pair or a bond, and ends at an atom or at the space where a new bond forms.
  • Heterolytic fission: both bonding electrons go to one atom, forming ions. Homolytic fission: one electron goes to each atom, forming radicals (species with an unpaired electron, written with a dot, for example Cl•).
  • A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor, for example OH⁻, CN⁻ or NH₃. An electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor, for example H⁺, NO₂⁺ or the δ+ end of Br₂.
  • Free-radical reactions are written with stages: initiation, propagation and termination.

4Isomerism

Key definitions

Structural isomers: compounds with the same molecular formula but a different structural formula.

Stereoisomers: compounds with the same structural formula but a different arrangement of atoms in space.

  • Chain isomers have different carbon skeletons, for example butane and methylpropane.
  • Position isomers have the functional group in different positions, for example propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol.
  • Functional group isomers have different functional groups, for example propanal and propanone, or ethanol and methoxymethane.
  • E/Z isomerism happens because rotation about a C=C bond is restricted, and each carbon of the C=C has two different groups attached.
  • CIP priority rules: on each carbon of the C=C, the attached atom with the higher atomic number has the higher priority. If the higher-priority groups are on the same side, the isomer is Z (zusammen); if they are on opposite sides, it is E (entgegen).
Worked example 2: E/Z naming

Is CH₃CH=CHCl with CH₃ and Cl on opposite sides of the double bond the E or Z isomer?

  1. Left-hand carbon: CH₃ (C, atomic number 6) beats H, so CH₃ has priority.
  2. Right-hand carbon: Cl (atomic number 17) beats H, so Cl has priority.
  3. The two priority groups are on opposite sides.

Answer: E-1-chloroprop-1-ene

Worked example 3: Counting structural isomers

Draw or name the structural isomers of C₄H₉Br.

  1. Straight chain: 1-bromobutane and 2-bromobutane.
  2. Branched chain: 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

Answer: There are four structural isomers. (2-bromobutane also has optical isomers.)

Common mistakes
  • Numbering a chain from the wrong end, or not listing substituent prefixes alphabetically.
  • Starting a curly arrow from an atom instead of from a lone pair or a bond.
  • Saying that any alkene shows E/Z isomerism. Each C of the C=C must carry two different groups, so but-1-ene does not.
Exam tips
  • In mechanism questions, marks are given for each curly arrow, each lone pair and each partial charge. Draw lone pairs on nucleophiles.
  • When you assign E/Z, write the atomic numbers on the diagram to show your working.
Summary
  • Formula types: empirical, molecular, general, structural, displayed and skeletal.
  • IUPAC: longest chain, lowest numbers, alphabetical prefixes.
  • Curly arrows show electron pairs; heterolytic fission gives ions and homolytic fission gives radicals.
  • Isomerism: structural (chain, position, functional group) or stereo (E/Z from restricted rotation, assigned using CIP priorities).
c-3-1.intro: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Before studying any reactions you need the language: how to name compounds, the different kinds of formula, how mechanisms are drawn, and the types of isomerism.

c-3-2.h:
1Fractional distillation of crude oil

  • Crude oil is a mixture of mainly alkanes. It is separated by fractional distillation, which relies on different boiling points.
  • The oil is heated and vaporised, then passed into a column that is hot at the bottom and cool at the top. Vapours rise until they reach a level cool enough to condense, and that fraction is collected there.
  • Long-chain alkanes have stronger van der Waals forces, so they boil higher and are collected near the bottom. Short chains (gases such as LPG, and petrol) come off at the top.

2Cracking

Key definitions

Cracking: breaking long-chain alkanes into shorter, more useful alkanes and alkenes by breaking C–C bonds.

Thermal crackingCatalytic cracking
conditionshigh temperature (up to about 1000 °C) and high pressure (up to 70 atm)slight pressure, high temperature (about 450 °C), zeolite catalyst
main productsa high percentage of alkenesmotor fuels and aromatic hydrocarbons
  • Why crack? There is more demand for short-chain fractions such as petrol, and alkenes are valuable feedstocks for polymers.
  • Example: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₈H₁₈ + 2C₂H₄.

3Combustion of alkanes

  • Complete combustion happens in plenty of oxygen: C₈H₁₈ + 12½O₂ → 8CO₂ + 9H₂O. Alkanes are good fuels because they release a lot of energy.
  • Incomplete combustion happens in limited oxygen. It produces CO (toxic, because it binds to haemoglobin) and carbon (soot), which causes breathing problems.
  • Pollutants from engines:
  • Unburned hydrocarbons and NOₓ form photochemical smog. NO forms because the high temperature in an engine lets N₂ and O₂ react.
  • SO₂ comes from sulfur impurities and causes acid rain.
  • CO₂ is a greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change.
  • Catalytic converters use Pt, Pd or Rh on a ceramic honeycomb: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂, and hydrocarbons + NO → CO₂ + N₂ + H₂O.
  • Flue gas desulfurisation removes SO₂ from power-station emissions using CaO or CaCO₃: CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃.
Worked example 1: Balancing a combustion equation

Write equations for the complete combustion of propane and for its incomplete combustion to carbon monoxide.

  1. Complete: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.
  2. Incomplete: C₃H₈ + 3½O₂ → 3CO + 4H₂O.

Answer: Less oxygen is needed for the incomplete combustion, which forms toxic CO.

4Chlorination of alkanes: free-radical substitution

In UV light, alkanes react with chlorine: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.

  1. Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl•. UV light breaks the Cl–Cl bond by homolytic fission.
  2. Propagation: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃, then •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•. The radical is regenerated, so this is a chain reaction.
  3. Termination: two radicals combine, for example Cl• + •CH₃ → CH₃Cl, or 2•CH₃ → C₂H₆, or 2Cl• → Cl₂.
  • Further substitution gives CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄. So the reaction gives a mixture of products and is not very useful for making one specific compound. An excess of methane favours CH₃Cl.
Worked example 2: Explaining a by-product

Explain why traces of ethane are found when methane reacts with chlorine.

  1. •CH₃ radicals form in the propagation stage.
  2. Two methyl radicals can combine in a termination step: •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆.

Answer: Ethane forms from a termination step between two methyl radicals.

Common mistakes
  • Writing the propagation steps so that they produce H• radicals. The first propagation step forms HCl and •CH₃.
  • Leaving out "UV light" as the condition for initiation.
  • Mixing up the conditions and products of thermal and catalytic cracking.
Exam tips
  • Learn the full chlorination mechanism, with the dots on the radicals, for any alkane. For example, ethane gives •C₂H₅.
  • For pollution questions, give the pollutant, its source, its effect, and how it is removed.
Summary
  • Fractional distillation separates crude oil by boiling point.
  • Cracking: thermal cracking (high T and P) gives alkenes; catalytic cracking (zeolite) gives fuels and aromatics.
  • Complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O. Incomplete combustion gives CO and C. Catalytic converters remove CO, NOₓ and hydrocarbons.
  • Free-radical substitution: initiation, propagation and termination in UV light, giving a mixture of products.
c-3-2.intro: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, obtained from crude oil. This topic covers fractional distillation, cracking, combustion and its pollutants, and free-radical substitution with chlorine.

c-3-3.h:
1The C–X bond

  • Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polar: C^{\delta+}–X^{\delta-}. The δ+ carbon is attacked by nucleophiles.
  • Reactivity depends on bond enthalpy, not on polarity. C–I is the weakest bond, so iodoalkanes react fastest, even though the C–I bond is the least polar. The order of reactivity is C–I > C–Br > C–Cl > C–F.
  • Comparing rates of hydrolysis. Warm each halogenoalkane with aqueous AgNO₃ in ethanol. Water acts as the nucleophile, and the halide ion released forms a precipitate. The yellow AgI precipitate appears first, then cream AgBr, then white AgCl.

2Nucleophilic substitution

A nucleophile (an electron-pair donor) replaces the halogen.

NucleophileConditionsProduct
OH⁻warm aqueous NaOH or KOH, under refluxalcohol
CN⁻KCN in ethanol and water, warmnitrile (the carbon chain gets one carbon longer)
NH₃excess concentrated ammonia in ethanol, heated under pressureprimary amine
  • Mechanism: the lone pair on the nucleophile attacks the δ+ C (curly arrow from the lone pair to C). The C–X bond breaks heterolytically (curly arrow from the bond to X), and X⁻ leaves.
  • With ammonia, two molecules of NH₃ are used: the second removes H⁺ from the intermediate. For example, CH₃CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br. Excess NH₃ reduces further substitution to secondary and tertiary amines.
  • With cyanide, bromoethane gives propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN.

3Elimination

  • With hot KOH in ethanol (no water), OH⁻ acts as a base. It removes an H⁺ from the carbon next to the C–X carbon, forming an alkene: CH₃CHBrCH₃ + KOH → CH₂=CHCH₃ + KBr + H₂O.
  • Mechanism: the OH⁻ lone pair attacks an H on the adjacent carbon. That C–H bond's electrons move to form the C=C, and the C–Br bond breaks to release Br⁻.
  • Unsymmetrical halogenoalkanes can give more than one alkene, including E/Z isomers. For example, 2-bromobutane gives but-1-ene, E-but-2-ene and Z-but-2-ene.

4Substitution or elimination?

Favours substitutionFavours elimination
aqueous solventethanol solvent
warmhot
primary halogenoalkanestertiary halogenoalkanes
Worked example 1: Predicting the product

Name the organic product when 1-bromopropane is (a) warmed with aqueous NaOH and (b) heated with KOH in ethanol.

  1. (a) Aqueous OH⁻ acts as a nucleophile and replaces Br, giving an alcohol.
  2. (b) KOH in ethanol acts as a base and removes HBr, giving an alkene.

Answer: (a) propan-1-ol (b) propene

Worked example 2: Explaining relative rates

Explain why 1-iodobutane is hydrolysed faster than 1-chlorobutane, even though the C–Cl bond is more polar.

  1. The rate depends on how easily the C–X bond breaks.
  2. The C–I bond enthalpy (about 228 kJ mol⁻¹) is much lower than that of C–Cl (about 346 kJ mol⁻¹).

Answer: The weaker C–I bond breaks more easily, so the reaction is faster. Bond enthalpy matters more than polarity.

5Ozone depletion

  • Ozone in the upper atmosphere absorbs harmful UV radiation: O₃ ⇌ O₂ + O. UV causes skin cancer and cataracts.
  • CFCs were used in aerosols and refrigerants. In the upper atmosphere, UV breaks their C–Cl bonds to release Cl• radicals, which catalyse the breakdown of ozone:
\text{Cl}\bullet+\text{O}_3\rightarrow\text{ClO}\bullet+\text{O}_2
\text{ClO}\bullet+\text{O}_3\rightarrow\text{Cl}\bullet+2\text{O}_2
  • Overall: 2O₃ → 3O₂. One Cl• radical can destroy thousands of ozone molecules because it is regenerated.
  • NO• radicals from aircraft and lightning act in the same way.
  • Chemists' role. Research confirmed the link between CFCs and the ozone hole, and legislation (the Montreal Protocol) banned CFCs. Chemists developed alternatives such as HFCs, which contain no chlorine.
Common mistakes
  • Saying that C–F is the most reactive "because it is most polar". Bond enthalpy controls the rate.
  • Using aqueous KOH for elimination. Use ethanolic KOH, heated.
  • Forgetting that the Cl• radical is regenerated, which is why it acts as a catalyst.
Exam tips
  • In mechanisms, show the δ+ and δ− charges, the lone pair on the nucleophile, both curly arrows, and the halide ion as a product.
  • In elimination, the first curly arrow goes from OH⁻ to an H on the adjacent carbon, not to the C–X carbon.
Summary
  • The C–X bond is polar, but bond enthalpy controls reactivity: iodoalkanes react fastest.
  • Nucleophilic substitution with OH⁻(aq) gives an alcohol, with CN⁻ a nitrile, and with excess NH₃ an amine.
  • Elimination with hot ethanolic KOH gives alkenes.
  • Cl• from CFCs catalyses the breakdown of O₃. CFCs have been replaced by HFCs.
c-3-3.intro: Halogenoalkanes contain a polar C–X bond, which makes them open to attack by nucleophiles and bases. This topic covers nucleophilic substitution, elimination, how the two compete, and how CFCs damage the ozone layer.

c-3-4.h:
1Structure, bonding and reactivity

  • General formula CₙH₂ₙ for alkenes with one C=C.
  • The C=C is made of a σ bond and a π bond. The π bond is formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals, above and below the plane of the molecule.
  • The π bond is a region of high electron density, so it attracts electrophiles. It is weaker than the σ bond, which is why alkenes are more reactive than alkanes.
  • Rotation about the C=C is restricted, which gives E/Z isomerism.

2Electrophilic addition

ReagentConditionsProduct
HBrroom temperaturebromoalkane
Br₂room temperature, in an organic solvent or as bromine waterdibromoalkane
conc. H₂SO₄, then watercold acid, then warm with wateralcohol (H₂SO₄ is a catalyst overall)

Mechanism with HBr:

  1. The π electrons attack the δ+ H of H–Br. The H–Br bond breaks heterolytically, with both electrons going to Br.
  2. This forms a carbocation and a Br⁻ ion.
  3. The lone pair on Br⁻ attacks the positive carbon.

With Br₂: the bromine molecule is non-polar, but as it approaches the electron-rich C=C its electrons are repelled, inducing a dipole (Br^{\delta+}–Br^{\delta-}). After that the mechanism is the same as for HBr.

  • Test for unsaturation. Shake with bromine water. It changes from orange to colourless with an alkene. With an alkane it stays orange.

3Unsymmetrical alkenes: major and minor products

  • Adding HBr to propene can form two carbocations. The secondary carbocation, CH₃C⁺HCH₃, is more stable than the primary one, CH₃CH₂C⁺H₂.
  • Stability order: tertiary > secondary > primary. Alkyl groups have a positive inductive effect: they push electrons towards the positive carbon and spread out its charge.
  • The more stable carbocation forms faster, so 2-bromopropane is the major product and 1-bromopropane the minor one.
Worked example 1: Major product

Name the major product of the reaction of 2-methylpropene with HBr, and explain why it forms.

  1. The H can add to either carbon of the C=C. If it adds to the CH₂ end, a tertiary carbocation, (CH₃)₃C⁺, forms.
  2. A tertiary carbocation is the most stable, because three alkyl groups donate electron density.

Answer: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, formed through the more stable tertiary carbocation.

Worked example 2: Addition of sulfuric acid

Ethene reacts with cold concentrated H₂SO₄, and the product is warmed with water. Name the intermediate and the final product.

  1. Electrophilic addition of H₂SO₄ gives ethyl hydrogensulfate, CH₃CH₂OSO₂OH.
  2. Hydrolysis with water gives ethanol and re-forms H₂SO₄.

Answer: Ethyl hydrogensulfate, then ethanol.

4Addition polymers

  • Alkenes join together through their C=C bonds to make addition polymers. Poly(ethene) is made from ethene, and poly(propene) from propene.
  • To draw a repeating unit, open the C=C, put the substituents on the two carbons, and add extension bonds through square brackets with n.
Worked example 3: Drawing a repeating unit

Draw the repeating unit of poly(chloroethene) (PVC).

  1. The monomer is CH₂=CHCl.
  2. Open the double bond and keep the Cl on one carbon.

Answer: –[CH₂–CHCl]ₙ–

  • Properties. Poly(alkenes) are saturated, with only strong C–C and C–H bonds, so they are unreactive and not biodegradable.
  • PVC is rigid. Adding a plasticiser pushes the polymer chains apart, weakening the forces between them, so the chains slide and the material becomes flexible. Rigid PVC is used for window frames and pipes; flexible PVC for cable insulation.
Common mistakes
  • Drawing the first curly arrow from the H of HBr to the C=C. It starts from the double bond and goes to the H.
  • Saying that the major product forms because "the Br goes to the carbon with fewer H". Explain using carbocation stability.
  • Drawing a polymer repeating unit with a C=C still in it.
Exam tips
  • In the Br₂ mechanism, show the induced dipole on Br₂ and the curly arrow from the Br–Br bond to Br^{\delta-}.
  • For "explain the major product", draw both carbocations, label them primary, secondary or tertiary, and state their relative stability.
Summary
  • The C=C is a σ bond plus a π bond. The π bond is electron-rich and attacks electrophiles.
  • Electrophilic addition of HBr, Br₂ and H₂SO₄ goes through a carbocation. Bromine water decolourises.
  • Carbocation stability is tertiary > secondary > primary, which decides the major product.
  • Addition polymers are unreactive. Plasticisers make PVC flexible.
c-3-4.intro: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with a C=C double bond. The electron-rich double bond makes them react by electrophilic addition. This topic also covers addition polymers.
secs: Unsymmetrical alkenes: major and minor products

c-3-5.h:
1Classifying alcohols

TypeCarbon bonded to OH hasExample
primary (1°)one alkyl grouppropan-1-ol
secondary (2°)two alkyl groupspropan-2-ol
tertiary (3°)three alkyl groups2-methylpropan-2-ol

2Production of ethanol

1. Fermentation of glucose

\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\rightarrow2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}+2\text{CO}_2
  • Conditions: yeast enzymes, anaerobic, about 35 °C, in aqueous solution. The ethanol is separated by fractional distillation.
  • The temperature is a compromise. It must be warm enough for a reasonable rate, but not so hot that the enzymes are denatured.
  • Advantages: it uses renewable sugar crops and needs little energy. Disadvantages: it is slow, it is a batch process, the ethanol is impure, and it uses farmland.

2. Hydration of ethene

\text{C}_2\text{H}_4(\text{g})+\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{g})\rightleftharpoons\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(\text{g})
  • Conditions: phosphoric acid catalyst, 300 °C, 6–7 MPa. It is fast, continuous and gives pure ethanol, but it uses non-renewable crude oil.

3Biofuels and carbon neutrality

Key definitions

Carbon neutral: an activity with no net annual emission of carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.

  • Bioethanol is sometimes called carbon neutral. Photosynthesis takes in 6CO₂, then fermentation releases 2CO₂ and combustion releases 4CO₂, so these cancel.
  • In practice it is not fully carbon neutral, because fossil fuels are burned for farming, transport, making fertiliser and distillation.

4Oxidation of alcohols

The oxidising agent is acidified potassium dichromate(VI), K₂Cr₂O₇ with H₂SO₄. It changes from orange to green as Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to Cr³⁺. The oxygen from the oxidising agent is written [O].

AlcoholConditionsProduct
primarydistil immediately, so the aldehyde is removed as it formsaldehyde
primaryheat under reflux with excess oxidising agentcarboxylic acid
secondaryheat under refluxketone
tertiary—not oxidised; the solution stays orange
Key equations
\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}+[\text{O}]\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}+\text{H}_2\text{O}
\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}+2[\text{O}]\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}+\text{H}_2\text{O}
\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3+[\text{O}]\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3+\text{H}_2\text{O}
  • Distinguishing an aldehyde from a ketone. Tollens' reagent ([Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺), warmed, gives a silver mirror with an aldehyde. Fehling's solution (or Benedict's), warmed, changes from blue to a brick-red precipitate (Cu₂O) with an aldehyde. Ketones give no change in either test.
Worked example 1: Predicting oxidation products

Butan-2-ol is heated under reflux with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. Name the product, state the colour change, and write the equation.

  1. Butan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol, so it is oxidised to a ketone.
  2. The dichromate is reduced from orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ to green Cr³⁺.
  3. CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ + [O] → CH₃COCH₂CH₃ + H₂O.

Answer: Butanone; orange to green.

5Dehydration (elimination)

  • Heating an alcohol with concentrated H₃PO₄ or H₂SO₄ (acid catalyst) eliminates water to form an alkene: CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O.
  • Mechanism: the OH is protonated by H⁺ and leaves as H₂O, giving a carbocation. Then an H⁺ is lost from the adjacent carbon to form the C=C.
  • This gives a route to polymers from renewable sources (bio-ethanol to ethene to poly(ethene)) without using crude oil.
  • Unsymmetrical alcohols can give a mixture of alkenes, including E/Z isomers. For example, butan-2-ol gives but-1-ene and E- and Z-but-2-ene.
Worked example 2: Products of dehydration

Give the structures of all the alkenes formed when pentan-2-ol is dehydrated.

  1. The H can be lost from C1 or from C3.
  2. Loss from C1 gives pent-1-ene. Loss from C3 gives pent-2-ene, which has E and Z forms.

Answer: pent-1-ene, E-pent-2-ene and Z-pent-2-ene

Required practical 5: distillation of a product
  • To prepare an aldehyde, add acidified dichromate dropwise to warm ethanol and distil immediately. Keep the receiver cool in ice; ethanal boils at 21 °C.
  • To prepare a carboxylic acid, heat under reflux. The vapours condense and drip back, so the volatile aldehyde intermediate is fully oxidised. Then distil off the product.
  • Add anti-bumping granules and heat with a water bath or an electric heater. Never seal the apparatus.
Common mistakes
  • Saying that tertiary alcohols are oxidised "to ketones". They are not oxidised, because there is no H on the C–OH carbon.
  • Mixing up distillation (to collect the aldehyde) with reflux (to make the acid).
  • Saying that bioethanol is fully carbon neutral without mentioning the energy used in production.
Exam tips
  • Use [O] in oxidation equations and balance with H₂O. Examiners accept this for organic oxidation.
  • In "compare the two methods" questions, cover rate, purity, the type of process, the raw materials (renewable or not) and the energy needed.
Summary
  • Ethanol is made by fermentation (yeast, 35 °C, anaerobic) or by hydration of ethene (H₃PO₄, 300 °C, 6–7 MPa).
  • Bioethanol is not fully carbon neutral in practice.
  • Oxidation with H⁺/Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange to green): primary gives an aldehyde (distil) or a carboxylic acid (reflux); secondary gives a ketone; tertiary has no reaction.
  • Tollens' and Fehling's tests identify aldehydes. Dehydration with a concentrated acid gives alkenes.
c-3-5.intro: Alcohols contain the –OH group. This topic covers how ethanol is made (fermentation and hydration), the debate over biofuels, the oxidation of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols, and dehydration to alkenes.

c-3-6.h:
1Test-tube tests for functional groups

Functional groupTestPositive result
alkene (C=C)shake with bromine waterorange → colourless
primary or secondary alcoholwarm with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇orange → green
tertiary alcoholwarm with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇stays orange
aldehydewarm with Tollens' reagentsilver mirror
aldehydewarm with Fehling's solutionblue solution → brick-red precipitate
carboxylic acidadd NaHCO₃ or Na₂CO₃effervescence; the CO₂ turns limewater milky
halogenoalkanewarm with NaOH(aq), acidify with HNO₃, then add AgNO₃white, cream or yellow precipitate
Required practical 6: identifying functional groups
  • Use small volumes in test tubes and warm in a water bath, never over a flame, because many organic compounds are flammable. Tollens' reagent must be freshly prepared.
  • Do the tests in a logical order. For example, test with NaHCO₃ for an acid first, then Tollens' for an aldehyde, then dichromate to distinguish primary/secondary alcohols from tertiary ones.

2High-resolution mass spectrometry

  • High-resolution mass spectrometry measures m/z to 4 or 5 decimal places. This distinguishes compounds that have the same integer M_r but different molecular formulae.
  • Uses precise atomic masses: ¹H = 1.0078, ¹²C = 12.0000, ¹⁶O = 15.9949, ¹⁴N = 14.0031.
Worked example 1: Choosing a molecular formula

A compound has a molecular ion at m/z = 44.0262. Is it CO₂, C₃H₈ or C₂H₄O?

  1. CO₂ = 12.0000 + 2(15.9949) = 43.9898.
  2. C₃H₈ = 3(12.0000) + 8(1.0078) = 44.0624.
  3. C₂H₄O = 24.0000 + 4.0312 + 15.9949 = 44.0261.

Answer: C₂H₄O, whose precise mass matches 44.0262.

3Infrared spectroscopy

  • Covalent bonds absorb IR radiation at characteristic frequencies, which makes them vibrate more (stretch or bend). An IR spectrum plots % transmittance against wavenumber (cm⁻¹); absorptions appear as dips.
BondWavenumber (cm⁻¹)Appearance
O–H (alcohols)3230–3550broad
O–H (carboxylic acids)2500–3000very broad
N–H (amines)3300–3500medium
C–H2850–3300sharp
C=O1680–1750strong, sharp
C=C1620–1680medium
C–O1000–1300strong
  • The fingerprint region (below about 1500 cm⁻¹) is unique to each compound. Comparing it with a database spectrum identifies the compound exactly. It also shows impurities, which give extra peaks.
  • Greenhouse gases. CO₂, CH₄ and H₂O absorb IR radiation emitted by the Earth's surface, which leads to global warming.
Worked example 2: Interpreting an IR spectrum

A compound C₃H₆O₂ shows a very broad absorption at 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ and a strong peak at 1715 cm⁻¹. Identify it.

  1. A very broad absorption at 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ is the O–H of a carboxylic acid.
  2. The peak at 1715 cm⁻¹ is a C=O.
  3. Three carbons with COOH gives propanoic acid.

Answer: Propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH

Worked example 3: Following a reaction by IR

How could IR show that propan-1-ol has been fully oxidised to propanal?

  1. Propan-1-ol has a broad O–H absorption at 3230–3550 cm⁻¹.
  2. Propanal has a C=O absorption at about 1720 cm⁻¹ and no O–H.

Answer: The broad O–H peak disappears and a strong C=O peak appears.

Common mistakes
  • Mixing up the two O–H ranges: 3230–3550 cm⁻¹ for alcohols and 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ for acids.
  • Trying to read individual peaks in the fingerprint region. You compare its overall pattern with known spectra.
  • Saying that Fehling's solution gives a "silver mirror". That is Tollens' reagent; Fehling's gives a brick-red precipitate.
Exam tips
  • The data booklet gives the IR table. Quote the bond and its wavenumber range in your answer.
  • In combined-technique questions, use the molecular ion for M_r, IR for the functional groups, and the tests for confirmation.
Summary
  • Tests: bromine water for C=C, dichromate for 1°/2° alcohols, Tollens' or Fehling's for aldehydes, NaHCO₃ for acids.
  • High-resolution MS gives precise masses, which identify the molecular formula.
  • IR: bonds absorb at characteristic wavenumbers. The fingerprint region identifies the compound. Greenhouse gases absorb IR.
c-3-6.intro: How do chemists find out what an unknown organic compound is? This topic covers simple test-tube tests for functional groups, high-resolution mass spectrometry for molecular formulae, and infrared spectroscopy for identifying bonds.

c-1-8.h:
1Enthalpy definitions for Born–Haber cycles

Key definitions

Enthalpy of atomisation, ΔatH: the enthalpy change when 1 mol of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state. Example: ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g).

First ionisation energy: the enthalpy change to remove 1 mol of electrons from 1 mol of gaseous atoms. Example: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻.

First electron affinity: the enthalpy change when 1 mol of gaseous atoms each gains an electron, forming 1 mol of gaseous 1− ions. Example: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g). It is exothermic.

Second electron affinity: O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g). It is endothermic, because an electron is being added to a negative ion, which repels it.

Lattice enthalpy of formation: the enthalpy change when 1 mol of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions (exothermic). Lattice dissociation is the reverse (endothermic, same magnitude).

Enthalpy of hydration, ΔhydH: the enthalpy change when 1 mol of gaseous ions dissolves in water to form 1 mol of aqueous ions (exothermic).

Enthalpy of solution, ΔsolH: the enthalpy change when 1 mol of an ionic solid dissolves in enough water that the ions are separated and do not interact.

2Born–Haber cycles

A Born–Haber cycle uses Hess's law to find a lattice enthalpy, which can't be measured directly. Going round the cycle from the elements: ΔfH = ΔatH(metal) + IE(s) + ΔatH(non-metal) + EA(s) + LE(formation).

Worked example 1: Lattice enthalpy of MgCl₂

Use the following data (kJ mol⁻¹) to find the lattice enthalpy of formation of MgCl₂: ΔfH −642; ΔatH(Mg) +148; 1st IE +738; 2nd IE +1451; ΔatH(Cl) +121 (per mole of Cl atoms); EA(Cl) −349.

  1. Add up the steps from the elements to the gaseous ions. Two Cl atoms are needed: 148 + 738 + 1451 + 2(121) + 2(−349) = +1881.
  2. Then ΔfH = 1881 + LE, so LE = −642 − 1881.

Answer: LE(formation) = −2523 kJ mol⁻¹

  • Lattice enthalpy becomes more exothermic for smaller ions and higher charges, because the electrostatic attraction is stronger. For example, MgO is far more exothermic than NaCl.
  • Perfect ionic model comparison. A theoretical lattice enthalpy assumes perfectly spherical ions with only ionic bonding. If the Born–Haber (experimental) value is more exothermic than the theoretical value, the compound has some covalent character. This happens when a small, highly charged cation polarises a large anion, as in AgI or MgI₂.

3Dissolving

\Delta_{sol}H=\Delta_{LE}H(\text{dissociation})+\sum\Delta_{hyd}H
  • Hydration enthalpies are more exothermic for smaller ions with higher charges, because they attract the water molecules' dipoles more strongly. The δ− O faces cations; the δ+ H faces anions.
Worked example 2: Enthalpy of solution

Find ΔsolH of KCl. Lattice dissociation +711; ΔhydH K⁺ −322; ΔhydH Cl⁻ −364 kJ mol⁻¹.

  1. ΔsolH = 711 + (−322) + (−364).

Answer: +25 kJ mol⁻¹ (endothermic, so the solution gets colder)

4Entropy

Key definitions

Entropy, S: a measure of the number of ways that particles, and their energy, can be arranged. A higher S means more disorder. Units: J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

  • S increases from solid to liquid to gas, and when the number of gas moles increases. For a perfect crystal at 0 K, S = 0.
\Delta S=\sum S(\text{products})-\sum S(\text{reactants})

5Gibbs free energy and feasibility

\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S
  • A reaction is feasible (thermodynamically possible) when ΔG ≤ 0.
  • Convert ΔS to kJ (divide by 1000) before combining it with ΔH in kJ.
  • The temperature at which a reaction becomes feasible is found by setting ΔG = 0: T=\frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}.
  • A graph of ΔG against T is a straight line with gradient −ΔS and intercept ΔH.
ΔHΔSFeasible?
−+at all temperatures
+−never
−−at low T (below ΔH/ΔS)
++at high T (above ΔH/ΔS)
Worked example 3: Minimum temperature for feasibility

CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Find the lowest temperature at which it is feasible.

  1. Convert: ΔS = 0.161 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
  2. Set ΔG = 0: T = 178 / 0.161.

Answer: T ≈ 1106 K (about 833 °C)

  • A feasible reaction may still not happen, because the activation energy can be so high that the rate is negligible. Diamond turning into graphite is an example.
Common mistakes
  • Mixing J and kJ in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
  • Forgetting to double the atomisation and electron affinity terms when there are two halide ions (as in MgCl₂).
  • Mixing up the signs of formation and dissociation lattice enthalpies. State which one you mean.
  • Using °C instead of K.
Exam tips
  • Write every Born–Haber definition with state symbols and "1 mol". Examiners often ask for one definition plus an equation.
  • When you explain lattice enthalpy trends, always mention ionic radius, ionic charge and the strength of electrostatic attraction.
Summary
  • Born–Haber: ΔfH = the sum of atomisation, IE, EA and LE. Use it to find LE.
  • LE is more exothermic for small, highly charged ions. An experimental value more exothermic than theoretical means covalent character.
  • ΔsolH = LE(dissociation) + ΣΔhydH.
  • ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. The reaction is feasible when ΔG ≤ 0, and T = ΔH/ΔS at the switch-over.
c-1-8.intro: Thermodynamics explains why ionic lattices form and whether a reaction is feasible at all. This topic covers Born–Haber cycles, lattice, hydration and solution enthalpies, perfect ionic model comparisons, entropy and Gibbs free energy.

c-1-9.h:
1Rate equations and orders

\text{rate}=k[\text{A}]^m[\text{B}]^n
Key definitions

Order with respect to a reactant: the power of its concentration in the rate equation (0, 1 or 2 at A-level).

Overall order: the sum of the individual orders, m + n.

Rate constant, k: the constant of proportionality in the rate equation. It is fixed at a given temperature.

  • Orders can only be found by experiment. They are not taken from the balanced equation.
  • Zero order: changing the concentration has no effect on the rate. First order: doubling the concentration doubles the rate. Second order: doubling the concentration ×4 the rate.
Key equations
Overall orderUnits of k
0mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
1s⁻¹
2mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹
3mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹
Worked example 1: Finding orders from initial rates

For A + B → products. Experiment 1: [A] = 0.10, [B] = 0.10, rate = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴. Experiment 2: [A] = 0.20, [B] = 0.10, rate = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴. Experiment 3: [A] = 0.10, [B] = 0.30, rate = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ (concentrations in mol dm⁻³, rates in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹). Find the rate equation and k.

  1. From 1 to 2, [A] ×2 and the rate ×4, so the order in A is 2.
  2. From 1 to 3, [B] ×3 and the rate ×3, so the order in B is 1.
  3. The rate equation is rate = k[A]²[B]. Using experiment 1: k=\frac{2.0\times10^{-4}}{(0.10)^2(0.10)}=0.20.

Answer: rate = k[A]²[B]; k = 0.20 mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹

2Temperature and the Arrhenius equation

k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}
\ln k=-\frac{E_a}{R}\cdot\frac1T+\ln A
  • A rise in temperature increases k, so the rate increases. Concentrations are unchanged.
  • A plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with gradient -E_a/R and intercept \ln A. Use R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and T in K.
Worked example 2: Activation energy from a graph

A plot of ln k against 1/T has gradient −6500 K. Calculate Eₐ.

  1. Gradient = −Eₐ/R, so Eₐ = 6500 × 8.31.
  2. That is 54 015 J mol⁻¹.

Answer: Eₐ ≈ 54 kJ mol⁻¹

3Finding orders from graphs

  • Concentration–time graph. Zero order gives a straight line with a constant gradient. First order gives a curve with a constant half-life. Second order gives a curve whose half-life increases.
  • Rate–concentration graph. Zero order is a horizontal line. First order is a straight line through the origin. Second order is a curve (a parabola). A plot of rate against [A]² is a straight line for second order.
  • The rate at a given time is the gradient of the tangent to the concentration–time curve.
  • For first order, k=\frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}.
Required practical 7: measuring rate
  • Initial rate (clock) method. In the iodine clock, a fixed small amount of thiosulfate is added, so the blue-black colour appears when a fixed amount of iodine has formed. The initial rate is proportional to 1/time. Repeat with different starting concentrations of one reactant at a time.
  • Continuous monitoring. Follow one reaction over time, for example by colorimetry, gas volume or titrating samples that have been quenched. Plot concentration against time and draw tangents.

4Rate-determining step

Key definitions

Rate-determining step (RDS): the slowest step in a mechanism. It controls the overall rate.

  • Species that appear in the rate equation, and in the right numbers, are involved in the RDS or in steps before it. A zero-order reactant appears only after the RDS.
  • Example: for 2-bromo-2-methylpropane + OH⁻, rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr]. So the RDS involves only the halogenoalkane, which ionises to a carbocation first; OH⁻ attacks afterwards.
Common mistakes
  • Taking the orders from the coefficients in the balanced equation.
  • Forgetting to convert °C to K, or Eₐ from J to kJ.
  • Saying that a catalyst or a higher temperature changes the orders. Temperature changes k, not the orders.
Exam tips
  • In initial-rate tables, compare two experiments where only one concentration changes. If no such pair exists, use one known order to find the other.
  • Always give units for k. Derive them by rearranging k = rate ÷ (concentration terms).
Summary
  • rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, with orders from experiment only.
  • The units of k depend on the overall order. k increases with temperature: ln k = −Eₐ/RT + ln A.
  • Graph shapes identify the order. First order has a constant half-life.
  • The rate equation shows which species are in the rate-determining step.
c-1-9.intro: Rate equations show exactly how the rate depends on each concentration. This topic covers orders, the rate constant and its units, the Arrhenius equation, finding orders from experiments and graphs, and linking the rate equation to the rate-determining step.

c-1-10.h:
1Mole fraction and partial pressure

Key definitions

Mole fraction, x: the number of moles of a gas divided by the total number of moles of gas.

Partial pressure, p: the pressure a gas would exert if it alone occupied the whole volume. It equals mole fraction × total pressure.

Key equations
x_A=\frac{n_A}{n_{total}}
p_A=x_A\times P_{total}
\sum p=P_{total}
  • The mole fractions of all the gases add up to 1.

2The equilibrium constant Kp

For a\text{A(g)}+b\text{B(g)}\rightleftharpoons c\text{C(g)}+d\text{D(g)}:

K_p=\frac{(p_C)^c(p_D)^d}{(p_A)^a(p_B)^b}
  • Only gases are included. Kp is for homogeneous gas equilibria. Use round brackets or p, not square brackets.
  • Units: substitute kPa (or Pa or atm) for each term and cancel.
Worked example 1: Calculating Kp

For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), 1.00 mol of N₂O₄ is heated in a sealed container until 0.40 mol has dissociated. The total pressure is 150 kPa. Calculate Kp.

  1. Equilibrium moles: N₂O₄ is 1.00-0.40=0.60; NO₂ is 2\times0.40=0.80. The total is 1.40.
  2. Mole fractions: N₂O₄ =0.60/1.40=0.429; NO₂ =0.80/1.40=0.571.
  3. Partial pressures: N₂O₄ =64.3 kPa; NO₂ =85.7 kPa.
  4. K_p=\frac{85.7^2}{64.3}=114.

Answer: Kp ≈ 114 kPa

Worked example 2: Using Kp to find a partial pressure

For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), Kp = 50 at a certain temperature. At equilibrium p(H₂) = p(I₂) = 20 kPa. Find p(HI).

  1. 50=\frac{p_{HI}^2}{20\times20}, so p_{HI}^2=20000.
  2. p_{HI}=\sqrt{20000}.

Answer: p(HI) ≈ 141 kPa (Kp has no units here)

3Homogeneous systems and links to Kc

  • A homogeneous equilibrium has all species in the same phase (here, all gases). Kp is used for these systems at A-level.
  • Kp and Kc describe the same equilibrium. Kp uses partial pressures because, for gases, pressure is easy to measure and is proportional to concentration at a fixed temperature (p=\frac{n}{V}RT).
  • The more product there is at equilibrium, the larger Kp. A value of Kp much greater than 1 means the equilibrium lies well to the right.
Worked example 3: Partial pressures from a percentage

The Haber process gives an equilibrium mixture of 15% NH₃, 21% N₂ and 64% H₂ by moles at a total pressure of 20 000 kPa. Write the expression for Kp and calculate it.

  1. K_p=\frac{p_{NH_3}^2}{p_{N_2}\,p_{H_2}^3}
  2. Partial pressures: NH₃ =0.15\times20000=3000 kPa; N₂ =4200 kPa; H₂ =12800 kPa.
  3. K_p=\frac{3000^2}{4200\times12800^3}=\frac{9.0\times10^6}{8.81\times10^{15}}=1.0\times10^{-9}.
  4. Units: \frac{\text{kPa}^2}{\text{kPa}^4}=\text{kPa}^{-2}.

Answer: Kp ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ kPa⁻²

4Effect of changing conditions

  • Temperature is the only factor that changes Kp. If the forward reaction is exothermic, increasing the temperature decreases Kp, and the equilibrium shifts left to restore the ratio. If it is endothermic, Kp increases.
  • Changing the total pressure changes the partial pressures, but Kp stays the same. The equilibrium position shifts (Le Chatelier) until the expression equals Kp again.
  • Example: for N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ (endothermic forward), heating increases Kp, so the mixture becomes browner because there is more NO₂. Increasing the pressure moves the equilibrium to the left (fewer gas moles), but Kp is unchanged.
  • A catalyst has no effect on Kp or the equilibrium position; equilibrium is only reached faster.
Common mistakes
  • Including solids or liquids in Kp.
  • Forgetting that the dissociation of one mole of N₂O₄ makes two moles of NO₂ when you calculate the equilibrium moles.
  • Using the initial total moles instead of the equilibrium total to find mole fractions.
Exam tips
  • Set up a table with rows for initial moles, change, equilibrium moles, mole fraction and partial pressure. It keeps the method marks safe.
  • Check that the partial pressures add up to the total pressure.
Summary
  • Mole fraction = n/n(total). Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure.
  • Kp uses partial pressures of gases only. Find the units by cancelling.
  • Only temperature changes Kp. Pressure and catalysts do not.
c-1-10.intro: For reactions between gases it is natural to use pressures instead of concentrations. This topic covers mole fractions, partial pressures, writing Kp expressions, calculating Kp and its units, and how conditions affect Kp.
secs: Homogeneous systems and links to Kc

c-1-11.h:
1Half-cells and electrode potentials

  • A half-cell is an element in contact with a solution of its ions, for example Zn in Zn²⁺(aq). It can also be two ions of the same element with a platinum electrode, for example Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ with Pt.
  • Two half-cells are joined by a wire (which carries electrons) and a salt bridge (filter paper soaked in KNO₃(aq), which carries ions and completes the circuit without reacting).
  • Platinum is used when there is no solid metal in the half-cell, because it is inert and conducts.
Key definitions

Standard electrode potential, E⦵: the emf of a half-cell measured against the standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions: 298 K, 100 kPa, and 1.00 mol dm⁻³ solutions.

2Cell notation and E°cell

  • Conventional representation. Write the more negative electrode on the left, oxidised species next to the salt bridge: Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s). A single line is a phase boundary; a double line is the salt bridge. Pt goes on the outside, for example Pt | Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺.
E^\ominus_{cell}=E^\ominus_{right}-E^\ominus_{left}=E^\ominus_{(+)}-E^\ominus_{(-)}
  • The more negative electrode is where oxidation happens; electrons flow from it through the wire to the more positive electrode.
Worked example 1: Calculating E°cell and writing the reaction

E⦵ values: Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V; Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V. Find E⦵cell and write the overall equation.

  1. Ag⁺/Ag is more positive, so it is the right-hand (positive) electrode, where Ag⁺ is reduced. Zn is oxidised.
  2. E⦵cell = +0.80 − (−0.76) = +1.56 V.
  3. Combine the half-equations with equal electrons: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ and 2Ag⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2Ag.

Answer: E⦵cell = +1.56 V; Zn + 2Ag⁺ → Zn²⁺ + 2Ag

3The electrochemical series and feasibility

  • In a list of half-equations written as reductions and ordered by E⦵: the more positive E⦵, the better the oxidising agent (the species on the left, such as F₂ or Cl₂). The more negative E⦵, the better the reducing agent (the species on the right, such as Li or Zn).
  • A reaction is feasible if E⦵cell is positive. That is the case when the oxidising agent's half-cell has a more positive E⦵ than the reducing agent's.
  • Feasible reactions may still be slow (high activation energy). Non-standard concentrations also change the actual emf.
Worked example 2: Predicting feasibility

Will acidified MnO₄⁻ (E⦵ = +1.51 V) oxidise Cl⁻ to Cl₂ (Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V)?

  1. MnO₄⁻ is reduced and Cl⁻ is oxidised.
  2. E⦵cell = 1.51 − 1.36 = +0.15 V, which is positive.

Answer: Yes, it is feasible. (This is why KMnO₄ titrations use H₂SO₄, not HCl.)

Required practical 8: measuring the emf of a cell
  • Clean the metal electrodes with emery paper. Make up a salt bridge from filter paper soaked in saturated KNO₃. Connect a high-resistance voltmeter, so almost no current flows and you measure the emf.
  • Use 1.00 mol dm⁻³ solutions at 298 K if you want standard values.

4Commercial cells

  • Non-rechargeable cells (for example alkaline zinc–manganese dioxide cells) are thrown away once the reactants are used up.
  • Rechargeable cells have reactions that can be reversed by applying a current. In the lithium-ion cell, the positive electrode reaction on discharge is Li⁺ + CoO₂ + e⁻ → Li⁺[CoO₂]⁻ and the negative electrode reaction is Li → Li⁺ + e⁻. These are reversed when the cell is charged. Lithium-ion cells are used in phones and laptops. You may be given data for other cells and asked to work out their electrode reactions.
  • Fuel cells are supplied continuously with fuel and oxygen, and are never recharged. In the alkaline hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell:
\text{negative: } \text{H}_2+2\text{OH}^-\rightarrow2\text{H}_2\text{O}+2\text{e}^-\quad(E^\ominus=-0.83\text{ V})
\text{positive: } \text{O}_2+2\text{H}_2\text{O}+4\text{e}^-\rightarrow4\text{OH}^-\quad(E^\ominus=+0.40\text{ V})
  • The overall reaction is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, with E⦵cell = 1.23 V.
  • Benefits and risks. Fuel cells produce only water at the point of use and are more efficient than combustion. However, hydrogen is flammable and hard to store, and it is often made using fossil fuels. Cells in general contain toxic or flammable chemicals and need to be recycled safely.
Common mistakes
  • Subtracting the potentials the wrong way round. Use right − left, or positive − negative. A feasible cell has a positive E⦵cell.
  • Saying the salt bridge carries electrons. It carries ions; electrons go through the wire.
  • Forgetting that changing the stoichiometric coefficients does not change E⦵ values.
Exam tips
  • For "which is the strongest oxidising agent?", look for the most positive E⦵ and choose the species on the left of that half-equation.
  • When you draw a cell, label the salt bridge, the high-resistance voltmeter, the electrodes, the solutions (1.00 mol dm⁻³) and the temperature (298 K).
Summary
  • E⦵ is measured against the SHE (0.00 V) at 298 K, 100 kPa and 1.00 mol dm⁻³.
  • E⦵cell = E⦵(right) − E⦵(left). The more negative electrode is oxidised, and the reaction is feasible if E⦵cell > 0.
  • Lithium-ion cells are rechargeable. Fuel cells use H₂ and O₂ to make water at 1.23 V.
c-1-11.intro: Electrochemical cells turn the energy of redox reactions into electricity. This topic covers electrode potentials, the standard hydrogen electrode, cell notation, calculating E°cell and predicting feasibility, and commercial cells: non-rechargeable, rechargeable and fuel cells.

c-1-12.h:
1Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases

Key definitions

Brønsted–Lowry acid: a proton (H⁺) donor.

Brønsted–Lowry base: a proton acceptor.

Strong acid: completely dissociates in water, for example HCl, HNO₃ and H₂SO₄.

Weak acid: only partially dissociates, for example ethanoic acid. It sets up an equilibrium.

  • When an acid reacts with water, water acts as a base: HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻. Often this is simplified to HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻.
  • Acid–base reactions involve transfer of a proton.

2pH and Kw

\text{pH}=-\log_{10}[\text{H}^+]
[\text{H}^+]=10^{-\text{pH}}
K_w=[\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-]=1.00\times10^{-14}\text{ mol}^2\text{ dm}^{-6}\text{ at 298 K}
  • In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = \sqrt{K_w}. Water is neutral at any temperature. Its pH is only 7 at 298 K: Kw increases with temperature, so the neutral pH falls.
  • Strong acid: [H⁺] = concentration of acid (monoprotic). For example, 0.050 mol dm⁻³ HCl has pH = 1.30.
  • Strong base: find [OH⁻], then [H⁺] = Kw/[OH⁻]. For example, 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NaOH: [H⁺] = 10⁻¹³, pH = 13.00.

3Weak acids: Ka and pKa

K_a=\frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]}
\text{p}K_a=-\log_{10}K_a
  • For a weak acid on its own, assume [H⁺] = [A⁻] and that [HA] at equilibrium ≈ the starting concentration. Then [\text{H}^+]=\sqrt{K_a\times[\text{HA}]}.
  • A larger Ka (smaller pKa) means a stronger acid.
Worked example 1: pH of a weak acid

Find the pH of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ propanoic acid, Ka = 1.35 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³.

  1. [\text{H}^+]^2=1.35\times10^{-5}\times0.100=1.35\times10^{-6}.
  2. [\text{H}^+]=1.16\times10^{-3} mol dm⁻³.
  3. pH =-\log(1.16\times10^{-3}).

Answer: pH = 2.93

Worked example 2: pH after mixing a strong acid and a strong base

25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl is mixed with 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. Find the pH.

  1. Moles of H⁺ = 2.50 × 10⁻³; moles of OH⁻ = 2.00 × 10⁻³. The excess H⁺ is 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
  2. The total volume is 45.0 cm³, so [H⁺] = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ / 0.0450 = 0.0111 mol dm⁻³.

Answer: pH = 1.95

4Titration curves and indicators

Acid + basepH at equivalenceSuitable indicator
strong + strong7phenolphthalein or methyl orange
weak acid + strong baseabove 7 (about 8–9)phenolphthalein (range 8.2–10)
strong acid + weak basebelow 7 (about 5)methyl orange (range 3.1–4.4)
weak + weakno sharp jumpnone suitable
  • An indicator is suitable if its colour-change range lies completely within the vertical section of the curve.
  • Half-neutralisation. At half the equivalence volume, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa. This is a quick way to find Ka from a curve.
Required practical 9: pH curves
  • Calibrate the pH meter with buffer solutions first. Add the base in small portions, and in drops near the end point. Record the pH after each addition, then plot pH against volume.
  • Read the equivalence volume at the middle of the vertical section, and pKa at half that volume.

5Buffers

Key definitions

Buffer: a solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added, or when it is diluted.

  • Acidic buffer: a weak acid and its salt, for example CH₃COOH and CH₃COONa. There is a large reservoir of both HA and A⁻.
  • Add H⁺: it reacts with A⁻ to form HA, so the equilibrium HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ shifts left.
  • Add OH⁻: it reacts with H⁺ (or with HA) to form water. More HA dissociates, so the equilibrium shifts right.
  • In both cases the ratio [HA]/[A⁻] changes very little.
  • Basic buffer: a weak base and its salt, for example NH₃ and NH₄Cl.
  • Uses: shampoos, biological systems (blood is buffered at about pH 7.4 by H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻), and calibrating pH meters.
[\text{H}^+]=K_a\times\frac{[\text{HA}]}{[\text{A}^-]}
Worked example 3: pH of a buffer

A buffer contains 0.20 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ sodium ethanoate. Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵. Find its pH, then the pH after 0.010 mol of HCl is added to 1.00 dm³ of it.

  1. [\text{H}^+]=1.74\times10^{-5}\times\frac{0.20}{0.10}=3.48\times10^{-5}, so pH = 4.46.
  2. Adding HCl turns A⁻ into HA. Now HA = 0.21 mol and A⁻ = 0.09 mol.
  3. [\text{H}^+]=1.74\times10^{-5}\times\frac{0.21}{0.09}=4.06\times10^{-5}, so pH = 4.39.

Answer: pH 4.46, falling only to 4.39 when the acid is added.

Common mistakes
  • Using the weak-acid formula \sqrt{K_a[\text{HA}]} for a buffer. Buffers contain added A⁻, so use K_a\times\frac{[\text{HA}]}{[\text{A}^-]}.
  • Forgetting to divide by the total volume after mixing.
  • Giving pH to the wrong precision. Use 2 decimal places.
Exam tips
  • For buffer explanations, always write the equilibrium, say what the added H⁺ or OH⁻ reacts with, and say that the ratio [HA] : [A⁻] stays almost constant.
  • For pH of diprotic acids such as H₂SO₄ at A-level, assume [H⁺] = 2 × concentration only if the question says so.
Summary
  • Acids are proton donors. pH = −log[H⁺]. Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K.
  • Weak acid: Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. For the acid alone, [H⁺] = √(Ka[HA]).
  • At half-neutralisation pH = pKa. Choose an indicator whose range lies in the steep part of the curve.
  • Buffers resist pH change because they hold reservoirs of HA and A⁻. [H⁺] = Ka[HA]/[A⁻].
c-1-12.intro: Acids and bases are proton donors and acceptors. This topic covers pH, the ionic product of water, strong and weak acids and bases, Ka and pKa, titration curves and indicators, and buffers, all with calculations.

c-2-4.h:
1Reactions of sodium and magnesium with water

  • Sodium reacts vigorously with cold water. It melts into a ball, fizzes and moves about: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. The solution formed has pH 13–14.
  • Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water, forming Mg(OH)₂, which is only slightly soluble (pH about 9–10). It burns in steam: Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂.

2Reactions with oxygen

ElementObservationEquation
Nayellow flame, white solid4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O
Mgbrilliant white flame, white solid2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
Alwhite flame, white solid4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃
Siburns when heated stronglySi + O₂ → SiO₂
Pwhite flame, white fumesP₄ + 5O₂ → P₄O₁₀
Sblue flame, choking gasS + O₂ → SO₂
  • In each oxide the element shows its highest oxidation state (equal to its group number), except S, which forms SO₂ (+4). SO₃ (+6) needs a catalyst.

3Structure and melting points of the oxides

OxideStructure and bondingMelting point
Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃giant ionic latticehigh; MgO is highest because the Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions carry high charges and are small
SiO₂macromolecular (giant covalent)very high
P₄O₁₀, SO₂, SO₃simple molecularlow; only van der Waals forces and dipole–dipole forces between molecules are overcome
  • Al₂O₃ has a lower melting point than MgO even though Al³⁺ has a higher charge. The very small, highly charged Al³⁺ ion polarises the oxide ion, giving the bonds some covalent character.

4Oxides with water

OxideWith waterpH
Na₂ONa₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH13–14
MgOMgO + H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ (slightly soluble)about 9–10
Al₂O₃, SiO₂insoluble7
P₄O₁₀P₄O₁₀ + 6H₂O → 4H₃PO₄0–1
SO₂SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃2–3
SO₃SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄0–1
  • Ionic oxides contain O²⁻ ions, which react with water to form OH⁻, so they are basic. Covalent oxides form acids, so they are acidic.

5Acid–base character

  • Basic oxides (Na₂O, MgO) react with acids: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O.
  • Amphoteric Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids and bases:
\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3+6\text{HCl}\rightarrow2\text{AlCl}_3+3\text{H}_2\text{O}
\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3+2\text{NaOH}+3\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow2\text{NaAl(OH)}_4
  • Acidic oxides (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂, SO₃) react with bases. For example, SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O (with hot, concentrated NaOH); P₄O₁₀ + 12NaOH → 4Na₃PO₄ + 6H₂O; SO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₃ + H₂O.
Worked example 1: Explaining the pH of an oxide solution

Explain why sodium oxide forms a strongly alkaline solution but phosphorus(V) oxide forms a strongly acidic one.

  1. Na₂O is ionic. Its O²⁻ ions react with water: O²⁻ + H₂O → 2OH⁻.
  2. P₄O₁₀ is simple molecular and covalent. It reacts with water to form phosphoric(V) acid, which releases H⁺ ions.

Answer: Ionic oxides give OH⁻ ions (pH 14); covalent non-metal oxides give acids (pH about 0).

Worked example 2: Writing a neutralisation equation

Write an equation for the reaction of sulfur trioxide with sodium hydroxide.

  1. SO₃ is an acidic oxide. With water it gives H₂SO₄, which is neutralised by 2NaOH.

Answer: SO₃ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O

Common mistakes
  • Saying that SiO₂ is acidic "because it dissolves in water to form an acid". It is insoluble; it is acidic because it reacts with bases.
  • Writing P₂O₅ instead of the molecular formula P₄O₁₀.
  • Forgetting that Al₂O₃ is amphoteric. You need an equation with an acid and an equation with a base.
Exam tips
  • Link the structure to the property: ionic oxides are basic and have high melting points; covalent oxides are acidic. Mention the oxide ion reacting with water.
Summary
  • Na reacts vigorously and Mg slowly with water. All the elements burn in O₂.
  • Oxides: Na₂O, MgO and Al₂O₃ are ionic; SiO₂ is giant covalent; P₄O₁₀, SO₂ and SO₃ are simple molecular.
  • Character: basic (Na, Mg), amphoteric (Al), acidic (Si, P, S). The pH of oxide solutions falls from 14 to about 0 across the period.
c-2-4.intro: Across Period 3 the elements change from metals to non-metals, and their oxides change from basic to acidic. This topic covers the reactions of the elements with water and oxygen, and the structure, bonding and acid–base behaviour of the oxides.
secs: Reactions of sodium and magnesium with water
Structure and melting points of the oxides

c-2-5.h:
1General properties

Key definitions

Transition metal: an element that forms at least one stable ion with an incomplete d sub-shell. Sc and Zn are not included: Sc³⁺ is 3d⁰ and Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰.

  • The four characteristic properties are complex formation, coloured ions, variable oxidation states and catalytic activity. They all come from the incomplete d sub-shell.

2Complexes, ligands and shapes

Key definitions

Ligand: a molecule or ion that donates a lone pair of electrons to a central metal ion, forming a co-ordinate bond.

Complex: a central metal atom or ion surrounded by ligands.

Co-ordination number: the number of co-ordinate bonds to the central metal ion.

  • Monodentate ligands (H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻) form one bond. Bidentate ligands (ethane-1,2-diamine, written en; and ethanedioate, C₂O₄²⁻) form two. Multidentate EDTA⁴⁻ forms six.
  • Shapes: octahedral with 6 small ligands, for example [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺. Tetrahedral with 4 larger Cl⁻ ligands, for example [CuCl₄]²⁻. Square planar, for example cisplatin [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]. Linear, for example [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ in Tollens' reagent.
  • Isomerism. Square planar and octahedral complexes can show cis–trans isomerism: cisplatin is the cis isomer. Octahedral complexes with three bidentate ligands, such as [Ni(en)₃]²⁺, show optical isomerism, existing as non-superimposable mirror images.
  • Haem is an iron(II) complex with a multidentate ligand. O₂ binds to the Fe²⁺ in haemoglobin. CO is toxic because it binds more strongly than O₂ and replaces it.

3Ligand substitution and the chelate effect

  • H₂O and NH₃ are similar in size, so substitution keeps the co-ordination number at 6: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 6NH₃ → [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺ + 6H₂O. With copper the substitution is partial: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 4H₂O, giving a deep blue solution.
  • Cl⁻ is larger, so the co-ordination number changes from 6 to 4: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CuCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O. The colour goes from blue to yellow-green, and the shape from octahedral to tetrahedral.
  • The chelate effect. Multidentate ligands form more stable complexes. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + EDTA⁴⁻ → [Cu(EDTA)]²⁻ + 6H₂O turns 2 particles into 7, so entropy increases greatly (ΔS is positive). ΔH is close to zero because similar bonds are broken and made, so ΔG is negative.

4Formation of coloured ions

  • In a complex, the ligands split the d orbitals into two energy levels. An electron absorbs a photon to jump up the gap, ΔE. The colour we see is the light that is not absorbed (the complementary colour).
\Delta E=h\nu=\frac{hc}{\lambda}
  • The colour changes with oxidation state, co-ordination number and ligand, because each of these changes ΔE.
  • Colorimetry. Measure the absorbance of standard solutions and plot a calibration curve. Then read the concentration of the unknown from it. Use a filter of the complementary colour.

5Variable oxidation states

  • Vanadium. Zinc in acid reduces vanadium step by step: VO₂⁺ (V, yellow) → VO²⁺ (IV, blue) → V³⁺ (III, green) → V²⁺ (II, violet).
  • The redox potential of a transition metal ion depends on pH and on the ligand. For example, Cr(III) is oxidised to Cr(VI) more easily in alkali, and silver forms the stable complex [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺.
  • Tollens' reagent is [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺. It is reduced to silver by aldehydes, giving a silver mirror.
  • Redox titrations use KMnO₄ in acid, which is its own indicator: the end point is the first permanent pale pink.
Key equations
\text{MnO}_4^-+8\text{H}^++5\text{Fe}^{2+}\rightarrow\text{Mn}^{2+}+4\text{H}_2\text{O}+5\text{Fe}^{3+}
2\text{MnO}_4^-+16\text{H}^++5\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}\rightarrow2\text{Mn}^{2+}+8\text{H}_2\text{O}+10\text{CO}_2
Worked example 1: Redox titration

25.0 cm³ of Fe²⁺(aq) needs 21.60 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄. Find [Fe²⁺].

  1. Moles of MnO₄⁻ =0.0200\times0.02160=4.32\times10^{-4} mol.
  2. The ratio is 1 MnO₄⁻ : 5 Fe²⁺, so moles of Fe²⁺ =2.16\times10^{-3} mol.
  3. [\text{Fe}^{2+}]=2.16\times10^{-3}/0.0250.

Answer: 0.0864 mol dm⁻³

Worked example 2: Explaining a colour

Explain why [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is blue.

  1. Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, an incomplete d sub-shell. The water ligands split the d orbitals.
  2. An electron absorbs light in the red–orange region to jump across the gap ΔE.
  3. The remaining wavelengths are transmitted or reflected.

Answer: The ion absorbs red/orange light, so we see the complementary colour, blue.

6Catalysts

  • Heterogeneous catalysts are in a different phase from the reactants. Reactants adsorb onto active sites, bonds weaken, the reaction happens, and the products desorb.
  • Contact process: V₂O₅ catalyses the conversion of SO₂ to SO₃. Step 1: SO₂ + V₂O₅ → SO₃ + V₂O₄. Step 2: V₂O₄ + ½O₂ → V₂O₅.
  • Haber process: iron catalyses the formation of NH₃.
  • Catalysts are spread on a support (for example a ceramic honeycomb) to maximise the surface area and reduce cost. They are poisoned by impurities that block the active sites, for example sulfur on the iron in the Haber process, or lead in catalytic converters.
  • Homogeneous catalysts are in the same phase. They work through an intermediate species.
  • Fe²⁺ catalyses S₂O₈²⁻ + 2I⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ + I₂. The two negative ions repel each other, so the direct reaction is slow. Instead: S₂O₈²⁻ + 2Fe²⁺ → 2SO₄²⁻ + 2Fe³⁺, then 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂.
  • Autocatalysis: Mn²⁺, a product, catalyses the reaction between MnO₄⁻ and C₂O₄²⁻. The reaction starts slowly, then speeds up.
Common mistakes
  • Calling Zn a transition metal. Its only ion, Zn²⁺, has a full d sub-shell.
  • Saying a complex is coloured because it "emits" light. It absorbs some wavelengths; we see the rest.
  • Writing the co-ordination number as the number of ligands. For bidentate ligands it is double the number of ligands.
Exam tips
  • For the chelate effect, always give the change in the number of particles, the sign of ΔS, ΔH ≈ 0, and therefore ΔG < 0.
  • Learn the vanadium colours in order: yellow, blue, green, violet.
Summary
  • A transition metal forms an ion with an incomplete d sub-shell. Its properties are complexes, colour, variable oxidation states and catalysis.
  • Ligands donate lone pairs. Shapes are octahedral, tetrahedral, square planar or linear. Multidentate ligands are more stable (the chelate effect, from entropy).
  • Colour comes from d-electron transitions: ΔE = hν, and it changes with oxidation state, ligand and co-ordination number.
  • KMnO₄ titrations: 1 MnO₄⁻ reacts with 5 Fe²⁺.
  • Heterogeneous catalysts work by adsorption (V₂O₅, Fe); homogeneous ones work through intermediates (Fe²⁺ with S₂O₈²⁻ and I⁻); Mn²⁺ is an autocatalyst.
c-2-5.intro: Transition metals (Ti to Cu) have partly filled d sub-shells, which gives them their characteristic properties: complex ions, colours, variable oxidation states and catalytic activity. This is one of the largest topics in the course.
secs: Ligand substitution and the chelate effect

c-2-6.h:
1Metal–aqua ions and acidity

  • In water, these metal ions form octahedral [M(H₂O)₆]ⁿ⁺ ions: Fe²⁺ (pale green), Cu²⁺ (blue), Fe³⁺ (violet, often yellow-brown in solution because of hydrolysis) and Al³⁺ (colourless).
  • The metal ion polarises the O–H bonds in its water ligands, so a water ligand can release H⁺:
[\text{Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{3+}+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons[\text{Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_5\text{(OH)}]^{2+}+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+
  • 3+ ions are more acidic than 2+ ions (with a pH of about 3 compared with about 6). M³⁺ has a higher charge-to-size ratio (charge density), so it polarises the water ligands more strongly, weakening their O–H bonds and releasing H⁺ more readily.

2Reactions with hydroxide and ammonia

Both OH⁻ and NH₃ act as bases: they remove H⁺ ions from the water ligands until a neutral hydroxide precipitates.

IonFew drops of NaOH or NH₃Excess NaOHExcess NH₃
[Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (green)green precipitate of Fe(H₂O)₄(OH)₂; it turns brown in air (oxidised to Fe(III))no changeno change
[Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (blue)blue precipitate of Cu(H₂O)₄(OH)₂no changedissolves to give a deep blue solution of [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺
[Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (yellow/violet)brown precipitate of Fe(H₂O)₃(OH)₃no changeno change
[Al(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (colourless)white precipitate of Al(H₂O)₃(OH)₃dissolves to give a colourless solution of [Al(OH)₄(H₂O)₂]⁻no change
Key equations
[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}+2\text{OH}^-\rightarrow\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4\text{(OH)}_2+2\text{H}_2\text{O}
[\text{Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{3+}+3\text{NH}_3\rightarrow\text{Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_3\text{(OH)}_3+3\text{NH}_4^+
\text{Al(H}_2\text{O)}_3\text{(OH)}_3+\text{OH}^-\rightarrow[\text{Al(OH)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2]^-+\text{H}_2\text{O}
\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4\text{(OH)}_2+4\text{NH}_3\rightarrow[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2]^{2+}+2\text{H}_2\text{O}+2\text{OH}^-
  • Amphoteric behaviour: aluminium hydroxide dissolves in both acid and excess alkali. With acid: Al(H₂O)₃(OH)₃ + 3H⁺ → [Al(H₂O)₆]³⁺.
  • Note that excess ammonia does ligand substitution only with copper here. Excess NaOH removes a further proton only from aluminium.

3Reactions with carbonate

  • 2+ ions (weakly acidic) form metal carbonate precipitates: [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → FeCO₃ + 6H₂O, a green precipitate. Cu²⁺ gives a blue-green precipitate of CuCO₃.
  • 3+ ions are acidic enough to react with carbonate to release CO₂ gas (effervescence), forming the hydroxide precipitate instead:
2[\text{Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{3+}+3\text{CO}_3^{2-}\rightarrow2\text{Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_3\text{(OH)}_3+3\text{CO}_2+3\text{H}_2\text{O}
  • So Fe³⁺ gives a brown precipitate with bubbles, and Al³⁺ gives a white precipitate with bubbles.
Worked example 1: Identifying an ion
