A solution gives a white precipitate with a few drops of NaOH(aq). The precipitate dissolves in excess NaOH but not in excess ammonia. With Na₂CO₃ it gives a white precipitate and bubbles. Identify the ion and explain the bubbles.

  1. A white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH is amphoteric Al(OH)₃.
  2. The bubbles are CO₂. Al³⁺ is a 3+ ion, acidic enough to react with carbonate.

Answer: [Al(H₂O)₆]³⁺. The acidic 3+ aqua ion releases H₃O⁺, which reacts with CO₃²⁻ to give CO₂.

Worked example 2: Explaining relative acidity

Explain why a solution of iron(III) chloride is more acidic than a solution of iron(II) chloride of the same concentration.

  1. Fe³⁺ has a higher charge and a smaller radius than Fe²⁺, so its charge density is higher.
  2. It polarises the O–H bonds of the water ligands more, so H⁺ is released more readily.

Answer: [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ dissociates to a greater extent, so [H₃O⁺] is higher and the pH is lower.

Required practical 11: identifying transition metal ions
  • Add NaOH(aq) dropwise, then in excess. Repeat with NH₃(aq) dropwise, then in excess. Repeat with Na₂CO₃(aq). Record the colours of the precipitates and solutions and any effervescence.
  • Leave the iron(II) hydroxide precipitate standing to see it turn brown as it is oxidised in air.
Common mistakes
  • Writing "Fe(OH)₂" without water ligands is acceptable in some answers, but AQA usually expects the full formulae, Fe(H₂O)₄(OH)₂ and so on.
  • Saying that Fe²⁺ produces CO₂ with carbonate. Only 3+ ions do.
  • Forgetting the charges when you balance the equation for the Cu–NH₃ substitution.
Exam tips
  • Learn the table as a grid of colours: Fe²⁺ green, Cu²⁺ blue, Fe³⁺ brown, Al³⁺ white. The excess reactions are only Cu with NH₃ (deep blue) and Al with NaOH (colourless).
Summary
  • [M(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is more acidic than [M(H₂O)₆]²⁺ because of its higher charge density.
  • OH⁻ and NH₃ deprotonate the aqua ions to give hydroxide precipitates. Excess NH₃ gives deep blue with Cu; excess OH⁻ dissolves Al(OH)₃.
  • Carbonate gives MCO₃ with 2+ ions, but M(OH)₃ and CO₂ with 3+ ions.
c-2-6.intro: Metal ions in water are surrounded by water ligands, and these metal–aqua ions behave as acids. This topic covers why 3+ ions are more acidic than 2+ ions, and the test-tube reactions of Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe³⁺ and Al³⁺ with hydroxide, ammonia and carbonate.

c-3-7.h:
1Key definitions

Key definitions

Stereoisomers: compounds with the same structural formula but a different arrangement of atoms in space. Optical isomerism is one type; E/Z isomerism is the other.

Chiral centre (asymmetric carbon): a carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups. Mark it with an asterisk, C*.

Enantiomers (optical isomers): a pair of molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.

Racemic mixture (racemate): an equimolar (50 : 50) mixture of two enantiomers.

2Spotting chiral centres

  • Check each sp³ carbon. A carbon with two H atoms (CH₂), or with two identical groups such as two CH₃ groups, cannot be chiral.
  • A carbon in a C=C or C=O is never a chiral centre, because it has only three groups and is planar.
  • Look along the whole chain. In butan-2-ol, C2 carries H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃, which are all different, so C2 is chiral. Propan-2-ol has two CH₃ groups on C2, so it is not chiral.
Worked example 1: Finding a chiral centre

Is 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid), CH₃CH(OH)COOH, chiral?

  1. Look at C2. It is bonded to H, OH, CH₃ and COOH.
  2. These are four different groups, so C2 is a chiral centre.
  3. C1 (COOH) has only three groups, and C3 (CH₃) has three identical H atoms, so neither is chiral.

Answer: Yes. C2 is chiral, so lactic acid has two enantiomers.

Worked example 2: Counting chiral centres

How many chiral centres are there in 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane, CH₃CHBrCHClCH₃?

  1. C2 has H, Br, CH₃ and CHClCH₃: four different groups.
  2. C3 has H, Cl, CH₃ and CHBrCH₃: four different groups.

Answer: Two chiral centres.

3Drawing enantiomers

  • Draw the chiral carbon as a tetrahedron: two bonds in the plane of the page, one wedge (towards you) and one dash (away from you).
  • Then draw its mirror image across a dashed mirror line. Equivalently, swap any two groups.
  • Check that the two drawings cannot be rotated to match.

4Plane-polarised light

  • Each enantiomer rotates the plane of plane-polarised light by the same angle but in opposite directions. This is why enantiomers are called optically active.
  • A racemic mixture is optically inactive, because the two rotations cancel out.
  • Enantiomers have identical physical properties (melting point, boiling point, density) and identical reactions with ordinary reagents. They behave differently only towards other chiral molecules, such as enzymes and receptors in the body.

5Forming racemic mixtures

  • The C=O group is planar. In nucleophilic addition, for example KCN then acid with ethanal, the CN⁻ can attack from either face with equal probability. This gives equal amounts of the two enantiomers of 2-hydroxypropanenitrile.
  • The same happens in electrophilic addition when a planar carbocation is attacked to make a new chiral centre. For example, HBr + but-1-ene gives racemic 2-bromobutane.
  • A reaction that makes only one enantiomer, such as an enzyme-catalysed reaction, gives an optically active product.
Worked example 3: Explaining an inactive product

Propanal reacts with HCN (from KCN and acid). Explain why the product is optically inactive.

  1. The product, 2-hydroxybutanenitrile, has a chiral centre: C2 is bonded to H, OH, CN and C₂H₅.
  2. The C=O in propanal is planar, so CN⁻ is equally likely to attack from above or below.
  3. Equal amounts of both enantiomers form, giving a racemic mixture.

Answer: The two enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions, so the effects cancel.

6Drugs and synthesis

  • Often only one enantiomer of a drug binds to the target receptor. The other may be inactive or harmful. The thalidomide tragedy is the classic example.
  • Synthetic routes through planar intermediates give racemates, which then need costly separation. Chemists use chiral catalysts or enzymes to make a single enantiomer instead.
Common mistakes
  • Saying that enantiomers have different boiling points, or that they react differently with ordinary reagents. They do not.
  • Drawing the "mirror image" as the same molecule rotated. Swap two groups or reflect it properly.
  • Forgetting that a racemic mixture has no overall effect on plane-polarised light.
Exam tips
  • For "explain why the product is optically inactive", make three points: the C=O (or carbocation) is planar; attack is equally likely from above and below; a racemic mixture forms, and the rotations cancel.
  • Always draw enantiomers in 3D, with wedges and dashes, and a mirror line.
Summary
  • A chiral carbon has four different groups. Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images.
  • Enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions; a racemate is inactive.
  • Attack on planar C=O groups or carbocations gives racemic mixtures.
  • Drugs often need a single enantiomer.
c-3-7.intro: Some molecules exist as two forms that are mirror images of each other but cannot be superimposed, like your left and right hands. This is optical isomerism. It matters a great deal in biology and in drug design.

c-3-8.h:
1Structure and naming

  • Aldehydes have the C=O at the end of the chain, as –CHO. Examples are ethanal (CH₃CHO) and propanal.
  • Ketones have the C=O within the chain, as R–CO–R′. Examples are propanone (CH₃COCH₃) and butanone.
  • The C=O is polar, C^{\delta+}=O^{\delta-}, and planar. The δ+ carbon is attacked by nucleophiles.

2Oxidation and tests

  • Aldehydes are oxidised to carboxylic acids by acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (orange to green): RCHO + [O] → RCOOH. Ketones are not oxidised.
TestAldehydeKetone
Tollens' reagent, [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, warmsilver mirror (Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag)no change
Fehling's solution (blue Cu²⁺ complex), warmbrick-red precipitate of Cu₂Ostays blue
acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, warmorange → greenstays orange

3Reduction with NaBH₄

  • NaBH₄ in aqueous or alcoholic solution reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols. The reducing agent is written [H].
\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}+2[\text{H}]\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}
\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3+2[\text{H}]\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3
  • Mechanism (nucleophilic addition). The hydride ion, H⁻, from NaBH₄ attacks the δ+ carbon, and the C=O π electrons move onto O, forming an alkoxide ion. The O⁻ then takes H⁺ from water, giving –OH.

4Addition of cyanide: making hydroxynitriles

  • Carbonyl compounds react with KCN followed by dilute acid (or HCN) to form hydroxynitriles. For example, propanone gives 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile, (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN. This adds a carbon to the chain.
  • Mechanism: the lone pair on CN⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon, the C=O π electrons move to O to give O⁻, and the O⁻ is protonated by H⁺ (or HCN).
  • Hazards. KCN is highly toxic if swallowed or absorbed, and HCN is a toxic gas. KCN is used in preference to HCN because it is a solid, which is less likely to be inhaled, and it gives a higher concentration of the CN⁻ nucleophile. Work in a fume cupboard.
  • With aldehydes and unsymmetrical ketones the product is chiral. Because the C=O is planar, attack from either side gives a racemic mixture.
Worked example 1: Naming a hydroxynitrile

Name the product of ethanal with KCN and dilute acid, and say whether it is optically active.

  1. CH₃CHO + HCN → CH₃CH(OH)CN.
  2. The longest chain, including the CN carbon, has 3 carbons. The OH is on C2: 2-hydroxypropanenitrile.
  3. C2 has four different groups (H, OH, CH₃, CN), so it is chiral. But the planar C=O is attacked equally from both sides, so a racemate forms.

Answer: 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, formed as a racemic mixture, so it is not optically active.

Worked example 2: Distinguishing isomers

Describe a test to distinguish propanal from propanone, two isomers of formula C₃H₆O.

  1. Warm each with Tollens' reagent in a water bath.
  2. Propanal (an aldehyde) is oxidised, so Ag⁺ is reduced to silver.

Answer: Propanal gives a silver mirror; propanone shows no change.

Worked example 3: Reduction product

Name the product when butanone is reduced with NaBH₄, and classify it.

  1. Butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, is a ketone, so reduction gives a secondary alcohol.
  2. The OH ends up on C2.

Answer: Butan-2-ol, a secondary alcohol (with a chiral C2, formed as a racemate).

Common mistakes
  • In the NaBH₄ mechanism, showing H⁺ attacking first. The nucleophile is H⁻.
  • In the HCN mechanism, starting the arrow from the C of CN⁻ incorrectly. It starts from the lone pair on carbon.
  • Saying that Fehling's solution gives a silver mirror.
Exam tips
  • Nucleophilic addition marks: the δ+ and δ− on C=O, the lone pair on the nucleophile, an arrow to C, an arrow from the C=O bond to O, the intermediate, then protonation.
Summary
  • Aldehydes are oxidised (Tollens' gives a silver mirror; Fehling's gives a brick-red precipitate); ketones are not.
  • NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols, by nucleophilic addition of H⁻.
  • KCN with acid gives hydroxynitriles by nucleophilic addition of CN⁻, often as racemates. KCN is highly toxic.
c-3-8.intro: Aldehydes and ketones both contain the carbonyl group, C=O. Aldehydes can be oxidised further and ketones cannot, which is the basis of the tests that tell them apart. Both undergo nucleophilic addition.

c-3-9.h:
1Carboxylic acids

  • Carboxylic acids are weak acids that partly dissociate: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺.
  • They react with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates to release CO₂, which is the test for an acid: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂.
  • They also react with metals (giving H₂) and with bases (giving a salt and water).

2Esters

  • Esterification: carboxylic acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water, using a concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst and warming. For example, CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O, which gives ethyl ethanoate.
  • Naming: the alcohol part comes first ("ethyl"), then the acid part ("ethanoate").
  • Uses: solvents, plasticisers for polymers, and perfumes and food flavourings, because many esters are sweet-smelling.
  • Hydrolysis. Acid hydrolysis (dilute acid, heat under reflux) is reversible and gives the acid and the alcohol. Base hydrolysis (NaOH, reflux) goes to completion and gives the carboxylate salt and the alcohol.

3Fats, soaps and biodiesel

  • Vegetable oils and animal fats are esters of propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol) with three long-chain fatty acids, known as triglycerides.
  • Hydrolysis with hot NaOH gives glycerol and the sodium salts of the fatty acids, which are soaps.
  • Biodiesel is a mixture of methyl esters of long-chain fatty acids. It is made by reacting vegetable oils with methanol and a strong-alkali catalyst (KOH).
Worked example 1: Products of ester hydrolysis

Name the products when methyl propanoate is heated under reflux with NaOH(aq).

  1. The ester is CH₃CH₂COOCH₃. The alcohol part is methyl and the acid part is propanoate.
  2. Alkaline hydrolysis gives the salt of the acid plus the alcohol.

Answer: Sodium propanoate, CH₃CH₂COONa, and methanol.

4Acylation: acyl chlorides and acid anhydrides

  • Acyl chlorides (RCOCl, e.g. ethanoyl chloride) and acid anhydrides ((RCO)₂O) are acylating agents.
Reacts withProduct from RCOCl (+ HCl)Product from (RCO)₂O (+ RCOOH)
watercarboxylic acidcarboxylic acid
alcoholesterester
ammoniaprimary amideprimary amide
primary amineN-substituted amideN-substituted amide
  • With ammonia and amines, the HCl reacts with excess base to form an ammonium salt.
  • Mechanism (nucleophilic addition–elimination), for acyl chlorides:
  1. The lone pair on the nucleophile (H₂O, ROH, NH₃ or RNH₂) attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π electrons move to O.
  2. The C=O re-forms and Cl⁻ is eliminated.
  3. Loss of H⁺ (taken by Cl⁻) gives the product and HCl.
  • Ethanoic anhydride is used industrially to make aspirin. It is cheaper than ethanoyl chloride, less corrosive, reacts less vigorously with water, and does not produce corrosive HCl fumes.
Worked example 2: Acyl chloride with an amine

Give the product and equation for ethanoyl chloride with methylamine.

  1. Methylamine is a primary amine, so the product is an N-substituted amide.
  2. CH₃COCl + CH₃NH₂ → CH₃CONHCH₃ + HCl. With excess amine, the HCl forms CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻.

Answer: N-methylethanamide.

Required practical 10: preparing an organic solid and an organic liquid
  • Solid (e.g. aspirin): react, collect the crude solid by vacuum filtration with a Büchner funnel, and then recrystallise. Dissolve the crude product in the minimum volume of hot solvent, filter hot to remove insoluble impurities, cool to crystallise, filter, wash with a little cold solvent, and dry.
  • Testing purity: a pure solid has a sharp melting point that matches the data-book value. Impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.
  • Liquid (e.g. an ester): distil, then shake with NaHCO₃(aq) in a separating funnel to remove acid, releasing the pressure often. Run off the aqueous layer, dry with anhydrous CaCl₂ or MgSO₄, and redistil, collecting the fraction at the boiling point.
Common mistakes
  • Writing the ester name the wrong way round. The alcohol part comes first.
  • Forgetting HCl as the second product of acyl chloride reactions, or forgetting that an anhydride gives a carboxylic acid instead.
  • Using "excess hot solvent" in recrystallisation. It must be the minimum, or the product stays dissolved.
Exam tips
  • The addition–elimination mechanism scores marks for: the lone pair and arrow to C; the arrow from C=O to O; the tetrahedral intermediate; C=O re-forming with Cl⁻ leaving; and the loss of H⁺.
Summary
  • Carboxylic acids are weak acids; they fizz with carbonates.
  • Esters come from acid + alcohol with an H₂SO₄ catalyst. They are hydrolysed by acid (reversible) or by NaOH (giving the salt).
  • Fats with NaOH give soaps and glycerol; with methanol and KOH they give biodiesel.
  • RCOCl and (RCO)₂O acylate water, alcohols, NH₃ and amines by addition–elimination.
c-3-9.intro: Carboxylic acids contain –COOH. Their derivatives (esters, acyl chlorides, acid anhydrides and amides) are made from them and turn up in flavours, fats, soaps, biodiesel and medicines such as aspirin.
secs: Acylation: acyl chlorides and acid anhydrides

c-3-10.h:
1Bonding in benzene

  • Benzene is a planar hexagonal molecule. Each carbon forms three σ bonds (to two carbons and one hydrogen), with bond angles of 120°.
  • Each carbon's remaining p orbital overlaps with those of its neighbours, forming a ring of delocalised π electrons above and below the plane.
  • Evidence against the Kekulé structure, which has three alternating C=C bonds:
  1. All six C–C bonds are the same length (0.139 nm), between a C–C single bond (0.154 nm) and a C=C double bond (0.134 nm).
  2. Enthalpy of hydrogenation. Cyclohexene gives −120 kJ mol⁻¹, so Kekulé benzene would be expected to give 3 × −120 = −360 kJ mol⁻¹. The measured value is only about −208 kJ mol⁻¹. Benzene is about 152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than predicted.
  3. Benzene does not decolourise bromine water under normal conditions, so it does not undergo addition.
  • Electrophilic substitution is preferred to addition because substitution keeps the delocalised ring, and with it the extra stability.
Worked example 1: Delocalisation energy

Hydrogenating cyclohexa-1,3-diene gives ΔH = −232 kJ mol⁻¹, and hydrogenating benzene gives −208 kJ mol⁻¹. Estimate the stabilisation of benzene relative to Kekulé benzene, using −120 kJ mol⁻¹ per C=C.

  1. Kekulé benzene would give 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹.
  2. The difference is −208 − (−360) = +152 kJ mol⁻¹.

Answer: Benzene is about 152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable. (The diene value, −232 ≈ 2 × −120, confirms that the per-C=C figure is sensible.)

2Nitration

  • Reagents: concentrated HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄, at 50 °C or below. Higher temperatures give multiple substitution.
  • Generating the electrophile: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻.

Mechanism:

  1. An arrow goes from the delocalised ring to the N of NO₂⁺.
  2. This forms an intermediate with a partial (broken) delocalised ring and a + charge, with the H and NO₂ on the same carbon.
  3. The C–H bond electrons return to the ring, re-forming the delocalised system, and H⁺ is lost. The H⁺ re-forms H₂SO₄ with HSO₄⁻, so H₂SO₄ acts as a catalyst.
  • Importance: nitration is used to make explosives such as TNT, and to make aromatic amines (by reduction of nitro compounds), which are used to make dyes.

3Friedel–Crafts acylation

  • Reagents: an acyl chloride (RCOCl) with an AlCl₃ catalyst, heated under reflux in a dry solvent. The product is a phenyl ketone, for example C₆H₆ + CH₃COCl → C₆H₅COCH₃ + HCl.
  • Generating the electrophile: RCOCl + AlCl₃ → RCO⁺ (the acylium ion) + AlCl₄⁻.
  • The mechanism is the same pattern as nitration. Then H⁺ + AlCl₄⁻ → AlCl₃ + HCl, which regenerates the catalyst.
  • Acylation is important because it makes C–C bonds to the ring, which is useful in synthesis.
Worked example 2: Friedel–Crafts product

Name the organic product of benzene with propanoyl chloride and AlCl₃, and give the electrophile.

  1. The electrophile is CH₃CH₂CO⁺, formed from CH₃CH₂COCl + AlCl₃.
  2. It substitutes for one H on the ring.

Answer: 1-phenylpropan-1-one, C₆H₅COCH₂CH₃.

Common mistakes
  • Drawing the intermediate with a full delocalised circle. It must be a partial ring (a horseshoe) open at the sp³ carbon, with a + charge.
  • Writing addition products for benzene.
  • Forgetting to show catalyst regeneration in equations.
Exam tips
  • Learn the three electrophile-forming equations (for NO₂⁺, RCO⁺ and AlCl₄⁻).
  • The horseshoe should cover 5 carbons and be open towards the carbon carrying the H and the new group.
Summary
  • Benzene is planar with delocalised π electrons; its bond lengths and its hydrogenation enthalpy disprove the Kekulé structure.
  • Nitration uses conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄ at 50 °C with the NO₂⁺ electrophile; it is used for explosives and amines.
  • Friedel–Crafts acylation uses RCOCl/AlCl₃ with the RCO⁺ electrophile and gives phenyl ketones.
  • Substitution keeps the stable ring.
c-3-10.intro: Benzene, C₆H₆, is unusually stable because of its ring of delocalised electrons. Unlike alkenes, it reacts by electrophilic substitution, which keeps the stable ring intact.

c-3-11.h:
1Classifying and naming

TypeStructureExample
primaryRNH₂ethylamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂
secondaryR₂NHdiethylamine
tertiaryR₃Ntrimethylamine
quaternary ammonium ionR₄N⁺tetramethylammonium
  • Phenylamine, C₆H₅NH₂, is the simplest aromatic amine.

2Preparation

Aliphatic amines

  • From a halogenoalkane with excess ammonia (in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube): CH₃CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br. Excess NH₃ reduces further substitution, but the product is usually a mixture.
  • By reducing nitriles with LiAlH₄ in dry ether, or with H₂ and a Ni catalyst: CH₃CN + 4[H] → CH₃CH₂NH₂. This gives only the primary amine, which is better for synthesis.

Aromatic amines

  • Reduce nitrobenzene with tin and concentrated HCl, then add NaOH: C₆H₅NO₂ + 6[H] → C₆H₅NH₂ + 2H₂O.
  • Aromatic amines are used to make dyes.

3Amines as bases

  • The lone pair on N accepts a proton: RNH₂ + H₂O ⇌ RNH₃⁺ + OH⁻. With acids, amines form salts: CH₃NH₂ + HCl → CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻.
  • Base strength depends on how available the lone pair is:
OrderReason
primary aliphatic amines (strongest)the alkyl group is electron-donating (positive inductive effect), so it increases electron density on N
ammonia—
aromatic amines (weakest)the N lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available
Worked example 1: Ranking base strength

Put ammonia, phenylamine and propylamine in order of base strength, strongest first, and explain.

  1. Propylamine: the propyl group pushes electrons onto N, so the lone pair is more available to accept H⁺.
  2. Ammonia has no alkyl group.
  3. Phenylamine: the lone pair overlaps with the ring's π system, so it is delocalised and less available.

Answer: propylamine > ammonia > phenylamine

4Amines as nucleophiles

Nucleophilic substitution with halogenoalkanes

  • A primary amine reacts again with the halogenoalkane, giving a secondary amine, then a tertiary amine, then a quaternary ammonium salt. For example, (CH₃)₃N + CH₃Br → (CH₃)₄N⁺Br⁻.
  • Mechanism: the N lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon and the halide leaves. Then a second amine or NH₃ molecule removes H⁺ from the N.
  • Quaternary ammonium salts with long alkyl chains are cationic surfactants, used in fabric softeners and hair conditioners.

Nucleophilic addition–elimination with acyl chlorides and anhydrides

  • These reactions give N-substituted amides: CH₃COCl + 2CH₃CH₂NH₂ → CH₃CONHCH₂CH₃ + CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺Cl⁻.
  • The mechanism is the same as for acyl chlorides with NH₃ (see the Carboxylic acids topic).
Worked example 2: Making a quaternary salt

Excess bromoethane reacts with ammonia. Name the final product.

  1. Each substitution replaces one H on the N with an ethyl group: NH₃ → EtNH₂ → Et₂NH → Et₃N.
  2. Et₃N attacks a fourth bromoethane, giving Et₄N⁺, which has no H left to lose.

Answer: Tetraethylammonium bromide, (CH₃CH₂)₄N⁺Br⁻.

Worked example 3: Choosing a synthesis route

Give two routes from 1-bromopropane to an amine, and say which gives a purer primary amine.

  1. Route A: excess NH₃ in ethanol, heated, gives propylamine, contaminated with secondary and tertiary amines.
  2. Route B: KCN in ethanol under reflux gives butanenitrile; reduction with LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni then gives butylamine. This adds one carbon.

Answer: Route B gives only a primary amine (with one more carbon). Route A gives a mixture.

Common mistakes
  • Saying that phenylamine is a stronger base "because benzene is electron-withdrawing" without mentioning delocalisation of the lone pair.
  • Forgetting that ammonia or amine must be in excess, and that a second molecule removes the H⁺.
  • Mixing up the reagents: Sn/HCl reduces nitrobenzene; LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni reduces nitriles.
Exam tips
  • In base-strength answers, always describe lone-pair availability on N.
  • Remember that the nitrile route extends the carbon chain by one.
Summary
  • Amines are primary, secondary or tertiary, plus quaternary ammonium ions.
  • Preparation: halogenoalkane + excess NH₃; nitrile + LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni; nitrobenzene + Sn/HCl.
  • Base strength: aliphatic amines > NH₃ > aromatic amines, depending on lone-pair availability.
  • As nucleophiles, amines give secondary and tertiary amines, quaternary salts (surfactants) and N-substituted amides.
c-3-11.intro: Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia in which one or more H atoms are replaced by carbon groups. The lone pair on nitrogen makes them both bases and nucleophiles.

c-3-12.h:
1Addition vs condensation polymers

  • Addition polymers form from alkenes; the C=C opens and nothing else is produced. The chain is non-polar C–C bonds.
  • Condensation polymers form when two different functional groups react, losing a small molecule (usually H₂O, or HCl if an acyl chloride is used) at every link.
  • Condensation monomers need two reactive groups each (e.g. a diol, a dicarboxylic acid, a diamine), so the chain can grow at both ends.

2Polyesters

  • Diol + dicarboxylic acid → polyester + water; the link is the ester group –COO–.
  • Terylene (PET): ethane-1,2-diol HOCH₂CH₂OH + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH. Used for drinks bottles and clothing fibres.

3Polyamides

  • Diamine + dicarboxylic acid (or diacyl dichloride) → polyamide; the link is the amide group –CONH–.
  • Nylon-6,6: hexane-1,6-diamine H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂ + hexanedioic acid HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH. Each monomer has 6 carbon atoms, hence "6,6".
  • Kevlar: benzene-1,4-diamine + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid. Its flat, rigid chains line up and form many hydrogen bonds between N–H and C=O on neighbouring chains, so it is very strong (bullet-proof vests).
  • Proteins are natural polyamides (polypeptides) made from amino acids.

4Working out monomers from a repeat unit

  • Find each ester or amide link and break it: put –OH back on the C=O side, and –H back on the O or N side.
  • With a diacyl dichloride monomer, the acid end is –COCl and HCl is lost instead of H₂O.
Worked example 1: Monomers from a repeat unit

Identify the monomers of the polymer with repeat unit –NH–(CH₂)₆–NH–CO–(CH₂)₄–CO–.

  1. Find the amide links, –CO–NH–, and break each one.
  2. Add –H to each N and –OH to each C=O.

Answer: H₂N–(CH₂)₆–NH₂ (hexane-1,6-diamine) and HOOC–(CH₂)₄–COOH (hexanedioic acid), which make nylon-6,6.

Worked example 2: Drawing a polyester

Draw the repeat unit of the polyester made from ethane-1,2-diol and butanedioic acid, HOOC(CH₂)₂COOH.

  1. Remove the OH from the acid and the H from the alcohol at each link, losing H₂O.
  2. Join them through –COO– ester links.

Answer: –[OCH₂CH₂O–CO(CH₂)₂CO]ₙ–

Worked example 3: Hydrolysis products

Nylon-6,6 is heated with HCl(aq). What forms?

  1. Acid hydrolysis breaks the amide links.
  2. The diacid is released as the free acid, and the diamine forms its ammonium salt in the acid.

Answer: Hexanedioic acid and the hexane-1,6-diammonium chloride salt, ClH₃N(CH₂)₆NH₃Cl.

5Hydrolysis and disposal

  • Ester and amide links are polar, so they are attacked by nucleophiles: they can be hydrolysed by acid or alkali and are biodegradable. Poly(alkenes) have only non-polar C–C and C–H bonds, so they are not.
  • Acid hydrolysis gives the dicarboxylic acid plus the diol (or the diamine as its ammonium salt); alkaline hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt plus the diol or diamine.
  • Landfill: cheap but uses land, and the polymer persists for years.
  • Incineration: releases energy that can generate electricity, but produces CO₂ and possibly toxic gases (e.g. HCl from PVC), which must be removed.
  • Recycling: saves raw materials (crude oil) and energy, but plastics must be collected and sorted, which is costly.
Common mistakes
  • Leaving an –OH or –H on the end of a repeat unit. A repeat unit has open bonds (trailing lines) at both ends.
  • Drawing the amide link backwards in the same chain; check that each link joins a C=O to an N–H.
  • Calling poly(ethene) a condensation polymer. No small molecule is lost, so it is an addition polymer.
Exam tips
  • Draw the repeat unit with the link shown in full: C=O with the O or N–H attached, then brackets and a subscript n.
  • Hydrogen bonding between polyamide chains (N–H···O=C) explains the strength of Kevlar and nylon. Polyesters have only dipole–dipole forces between their C=O groups.
Summary
  • Condensation polymers are made from monomers with two functional groups each, losing H₂O or HCl at every link.
  • Polyesters (e.g. Terylene) have –COO– links; polyamides (nylon-6,6, Kevlar, proteins) have –CONH– links.
  • Polar links can be hydrolysed, so these polymers are biodegradable. Disposal options are landfill, incineration and recycling.
c-3-12.intro: Condensation polymers such as polyesters and polyamides are made from monomers that each have two reactive groups, with a small molecule lost at every link. Their polar links also mean they can be broken down again.
secs: Working out monomers from a repeat unit

c-3-13.h:
1Amino acids

  • General structure: H₂N–CHR–COOH. Each amino acid has an amine group and a carboxylic acid group on the same carbon. Most are chiral, because the central carbon has H, NH₂, COOH and R.
  • In the solid and in neutral solution they exist as zwitterions, ⁺H₃N–CHR–COO⁻. The ionic attractions between zwitterions give amino acids high melting points.
ConditionsForm
acidic (low pH)⁺H₃N–CHR–COOH: the COO⁻ is protonated
at the isoelectric point⁺H₃N–CHR–COO⁻ (zwitterion)
alkaline (high pH)H₂N–CHR–COO⁻: the NH₃⁺ loses H⁺
Worked example 1: Forms of an amino acid at different pH

Draw alanine, H₂NCH(CH₃)COOH, as it exists at pH 1 and at pH 13.

  1. At pH 1 (excess H⁺), both groups are protonated: ⁺H₃NCH(CH₃)COOH.
  2. At pH 13 (excess OH⁻), both groups are deprotonated: H₂NCH(CH₃)COO⁻.

Answer: pH 1: ⁺H₃NCH(CH₃)COOH. pH 13: H₂NCH(CH₃)COO⁻.

2Proteins

  • Proteins are condensation polymers of amino acids joined by peptide (amide) links, –CONH–, with H₂O lost at each link.
  • Hydrolysis, by heating with 6 mol dm⁻³ HCl for several hours, breaks the peptide links and releases the amino acids, which are present as their ammonium salts in the acid.
LevelWhat it isHeld by
primarythe sequence of amino acidscovalent peptide bonds
secondaryα-helix or β-pleated sheethydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H of the backbone
tertiarythe overall 3D folding of the chainH-bonds, ionic attractions, and disulfide bridges (–S–S– between cysteine residues)
  • Thin-layer chromatography separates and identifies the amino acids from a hydrolysed protein. Amino acids are colourless, so they are located with ninhydrin spray (which gives purple spots) or with UV light. Each is identified by its R_f value.
Worked example 2: Dipeptides

How many different dipeptides can form from one glycine and one alanine?

  1. Either the NH₂ of glycine joins the COOH of alanine, or the other way round.
  2. That gives Gly-Ala and Ala-Gly, which have different sequences.

Answer: Two dipeptides.

3Enzymes

  • Enzymes are protein catalysts. Each has an active site with a specific 3D shape that is stereospecific: it binds only one enantiomer of a substrate.
  • Inhibitors are drugs that block the active site. They have a similar shape to the substrate and bind to the active site, stopping the substrate from binding.
  • Computer modelling helps design drugs that fit a target active site.

4DNA

  • DNA is a polymer of nucleotides. Each nucleotide is a phosphate group, the sugar 2-deoxyribose and one of four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G).
  • The sugar and phosphate groups alternate, forming the sugar–phosphate backbone. The phosphate links C3 of one sugar to C5 of the next.
  • There are two strands, wound as a double helix. They are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs: A–T (2 hydrogen bonds) and C–G (3 hydrogen bonds).

5The anticancer drug cisplatin

  • Cisplatin, cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], is a square planar platinum(II) complex.
  • In the cell, its two Cl⁻ ligands are replaced by nitrogen atoms of guanine bases on DNA (a ligand substitution reaction). This forms a cross-link that distorts the DNA and prevents replication, so the cancer cell cannot divide.
  • Adverse effects: cisplatin also affects healthy cells that divide rapidly, such as hair follicles, causing hair loss. It can also damage the kidneys. So the dose is carefully controlled.
Worked example 3: Why the cis isomer

Why is the trans isomer of [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] much less effective?

  1. In the cis isomer, the two Cl ligands are next to each other (at 90°), so the Pt can bond to two neighbouring guanines on the same strand.
  2. In the trans isomer, the leaving groups are on opposite sides (at 180°) and cannot bridge two neighbouring bases.

Answer: Only the cis shape allows the DNA cross-link to form.

Common mistakes
  • Drawing a zwitterion as H₂N–CHR–COO⁻ with no charge on N. A zwitterion has both charges.
  • Saying that the secondary structure is held by bonds between side chains. That is the tertiary structure; secondary structure involves hydrogen bonds in the backbone.
  • Pairing A with G, or giving C–G only 2 hydrogen bonds.
Exam tips
  • For cisplatin, name the bond formed: a co-ordinate bond from N of guanine to Pt, replacing Cl⁻.
  • For TLC questions, always say that amino acids are colourless and must be located with ninhydrin or UV light.
Summary
  • Amino acids are zwitterions; their form depends on pH.
  • Proteins are held by peptide links (primary structure), H-bonds (secondary) and H-bonds, ionic attractions and S–S bridges (tertiary). Hydrolysis and TLC identify the amino acids.
  • Enzymes are stereospecific; inhibitors block the active site.
  • DNA is a phosphate/deoxyribose backbone with A–T and C–G hydrogen-bonded base pairs.
  • Cisplatin binds guanine N atoms and stops replication, but it also has side effects.
c-3-13.intro: This topic applies organic chemistry to biology: amino acids and proteins, how enzymes work, the structure of DNA, and how the anticancer drug cisplatin acts on DNA.

c-3-14.h:
1Principles of a good synthesis

  • Use as few steps as possible, because every step loses some yield.
  • Choose reactions with a high atom economy and a high percentage yield.
  • Avoid hazardous solvents and starting materials where possible, and reduce waste. These are principles of green chemistry.
  • Look at how the carbon chain length changes. Reactions with KCN (on halogenoalkanes or carbonyls) and Friedel–Crafts acylation add carbon atoms.

2Key aliphatic conversions

FromToReagents and conditions
alkanehalogenoalkaneCl₂ or Br₂, UV light
alkenehalogenoalkaneHBr, room temperature
alkenealcoholsteam, H₃PO₄, 300 °C, 6–7 MPa
halogenoalkanealcoholNaOH(aq), warm
halogenoalkanealkeneKOH in ethanol, hot
halogenoalkanenitrileKCN in ethanol/water, reflux
halogenoalkaneamineexcess NH₃ in ethanol, heat under pressure
nitrileamineLiAlH₄, or H₂/Ni
primary alcoholaldehydeK₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, distil
primary alcohol or aldehydecarboxylic acidK₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, reflux
secondary alcoholketoneK₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, reflux
aldehyde or ketonealcoholNaBH₄ (aqueous)

alcoholalkeneconc. H₃PO₄ or H₂SO₄, heat

3Key aromatic conversions

FromToReagents and conditions
benzenenitrobenzeneconc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄, 50 °C
nitrobenzenephenylamineSn + conc. HCl, then NaOH

phenyl ketonesecondary alcoholNaBH₄

4Planning a route

  1. Draw the starting material and the target. Compare their functional groups and count the carbons.
  2. Work backwards from the target: "Which functional group could make this?"
  3. Write each step with its intermediate, its reagents and its conditions.
Worked example 1: Two-step synthesis

Plan a synthesis of propanoic acid from 1-bromopropane.

  1. Both have 3 carbons, so no carbon needs to be added.
  2. Step 1: NaOH(aq), warm (nucleophilic substitution), gives propan-1-ol.
  3. Step 2: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, excess, heated under reflux, gives propanoic acid.

Answer: 1-bromopropane → propan-1-ol → propanoic acid

Worked example 2: Extending the chain

Convert bromoethane into propylamine, CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂.

  1. The target has 3 carbons and the starting material has 2, so a carbon must be added. Use cyanide.
  2. Step 1: KCN in ethanol, reflux, gives propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN.
  3. Step 2: reduce with LiAlH₄ (or H₂/Ni), giving CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂.

Answer: bromoethane → propanenitrile → propylamine

Worked example 3: Aromatic route

Give a two-step route from benzene to 1-phenylethanol, C₆H₅CH(OH)CH₃.

  1. Step 1: Friedel–Crafts acylation with CH₃COCl and AlCl₃ gives phenylethanone, C₆H₅COCH₃.
  2. Step 2: reduce the ketone with NaBH₄, giving the secondary alcohol (as a racemate).

Answer: benzene → phenylethanone → 1-phenylethanol

Common mistakes
  • Leaving out conditions such as "reflux", "aqueous" or "in ethanol". These often carry the mark. For example, KOH in ethanol gives elimination, but in water it gives substitution.
  • Forgetting to add a carbon when the target is longer than the starting material.
  • Suggesting a direct one-step route that does not exist, for example alkane to alcohol.
Exam tips
  • Make a reaction map on one sheet of paper, with functional groups as the nodes and reagents on the arrows. Revise from it.
  • For every step, name the type of reaction too (e.g. nucleophilic substitution), since questions often ask for it.
Summary
  • Plan backwards from the target and keep the number of steps low.
  • Know every reagent and condition. KCN (and Friedel–Crafts acylation) adds carbons.
  • Choose safe, high-atom-economy routes and avoid hazardous solvents.
c-3-14.intro: Organic synthesis means planning a sequence of reactions that turns a starting material into a target molecule. You need to know every reaction in the course: its reagents, its conditions and the functional group change it makes.

c-3-15.h:
1How NMR works

  • Nuclei such as ¹H and ¹³C behave like tiny magnets. In a strong magnetic field they absorb radio-frequency radiation at a frequency that depends on their chemical environment, meaning the atoms near them.
  • The chemical shift, δ (in ppm), is measured relative to the standard tetramethylsilane (TMS), Si(CH₃)₄, which is set at δ = 0.
  • TMS is used because it gives one strong sharp peak (12 equivalent H atoms) upfield of most other signals, and it is inert, non-toxic and volatile, so it is easily removed.
  • Samples are dissolved in solvents without ¹H atoms, such as CDCl₃ (a deuterated solvent) or CCl₄, so the solvent does not give a signal.

2¹³C NMR

  • The number of peaks equals the number of different carbon environments.
  • The chemical shift shows the type of carbon. For example, C=O is at 160–220 ppm, C–O at 50–90 ppm, and alkyl carbons at 5–40 ppm.
  • Peaks are not split, and their heights are not used for counting atoms.
Worked example 1: ¹³C environments

How many peaks are there in the ¹³C spectrum of propan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂CHOH?

  1. The two CH₃ carbons are equivalent, because of symmetry.
  2. The CH carbon bonded to OH is different.

Answer: 2 peaks: one at about 25 ppm (CH₃) and one at about 64 ppm (C–O).

3¹H NMR

Three pieces of information come from a ¹H spectrum:

  1. Number of peaks: the number of different H environments.
  2. Integration: the relative peak areas, shown as an integration trace or a ratio, give the relative number of H atoms in each environment.
  3. Splitting (spin–spin coupling): follows the n + 1 rule. A signal is split into n + 1 lines by n H atoms on adjacent carbon atoms.
Neighbouring H atomsPattern
0singlet
1doublet
2triplet
3quartet
  • H atoms on O or N (in OH or NH) usually give a singlet and do not cause splitting.
  • Use the data-booklet table of chemical shifts. For example, R–CH₃ is at about 0.9 ppm, CH₃–CO at 2.1 ppm, CH₂–O at 3.3–4.3 ppm, CHO at 9–10 ppm, and COOH at 10–12 ppm.
Worked example 2: Predicting a ¹H spectrum

Predict the ¹H NMR spectrum of ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃.

  1. There are three environments: CH₃CO, OCH₂ and CH₂CH₃.
  2. The CH₃CO group has no adjacent H, so it gives a singlet with integration 3, at about 2.0 ppm.
  3. The OCH₂ group is next to CH₃, so it gives a quartet with integration 2, at about 4.1 ppm.
  4. The terminal CH₃ is next to CH₂, so it gives a triplet with integration 3, at about 1.3 ppm.

Answer: Three peaks, in the ratio 3 : 2 : 3 (singlet, quartet, triplet).

Worked example 3: Working out a structure

A compound C₃H₆O gives a ¹³C spectrum with 2 peaks, one at 205 ppm. Its ¹H spectrum has a single peak at 2.1 ppm. Identify it.

  1. The 205 ppm peak is a ketone or aldehyde C=O.
  2. Only one ¹H environment means all six H atoms are equivalent, with no splitting.
  3. Two CH₃ groups attached to C=O fit this.

Answer: Propanone, CH₃COCH₃

Common mistakes
  • Counting the H atoms in the group being split. The n in n + 1 refers to H atoms on the adjacent carbon.
  • Forgetting symmetry, which makes some environments equivalent.
  • Saying that TMS is used "because it is the solvent". It is the reference standard; the solvent is CDCl₃.
Exam tips
  • For structure questions, set out a table: δ, splitting, integration, deduction. Then draw the final structure.
Summary
  • δ is measured relative to TMS (0 ppm); samples use CDCl₃ or CCl₄ as the solvent.
  • ¹³C NMR: the number of peaks gives the number of C environments; the shift gives the C type.
  • ¹H NMR: peaks give environments, integration gives the H ratio, and splitting follows the n + 1 rule for adjacent H atoms.
c-3-15.intro: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy shows the different environments of hydrogen or carbon atoms in a molecule. It is the most powerful tool for working out an organic structure.

c-3-16.h:
1The principle

  • Every chromatography method has a stationary phase and a mobile phase.
  • Components separate because they have different balances between solubility in the mobile phase and retention by (adsorption onto) the stationary phase. A component that is held more strongly moves more slowly.

2Thin-layer chromatography (TLC)

  • The stationary phase is a thin layer of silica (SiO₂) or alumina (Al₂O₃) on a glass or plastic plate. The mobile phase is a solvent.
Key equations
R_f=\frac{\text{distance moved by spot}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}
  • Colourless spots are located with UV light, if the plate has a fluorescent layer, or by using a chemical locating agent such as iodine or ninhydrin.
  • To identify a compound, compare its R_f with that of a known substance in the same solvent and on the same type of plate.
Worked example 1: R_f calculation

A spot moves 3.6 cm while the solvent front moves 8.0 cm. Calculate R_f.

  1. R_f = 3.6 / 8.0 = 0.45.

Answer: R_f = 0.45 (no units, always between 0 and 1).

3Column chromatography (CC)

  • A column is packed with silica or alumina as the stationary phase, and a solvent (the eluent) is run through it.
  • The components come out at different times and are collected in separate fractions. This is used to purify products on a larger scale.

4Gas chromatography (GC)

  • The stationary phase is a liquid or solid coated inside a long, thin column in an oven. The mobile phase is an unreactive carrier gas, such as He or N₂.
  • The retention time is the time from injection to detection. It identifies a component when compared with known standards under the same conditions.
  • The area under each peak is proportional to the amount of that component.
  • GC–MS: the GC separates the components, then the mass spectrometer identifies each one from its molecular ion and fragmentation, by comparison with a database. It is used in forensics, airport security and drug testing.
Worked example 2: Interpreting a gas chromatogram

A gas chromatogram has two peaks with areas of 30 and 90 units. What percentage of the mixture is the second component?

  1. The total area is 120.
  2. The second component is 90 / 120 = 75%.

Answer: 75% (assuming the detector responds equally to both components).

Required practical 12: separation of species by TLC
  • Draw the TLC baseline in pencil, because ink would dissolve and run. Keep it above the solvent level.
  • Cover the tank so that the atmosphere is saturated with solvent vapour.
  • Mark the solvent front as soon as you remove the plate.
  • One spot in several different solvents suggests a pure compound.
  • Wear gloves, because locating agents and solvents are harmful, and handle the plate by its edges so that you do not contaminate it.
  • Two-way TLC: run the plate in one solvent, turn it through 90° and run it again in a second solvent. This separates spots that overlap in the first solvent.
Common mistakes
  • Drawing the baseline in pen, or putting it below the solvent level.
  • Calculating R_f from the top of the spot. Measure to the centre of the spot.
  • Saying that a longer retention time means "more of the substance". The amount comes from the peak area.
Exam tips
  • Explain separation in terms of the relative affinity of each component for the stationary phase and the mobile phase.
Summary
  • Every method has a stationary phase and a mobile phase; components separate by their relative affinity for each.
  • TLC uses R_f = spot distance ÷ solvent distance.
  • Column chromatography purifies larger amounts.
  • GC uses retention time and peak area; GC–MS identifies the components.
c-3-16.intro: Chromatography separates the substances in a mixture so that they can be identified and their purity checked. It is often the first step before spectroscopy.
